case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 13-11-2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 667 of 1993)
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Matin J: I agree with the judgment delivered by my brother ABM Khairul   Haque, J.

2. Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J: I agree with the judgment delivered by my brother ABM Khairul Haque, J.

3. ABM Khairul Haque J: This appeal is in respect of ejectment of a monthly tenant and for realisation of arrear rent and compensation.

<u>4. The facts leading to the filing of this appeal are that Alhaj Sadequr Rahman Chowdhury instituted a suit being Other Suit No. 121 of 1988 in the Court of First Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong, praying for a decree for ejectment and compensation against Mis. Anupam Traders represented by Abul Kashem Sowdagar and others, on the ground that the defendant is a defauIter and also for reconstruction of the house.The defendants contested the suit, contending, inter-alia, that they never defaulted in payment of rents, the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is defective, that the plaintiff never collected rents in time, rather used to accept as and when necessary, that the plea of reconstruction of the house is not correct. That on those grounds, the suit is liable to be dismissed.</u>

5. The learned Assistant Judge, on evidence found that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, was duly served upon the defendants, The learned Judge also found that he was a defaulter and that the reconstruction of the house is a necessity for the plaintiff. With these findings, the learned Judge by his Judgment and Order dated 28-8-1989, decreed the suit.

6. On appeal being Other Appeal No. 485 of 1989, however,' the Additional District Judge, set aside the decree and allowed the appeal.

7. Being aggrieved, the heirs of the deceased plaintiff filed a civil revisional application being Civil Revision No. 667 of 1993. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, agreed with the findings of the Appellate Court below and held that the defendant-opposite-parties were not defaulters in making payment of rent for the month of July. 1982 and that the plaintiff failed to prove his bonafide necessity in reconstructing the house. With these findings the Rule was discharged by its Judgment and Order dated 1-2-1993, passed by the High Court Division.

8. Leave was granted to consider as to whether the respondent-opposite-party was a defaulter or not.

<u>9. By now it is well settled that once a tenant is found to be a defaulter, he is liable to be evicted.</u>

10.The tenancy agreement between the parties stipulated payment of rent within the 7th day of the next month. It is found by all the Courts below that the rent for the month of July, 1982, was sent through money order on 12-8-1982, four days after the stipulated period.

11. The question is whether the defendant-tenant is a defaulter for the delay of the said four days.

12. The legal position in this respect has been contained in sub-section 5 of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963.

13. The said provision reads as follows:

Section 18

"(5) No tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of this section in respect of any premises unless, he pays the rent due by him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance within the time fixed in the contract with his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, or in the cases provided for in section 19, unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of such premises as provided in that section together with, in the case mentioned in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of that section, the cost of transmission referred to in that clause within the time specified in that section.

Explanation-A landlord shall not for the purpose of this sub-section be deemed to have refused to accept any rent unless the rent is remitted within the period referred to above in this sub-section by postal money order to the address of the landlord and the rent so remitted in returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered either on account of the landlord having refused to accept payment thereof or for any other cause."

<u>14. It is well settled that in order to avoid eviction the tenant must pay its monthly rentals either within the period of contract or in the absence of contract, within the fifteenth day of the month next following for which the rent is payable.</u>

15. But when a land-lord refuses to accept the rent, the tenant ought to remit the rent by postal money order within the aforesaid period. If it is returned, the rent must be deposited within a fortnight of the date on which the rent so remitted, was returned to the tenant as undelivered by the postal authorities.

16. In the instant case, the tenancy agreement stipulated payment of rent for the current month within the seventh day of the next month but on refusal by the land-lord, the rent for the month of July, 1982, was remitted by the postal money order admittedly on 12-8-1982, as such, there was a delay of 5 (five) days in remitting the monthly rental for the month of July.

<u>17. In that respect, the High Court Division committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record since it ignored the delay of the aforesaid 5(five) days in remitting the rent and its consequence. It is also well settled that once a defaulter is always a defaulter. This default is incurable unless it is waived by the land-lord expressly. Since it is apparent that there is a delay of 5 (five) days in payment of rent of the month of July, 1982, the respondent-tenant is liable to be evicted.</u>

18. In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal is allowed and the Judgment and Order passed by the High Court Division is set-aside.

Md Mozammel Hossain J : I agree with the judgment delivered by my brother ABM Khairul Haque J.

SK Sinha J: I deeply regret 'my inability to share the views of my learned brethren Mr ABM Khairul Haque J. The point involves in this appeal has a narrow compass to consider the tenor and purport of section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 (the Ordinance). To put is otherwise, whether, a tenant can be said to be a defaulter if (s) he offers rent within the time fixed in the contract to the landlord and on refusal by the landlord to accept the rent, the tenant remits the rent by money order within five days of such refusal.

21. The predecessor of the appellant Al-Haj Sadequr Rahman (landlord) instituted Other Class Suit No, 121 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong for eviction of the respondents (tenants) and realization of arrear rent. Short facts are that the tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the landlord in respect of the suit shop premises at a monthly rental of Taka 200 payable within 7th of next following month. The tenants: it is alleged, defaulted in payment of monthly rent from July, 1982 and in violation of the terms of contract they sublet a portion and altered another portion of the suit premises and that the landlord bonafide required the suit premises for remodelling.

22. The tenants contested the suit denying the material allegations made in the plaint. Their case is that the landlord accepted the rent till June, 1982, that they offered rent of July, 1982 in time when the landlord demanded enhanced rent of Taka 400 per month and refused to accept rent on the plea that he would accept the rent latter on as he had no receipt book, that they offered rent again but the landlord refused to accept the rent and thereafter on sensing the bad intention of the landlord, they sent the rent by money order on 14th August, 1982, which the landlord refused to accept on 14th August, 1982 and returned back on the following day, that thereafter they have been depositing rent in HRC Case No. 412 of 1988, that the landlord does not bonafide require the suit premises, that they are not defaulters and that the suit was instituted with malafide motive to evict them by false pretext.

23. The learned Assistant Judge by judgment and order dated 28th August, 1989 decreed the suit. On appeal by the tenants, the learned Additional District Judge, who heard the said appeal by judgment and order dated 29th September, 1992 reversed the judgment of the learned Assistant Judge and dismissed the suit. The heirs of the landlord thereupon moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 667 of 1993. A Single Bench of the High Court Division affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeal below.

24. As regards the pleas of bonafide requirement and subletting of a portion of the suit premises the learned Assistant Judge found them in favour of the landlord, but the Court of appeal below and the High Court Division concurrently held that the landlord.failed to substantiate the same on assigning reasons therefor. The learned counsel for the appellants frankly concedes that those findings are based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record and confines his submission on the point of default in the payment of monthly rent. As regards the plea of default, the learned Assistant Judge observed. the tenants could not escape from default in the payment of rent since the landlord claimed that the tenants had been paying rents irregularly and that they have been depositing rent before the Rent Controller irregularly violating the terms of the contract. The learned Assistant Judge has resolved the principal issue involved in the suit relying upon the claim of the landlord without reference to the evidence which is absolutely erroneous. It is not expected or desired from a Court of law to resolve the main issue involved in the suit on the basis of the 'alleged claim' of a party without considering the evidence on which the issue is rested.

25. Whether an alleged fact is a fact in issue or a relevant fact, the court can draw no inference from its existence till it believes it to exist; and it is obvious that the belief of the Court in existence of a given fact ought to proceed upon grounds, altogether independent of the relation of the fact to the object and nature of the proceeding in which its existence is to be determined. Judicial decisions must proceed upon imperfect materials and must be made at the risk of error. The learned Assistant Judge in fact made out a third case for, the claim of the landlord is that tenants did not pay rent for the month of July, 1982 as per terms of the contract for which they are defaulters. Despite there being no specific finding of the learned Assistant that the tenants did not pay rent of July, 1982 as per terms of the contract, the learned Additional District Judge on consideration of the evidence on record particularly the statements of Haji Abul Kashem (DW 1) made in course of cross-examination held that the tenants are not defaulters.

26. Learned Counsel for the appellants, however, submits that in view of the statement of DW 1, the tenants .can not avoid from eviction on the ground of default. The statements of DW 1 basing upon which the Court of appeal as well as the High Court Division held that the tenants are not defaulters are reproduced below:

“৮২ইং জুলাই মাসের ভাড়া আমরা দিতে গেলে বাদীপক্ষ ভাড়া নেওয়া হয় নাই। তার তারিখ মনে নাই। বাদী ভাড়া নিবেন ৪০০ টাকা ভাড়া বাড়াতে হবে, তা ভাড়া দেওয়ার ২/৩ দিন আগে জানায়। যেদিন ভাড়া দিতে যাই সেদিন রশিদ ছিলনা বলে ভাড়া নেয় নাই। পরবর্তীতে আবারও ভাড়া দিতে যাই কিন্তু পরে ভাড়া নিবে বলে জানায়, জুলাই মাসের ভাড়া আমি ১২-৮-৮২ ইং তারিখে মানিঅর্ডার করেছি।”

27. DW 1 stated that he offered rent but the landlord did not accept the same. Though he did not mention the date of offer but in the same breath, he said that the landlord refused to accept the rent on the plea that he would accept rent at enhanced rate of Taka 400 which he told him prior to 2/3 days of the date of payment. This statement proved that he offered rent before the expiry of the date fixed in the contract. He then said, on the day of offering rent the landlord represented that he had no receipt book and then also he went to pay rent but the landlord refused to accept the rent and then he remitted the rent by money order on 12th August, 1982. These statements were made in reply to the scattered questions put to him in course of cross-examination by the learned Advocate for the landlord. Therefore, these statements should be read conjointly along with those made in chief so that a correct conclusion could be reached as to whether the tenants in fact offered the rent in time and then remitted the same in accordance with section 18(5) of the Ordinance. Upon evaluating those statements minutely, the Court of Appeal below rightly held that the tenants had offered the rent within the stipulated time and after the refusal by the landlord they remitted the rent by money order in accordance with law. The Court of Appeal below thereupon arrived at the conclusion that the landlord had adopted devices with ulterior motive to evict the tenants.

28. These findings of the Court of Appeal being based upon proper sifting of the evidence on record and having been affirmed by the High Court Division, this Court would not ordinarily interfere with the concurrent findings of fact, the reason being that when the facts have been fairly tried by two Courts upon a proper consideration of the evidence, this Court being the ultimate Court of Appeal would not go behind the findings of fact unless there is sufficient ground for doing so i.e. a manifest error of law arriving at the finding. Since the learned Assistant Judge while finding the tenants as defaulters did not give any specific finding that the tenants did not offer or remit the rent of July, 1982 in terms of the contract, there is no merit in the contention of the learned counsel that the trial Court was justified in arriving at the conclusion that the tenants are defaulter.

29. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on consideration of the statements of law argued in the cases of AKM Shamsuddin Dr Aftab Uddin Ahmed, 12 BLD (AD) 81 = 43 DLR (AD) 230 and Ramjan Ali Mistry vs Hedayel Ullah, 31 DLR (AD) 183, the evidence of DW 1, observed "the defendant-opposite parties were required to pay the rent for the month of July, 1982 on or before 7th August, 1982. Accordingly, rent was tendered to the landlord by the defendant-opposite parties. But the plaintiff petitioners as landlords refused to accept the rent on some pleas in order to make the defendant-opposite parties are defaulters. Sensing this design of the plaintiff-petitioners, defendant-opposite Parties sent the rent by postal money order on 12th August, 1982 and on refusal to accept the same by the plaintiff petitioners the rent so sent was received back by the defendant-opposite parties through the postal authority on 15-8-1982. Defendant-opposite parties thereafter deposited the rent before the rent controller on 21-8-1982 and since then they continued to do so. It is therefore, clear that the defendant opposite parties were not defaulters."

30. Sub sections (1) and (5) of section 18 are relevant for our consideration which read as follows:

"( I) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, 1972, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and perform the conditions of the tenancy;

"(5) No tenant shall be entitled to the benefit. of this section in respect of any premises unless, he pays the rent due by him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance within the time fixed in the contract with his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, or in the cases provided for in section 19, unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of such premises as provided in that section together with, in the case mentioned in the clause (b) of sub-section (1) of that section, the cost of transmission referred to in that clause within the time specified in that section.

Explanation-A landlord shall not for the purposes of this sub-section be deemed to have refused to accept to accept any rent unless the rent is remitted within the period referred to above in this sub-section by postal money order to the address of the landlord and the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered either on account of the landlord having refused to accept payment thereof or for any other cause."

31. These provisions relate to the manner of payment of rent and the remittance of rent by money order, in case of refusal by the landlord in order to avoid eviction of a tenant. The protection given is that the tenant is required to pay the rent notwithstanding the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act or the Contract Act, to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance within the time fixed by the contract with the landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of month next following for which the rent is payable, or unless the ten- ant has deposited the rent in accordance with section 19. In the' Explanation' it is said that the rent should not have been deemed to have refused by the landlord unless the rent is remitted "within the period referred" in sub-section (5) of section 18.

<u>32. Law enjoins a tenant whether there is a contract or not, to pay rent within the time specified in section 18(5) i.e. till the last day fixed in the contract or in the absence of contract, by the fifteenth day or the next following month, as the case may be, and then the question of remittance of the rent by money order will come after the refusal by the landlord to accept the rent so offered by the tenant. If that being the position of law, then how a tenant would remit the rent within the period referred to above in this sub-section by postal money order mentioned in the 'Explanation? In the face of such ambiguity if any interpretation is given to the effect that the rent is required be remitted by money order within the time fixed in the contract or in the absence of the contract, within fifteenth day of the next following month for which the rent is due will be against the letter and spirit of section 18(5) because under this clause the fixed date for payment of rent has been stated in either cases but in case of refusal by the landlord nothing has been spelt out therein. Where a party was given time to do an act, he was entitled to do that during the course of that date or in other words, where a certain time is allowed for doing an act, the last day of that time is included for the purpose of performing that act.</u>

33. An 'Explanation' cannot be read into a definition as limiting or restricting the scope of the letter. It is appended to a section and becomes an integral part of it, and has no independent existence apart from it. There is, in the eye of law, only one enactment of which both the section and the Explanation are two inseparable parts. It is axiomatic that an 'Explanation' only explains and does not expand or add to the scope of the original section.

The 'Explanation' must be read so as to harmonise with and clear up any ambiguity in the main section. It should not be so construed as to widen or limiting the ambit of the section. (AIR 1967 SC 389). The construction of the 'Explanation' must depend upon its terms, and no theory of its purpose can be entertained unless it is to be inferred from the language used. The mere description of a certain provision, such as, 'Explanation' is not decisive of its true meaning. The interpretation most obviously depend on the words used therein, but this must be borne in mind that when the provision is capable of two interpretations, that should be adopted which fits the description. Reference in this connection is the case of state of Bombay vs United Motors, AIR 1958 (SC) 252. And the Chief function of 'Explanation' is to harmonise with and clear up any ambiguity in the main section. In short, the 'Explanation' must be interpreted according to its own tenor.

<u>34. Lord Denning in Seaford Court Estates Ltd vs Asher (1949) 2 KB 481 argued as under:</u>

<u>"A judge, believing himself to be fettered by the supposed rule that he must look to the language and nothing else, laments that the draftsmen have hot provided for this or that, or have been guilty of some or other ambiguity. It would certainly save the judges trouble if Acts of Parliament were drafted with divine prescience and perfect clarity. In the absence of it, when a defect appears a judge cannot simply fold this hands and blame the draftsman. He must set to work on the constructive task of finding the intention of Parliament, and he must do this not only from the language of the statute, but also from a consideration of the social conditions which gave rise to it, and of the mischief which it was passed to remedy, and then he must supplement the written would so as to give force and life to the intention of the legislature. That was clearly laid down by the resolution of the judges in Heydon's case, and it is the safest guide today. Good practical advice on the subject was given about the same time by Plowden---Put into homely metaphor it is this: A judge should ask himself the question: If the makers of the Act had themselves come across this rock in the texture of it how would they have straightened it out? He must then do as they would have done. A judge must not alter the material of which it is woven, but he can and should iron out the creases."</u>

<u>35. Now the crux of the point is when such rent should be remitted by money order after the refusal by the landlord? The true meaning of the expressions "within the period referred to" used in the 'Explanation' is that such rent should be remitted within fifteenth day of the refusal by the landlord. Thus, a tenant can avoid eviction if (s)he can fulfil three conditions, such as, (a) (s)he must pay rent within the time fixed in the contract, or in the absence of contract, within fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, (b) in case of refusal by the landlord in the Above case, such rent must be remitted within fifteenth day from the date of refusal, and ( c) when the landlord refuses to accept the rent remitted by postal money order by a tenant, the latter must deposit such rent within a fortnight of the date on which the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by postal authorities as undelivered in accordance with section 19(1).</u>

<u>36. The purpose for promulgating .the Ordinance has been clearly stated in the preamble of the Ordinance. It is said "whereas it is expedient to make better provisions for the control of rent of premises in (East Pakistan) Bangladesh." This preamble speaks of protection of the poor tenants from being harassed in the hands of landlords from any of the eventualities mentioned in Chapters-III, IV, V, VI and VII. A look into these provisions will show that this Ordinance interferes with landlords right to property and freedom of contract only for the limited purpose of protecting tenants from misuse of the landlords power to evict them, by asserting their superior rights in property or trying to exploit their position by extracting too high rents from helpless and poor tenants or trying to evict them on any grounds other than those mentioned in clauses (a) (b) (c) (d) and (e) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18. The object was not to deprive the landlords altogether of their rights in property which have to be respected. Another object was to make possible eviction of tenants who fail to carry out their obligation to pay rents to the landlords despite opportunities and protection given by law. The tenants can comply with the conditions set out in sub- sections (1), (2), (3), (4) and (5) of section 18 and section 19 of the Ordinance and defeat the landlords claim for eviction. However, if they fail to fulfill those conditions, they will not be able to claim the protection and in that event, there being no other protection available to them, they will be evicted by a decree of the Court.</u>

37. In Ramjan Ali Mistry vs Hedayetullah, 31 DLR (AD) 183, similar views have expressed in paragraph 5 as under:

"It is to be observed that East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 has made substantial encroachment into the tenancy law of the country, its purpose is to protect the tenant from ejectment from the tenanted premises and has given the tenant certain benefits, notwithstanding the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act or the Contract Act. The general law governing relationship of landlord and tenant relating to premises are to be kept in view, while interpreting the sections of the Ordinance. Under the Transfer of Property Act which is the general law governing the relationship of landlord and tenant for this kind of tenancy, the landlord has the right to terminate the tenancy by giving a notice to quit on the tenant in the manner prescribed under section 106 of the Act. This right has been substantially curtained by the Ordinance. The Ordinance, how- ever, has not totally done away with the operation of the provisions of Transfer of Property Act but has made serious encroachment on the rights of the parties in a tenancy agreement the right of landlord being curtailed."

38. The scheme and purpose of a statute is to be gathered from a reading of the enactment as a reading of the enactment as a whole. Purpose and policy of law cannot be defeated by dry literal construction of a provision of law. When a provision is capable of more than one construction, the one should be preferred which is in accord with the object of the legislation. According to Maxwell, the function of a Court is to interpret a statute according to the intent of the legislature and in doing so it must be bear in mind that its function is Jus dicere not jus dare. As regards role of the Court Salmond observed:-

"This traditional English view is the following. The duty of the judicature is to discover and to act upon the true intention of the legislature the men's or sententialegis. The essence of the law lies in its spirit, not in its letter, for the letter is significant only as being the external manifestation of the intention that underlies it. Nevertheless in all ordinary cases the Courts must be content to accept the literaegis as the exclusive and conclusive evidence of the sententialegis. They must in general take it absolutely for granted that the legislature has said what it meant, and meant what it has said. lt a scriptum est is the first principle of interpretation. Judges are not at liberty to add to or take from or modify the letter of the law, simply because they have reason to believe that the true sententialegis is the first principle of interpretation. Judges are not at liberty to add to or take from or modify the letter of the law simply because they have reason to believe that the true sententialegis is not completely or correctly expressed by it."

39. It is also to be noted that in ascertaining the intention of the legislature, the desirability or undesirability of one conclusion as compared with another is not relevant (1967) 1 AC 472). In Padmasund rao Rao (Dead) vs State of TN, AIR 2002 SC /334. it has observed that where literal construction would defeat the obvious intention of the legislation and would produce a wholly unreasonable result the Court must do violence to the words so as to achieve that obvious intention and produce a rational result. The Court is to consider the nature and design of the stature, the consequences which would follow from construing it one way or other and whether the object of the legislation will be defeated by a particular construction.

40. If two interpretations of a provision is possible, the Court will lean in favour of that construction which avoids absurdity and ensure smooth working of the system which the statue seeks to regulate. In BR Enterprise vs UP, AIR 1999 SC /867, it has been observed that where the plain and literal meaning of the provision in question is clearly show that it confers arbitrary, unanalyzed or unbridled power or it carries only one meaning which render the provision unconstitutional, there is no scope for reading down the questioned provision.

41. Bennion on Statute Law at page 139 argued that if a statutory benefit is given on specific condition being satisfied, the Court presumes that parliament intended the benefit to operate only when conditions are fulfilled in lawful manner. Beneficial provisions are added for general betterment in social interest and the Court should adopt a constructive approach so as not to exclude such provision. It is argued in Union of India vs Pradip Kumari, AIR 1995 SC 2259 that "In relation to beneficent legislation, the law is well settled that while construing the provisions of such legislation the Court should adopt a construction which advances the policy of the legislation to extend the benefit rather than a construction which has the effect of curtailing the benefit conferred by it."

42. Thus where the usual meaning of the words does not convey the object or the intention of the legislature, a more extended meaning may be given to them. If in a legislation, the general object of which is to benefit a particular class of person, any provision is ambiguous so that it is capable of two meaning one of which is to preserve the benefit and the other to take away the benefit, the meaning which preserve the benefit should be adopted. Ordinarily, the rule of benevolent construction has been applied while construing welfare legislations or provisions relating to relationship between weaker and stronger contracting parties. In Syam Sunder vs Ram Kumer; AIR 2001 SC 2472, it has been argued that the rule of beneficial construction is applied in interpretation of social legislation and legislation regulating the affair between the weaker and stronger parties.

43. Now let us consider some cases on the point referred to by the learned counsel. In Ramzan Ali's case, the tenant, as per agreement was required to pay monthly rent within 3rd day of the following month according to Bengali Calendar. It was found by the trial Court that the tenant failed to tender rent within time, and he deposited rent of Aswin and Kartick, 1380 BS before the Rent Controller not within the time prescribed by law. The High Court Division concurred with the findings of the Trial Court. It the context of the matter on consideration of all earlier decisions on the point and the provisions of sections 18 and 19 of the Ordinance, K Hossain, CJ argued as under:

"The tenant must pay rent in terms of the contract and in the absence of the contract within fifteenth day next following month on which rent falls due, if the landlord refuses to accept the rent tendered by the tenant. the ten- ant must remit the rent within the aforesaid fifteenth day of the following month by money order.  If the rent remitted by money order is refused, the tenant can deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within a fortnight from the date of the receipt of the undelivered rent sent through the postal authority, and when these conditions as prescribed in the Ordinance are fulfilled by the tenant, he gets the protection, authorize the protection from ejectment on ground of default in the payment of rent granted by the Ordinance is clearly taken away by the express language of sub-section (5) of section 18."

44. These views have been approved in MKD Rozariovs Hassan Movies, 41 DLR (AD) 135. In that case there was a tenancy agreement between the parties that the rent to be paid by the fifth of each current month. The period of tenancy expired but before such expiry the landlord informed the tenant that she would be required to pay enhanced rent and for that purpose she was required to renew the lease on fresh terms, to which, the tenant expressed her willingness to continue as tenant subject to payment of 10% enhanced rent. The parties could not reach to an amicable settlement about the amount of monthly rent. After the expiry of the tenancy tenure, the tenant offered rent of January, which the landlord refused to accept, whereupon she sent the rent by money order dated 8th February, 1984, and when it was returned back, she again remitted the rent of January, February and March, 1984, but without waiting for the acceptance by the landlord, she deposited rent before the Rent Controller on 13th March, 1984 in respect of those three months.

<u>45. The landlord thereupon instituted the suit for eviction treating the tenant as a tenant holding over after the expiry of tenure on the ground that the tenant did not renew the contract. It was alleged in the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act that as the rent of January and February was not paid in terms of the agreement the tenant was as 'undesirable tenant'. In the facts of the case, this Court observed that there is no provision of law for determining a tenancy of the ground of "the tenant becoming undesirable unless the tenant comes within the mischief of forfeiture under section 111 (g) of the TP Act." It was argued that "the tenant must offer rent of a month within the period fixed in the contract, if any, or within the fifteenth day of next month as referred to in section 18(5). If the rent offered is refused the tenant shall remit it by Money Order within the period fixed, and if the Money Order is returned undelivered, then the tenant shall deposit it with the rent controller within the fifteen days of return of Money Order". As the tenure of tenancy expired, this Court treated the tenancy as one "in the absence of such contract' mentioned in section 18(5) and decided the case accordingly. It was found that since the tenant was depositinz rent in accordance with section 19, she was not a defaulter, and accordingly, set aside the judgment of the High Court Division which held that the tenant was defaulter. These views have been approved in Kalu Mondal vs Begum Fazilatun Nessa, 46 DLR (AD) 53 and AKM Shamsuddin vs Dr Aftabuddin Ahmed, 12 BLD (AD) 81 = 43 DLR (AD) 230.</u>

<u>46. From the statements of law argued in the cases referred above and the provisions of law, I find that in the absence of a contract fixing the time to pay monthly rent a tenant will get the benefit of section 18(5), if(s)he remits rent by money order to the landlord within fifteenth day from the date of refusal, and a tenant who has entered into a contract with the landlord fixing a time to pay the rent will also get the same benefit of section 18(5), if (s)he remits the rent by postal money order within fifteenth day of the date of refusal and if the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered, (s)he must deposit such rent within a fortnight of the date on which the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant.</u>

<u>47. Now turning to the facts of this case, the tenants were required to pay monthly rent by the seventh of the month next following that for which the rent was payable. The Court of Appeal and the High Court Division on consideration of the evidence held that the tenants offered the rent of July 1982 within the stipulated time i.e. within 7th August, 1982 and that as the landlord had refused to accept the rent, the tenants remitted the rent by money order on the fifth day of refusal on 12th August, 1982 and then they deposited the rent on 21st August, 1982, which deposit was made within fifteenth day of the date of refusal by the landlord. The tenants having remitted the rent of July 1982 within fifteenth day of refusal, they were rightly found not defaulters in terms of section 18(5). In view of the above, the learned single Judge of the High Court Division is perfectly justified in holding that the tenants are "not defaulters in making payment of the rent for the month of July, 1982".</u>

48. There is, therefore; no merit in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant.

The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.
