case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated August 16, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No, 255 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is plaintiff's appeal by leave against the judgment dated August 16, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 255 of 2000 making absolute the Rule upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated October 28, 1999 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Gazipur in House Rent Appeal No.1 of 1998 dismissing the same and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated April 30, 1998 of the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Sadar, Gazipur in House Rent Case No.1 of 1997 decreeing the same.

2. The suit was filed seeking ejectment of the monthly tenant on the ground of bonafide requirement and for unauthorised activities as well as causing annoyance and disturbance to the other tenants.

3. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff' let out the premises in suit i.e. shop Nos. 1 and 2, to the defendant by an agreement dated September 1, 1988, that initially rent was fixed at Taka 2.50 per square foot but later on the rent was enhanced to Taka 3.00 per square foot but the defendant did not, pay the rent at enhanced rate, that three sons of the plaintiff are graduates but could not procure any employment and, as such, to provide these unemployed sons plaintiff requires the shop in question. It was also the case of the plaintiff that defendant without obtaining permission from him made construction on the southern side of the shop No.1 and also installed illegal electric connection in the shop, that the defendant caused disturbance to the other tenants of the market, that notices under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act were served on October 19, 1996 and December 2, 1996 terminating the tenancy but the defendant did not vacate the premises in suit, Hence the suit.

4. The suit was contested by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the defendant is not a monthly electable tenant as per the agreement, that he purchased the possessory right of the shop at a consideration of Taka 95,000 and running medicine business there, that in spite of payment of rent regularly the plaintiff did not grant receipt and thereupon he filed the House Rent Case No.1 of 1993 and depositing the rent in, the said case, that the house rent case was allowed by the trial Court and, as against that, plaintiff did not file any appeal, that plaintiff's case of default by the defendant in the payment of rent is not true and that she has some other shops in the market to meet her alleged requirement. Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit on the findings that the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant is of landlord and tenant, that the defendant without obtaining permission of' the landlord has made construction on the south side of the shop No.1 and this fact of making unauthorised construction is also admitted by the defendant, that the plaintiff requires the premises for her bonafide requirement, that defendant is causing disturbance to the other tenants.

6. The defendant went on appeal. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal on the findings that the defendant admitted that without the permission of the landlord he has made construction on the south side of the shop No. 1 and thereby made an extension of the shop No.1 and obtained unapproved electric connection that the plaintiff requires the shop in question for her bonafide use i.e. to make provision for her unemployed sons by starting business, that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served, that nothing has been brought on record from the side of the defendant to establish that he purchased, the possession of the shop for good and thereby plaintiff's title in the shop has been extinguished, that by purchase of possession of the shop defendant has not got the title of the shop.

7. The defendant moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. The said Division made the Rule absolute on the findings that the plaintiff received Taka 95,000 as 'salami' and thereupon, handed over possession of the premises in suit, that in the agreement by which the defendant was put into possession there is no clause to terminate the tenancy or to eject the tenant, that as the plaintiff has other shops in the market "requirement as made out by the landlord do not appear to be bonafide. Facts of the case also do not disclose that the landlord was pressingly in need of the suit shops. Moreover, under the terms of the agreement, on such requirement the tenancy could not be brought to an end. Secondly, the view of the appellate Court that when the possessory right was transferred that does not; debar the landlord from getting a decree for ejectment is wholly misconceived in the facts and circumstances of the case. It may be noted that the landlord is entitled to possession only in tenus of the agreement of lease as executed by him/her and not otherwise. After handing over the possession of the premises at a valid consideration the landlord voluntarily forfeits her right of possession on such flimsy ground of requirement". Thereupon, the Division set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

8. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division erred in law in not taking into consideration that the tenant has erected tinshed adjacent to the suit shop without obtaining permission of the landlord and has been creating obstruction in the construction of the market which is sufficient ground for ejectment of such kind of tenant" that the High Court Division in reversing the judgment of the lower appellate Court and thereupon, dismissing the suit has not taken into consideration that terms of the agreement cannot over side the provision of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991, that the concurrent finding of fact regarding plaintiff's bonafide requirement by the courts below has been reversed by the High Court Division without proper reasoning.

9. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the High Court Division was in error in holding that as possession of the premises in suit was made over to the defendant on receiving Taka 95,000 as advance, and there being nothing in the agreement of tenancy about termination of the tenancy on the ground of bona fide requirement, the plaintiff or, in other words, the landlord was not entitled to terminate the tenancy since by letting out the premises in suit on taking advance the landlord did neither transfer his title nor put an embargo on the statutory right of terminating tenancy in case of bonafide requirement. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel that the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that as the landlord received Taka 95,000 as premium for handing over possession of the premises in suit to the defendant and, as such, because of the said manner of handing over possession of the premises in suit, the plaintiff forfeited her right of taking possession upon ejectment of the tenant. In support of the aforesaid contention the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Mustaque Hossain vs Md Shajahan Miah and another reported in 57 DLR (AD) 60. In the reported case section 10 of the "বাড়ী ভাড়া নিয়ন্ত্রন আইন, ১৯৯১” (Act No.3 of 1991) (the Ain) came up for consideration. Section 10 of the Ain reads as:

"১০। প্রিমিয়াম ইত্যাদির দাবী নিষিদ্ধ- ভাড়া দেওয়া বা ভাড়া নবায়ন করা বা ভাড়���র মেয়াদ বৃদ্ধি করার কারণে কোন ব্যক্তি-

(ক) ভাড়ার অতিরিক্ত কোন প্রিমিয়াম, সালামী, জামানত বা অনুরূপ কোন অর্থ দাবী বা গ্রহণ করিতে বা প্রদানের জন্য বলিতে পারিবেন না, অথবা

(খ) নিয়ন্ত্রকের পূর্বানুমোদন ব্যতিরেকে, অগ্রীম ভাড়া হিসাবে এক মাসের ভাড়ার অতিরিক্ত টাকা দাবী বা গ্রহণ করিতে পারিবেন না।”

10. The fact of the aforementioned case was that the landlord, since required the premises in suit for the purpose of giving accommodation to his son to start business and thereupon terminated the tenancy. The tenant having had not vacated the premises, the landlord filed the suit. The suit was resisted by the tenant contending, amongst others, that he purchased the possession of the premises in suit on payment of Taka 3,00,000 and two lease deeds were executed between the landlord and the tenant fixing rent Taka 200 for each of the shop rooms. In the agreement between the landlord and the tenant, there was a clause whereby the tenant was given right to sell the possession of the suit shops to a 3rd party. It was the definite case of the tenant that he purchased the possession of the suit shop rooms on payment of Taka 3,00,000.

11. The provision of section 10 of the Ain prohibits the practice of receiving any premium, salami, security or any amount similar or akin to the same for letting out any premises and renewal of the tenancy or for extension of the tenancy. The provision of the said section also prohibits receiving of any amount exceeding rent of one month without permission of the House Rent Controller. So, it is seen that the provision of section 10 of the Ain prohibits the practice of handing over possession of the premises by the landlord receiving amount exceeding rent of one month with the stipulation of allowing the tenant to transfer his tenancy right or possession of the premises in suit to a 3rd party. In the background of the provision of law as in section 10 of the Ain, in the reported case, it has been observed: "Section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 makes the illegal practice of payment of salami prohibited and that the tenant is entitled to refund of the salami paid by him within 6 months of such payment under section 14 and the landlord was liable to pay fine for receiving salami under section 3 of the said Act. The widespread and long standing practice of voluntary payment of salami in the commercial world did not make the tenant a nonejectable one and no interest other than the tenancy right recognised by law could be created on payment of salami so as to prevent the tenant not liable to be ejected on specific legal ground for the purpose. Under section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act, the landlord is entitled to eject a tenant as soon as a monthly tenant is a defaulter or a landlord bonafide requires the premises or for building and rebuilding purpose.

12. "In that view of the matter, no question of any promissory estoppel arises on ground of acceptance of any salami, for making a tenant nonejectable, for such practice is not only prohibited by the said Act, but no right recognised by law could be attributed for acceptance of the salami to render the tenant non ejectable in accordance with law."

13. In the background of the law as in section 10 of the Ain and the decision of this Court in the reported case, we are of the view the High Court Division was in error in reversing the judgment of the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment of the trial Court on the view that as the landlord had handed over possession of the premises in suit upon receiving an amount more than one month's rent as advance, landlord forfeited his right of asking the tenant to hand over possession on the ground of bonafide requirement or seeking redress under the law in case of refusal by the tenant to hand over possession on the ground of bonafide requirement of the landlord.

14. The trial Court, on consideration of the materials on record, held that the landlord requires the premises in suit for bonafide requirement and the said finding and decision of the trial Court was affirmed by the appellate Court. The High Court Division has not made any finding negating the finding and decision of the courts below as regard the case of the plaintiff that she requires the premises in suit for her bonafide requirement i.e. for making provision for her unemployed sons by starting business, but has observed that plaintiff is not entitled to get back the possession of the premises in suit on the flimsy ground of bonafide requirement since she upon receiving good amount of money as advance handed over possession of the premises in suit and thereby she voluntarily forfeited her right of possession of the premises in suit.

<u>15. The law is now settled that a tenant who obtained possession of a premises upon making advance of an amount which is more than rent of one month of the premises in suit and in the agreement of the tenancy there is stipulation that the possession so obtained upon making advance would be transferable to a third party which the landlord would accept or the tenancy would be nonejectable, the stipulation so made in the agreement of tenancy being violative of the provision of section 10 of the Ain and also being void in view of the provision of section 23 of the Contract Act, the tenant would be an ejectable tenant on the ground of anyone of the grounds as are in section 18 of the Ain. Since in the instant case plaintiff proved her requirement of the premises in suit for her use and occupation and, as such, the defendant in the background of the discussions, made hereinabove was required to surrender the premises in suit and having had not done so voluntarily the plaintiff approached the Court for obtaining possession of the premises in suit for her bonafide use and occupation and, as such, the Court of first instance and the appellate Court in the background of the facts of the case were not in error in decreeing the suit.</u>

16. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that defendant having had admitted that he made unauthorised construction in, the premises in suit or, in other words, he without taking permission of the landlord made construction in the premises in suit so the tenancy of the defendant was liable to be forfeited, This aspect of the matter was also considered by the courts below while decreeing the suit but the High Court Division in reversing the judgment of the appellate Court below did not address itself at all to the said aspect of the matter. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant that evidence having been on record that the defendant by his activities is causing disturbance and .annoyance to the other tenants of the plaintiff and because of that the plaintiff is apprehensive of losing the tenants, the tenancy of the defendant was liable to be terminated in view of the provision of clause 'Ga' of section 18 of the Ain which reads as follows:

"(গ) ভাড়াটিয়া এমন আচরনের জন্য দোষী যাহা সংলগ্ন বা পাশ্ববর্তী বাড়ীর দখলকারীগণের নিকট উৎপাত বা বিরুক্তি স্বরূপ”

17. For the disposal of the appeal the submission so made need not be addressed.

18. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that while reversing the judgment and decree of the Courts below the submission of the respondent that plaintiff has other shops in the market and as such, plaintiff's case of bonafide requirement of the premises in suit is not entertain able weighed with the said Division.

<u>19. In the case of Abdus Salam Bepari vs Shamsun Nahar Bibi and others reported in 6 BLC (AD) 36, the question of ejectment of a tenant from a particular shop in a particular market on the ground of bonafide requirement while the landlord has some other shops in the same market or in the same building came up for consideration and it has been held that it is the landlord's choice to eject a tenant from a particular premises on the ground of bonafide requirement and that when the landlord's case of bona fide requirement is established then the relief sought for ejectment of a particular tenant from a particular premises would not be refused only because in the same locality or in the same building the landlord has other shops which have been let out and instead of proceeding against the others the landlord was proceeding against the shop in suit, but that would not disentitle the landlord to have the decree of ejectment sought in respect of the premises in suit. The aforesaid question also came up for consideration before this Court in the case of Zaher Ahmed vs Manik Sardar reported in 6 MLR (AD) 44 and therein it has been held-</u>

<u>"It is for the appellant to decide which premises out of many is required by him bona fide. The learned Single Judge took a wrong view that the appellant picked up the shop room let out to the respondent mala fide on the plea of bona fide requirement without requiring other shop rooms let out to other tenants for the reason that choice for other shop room will be confronted with the same argument leading to an absurd situation. The right of bona fide requirement is always with landlord but he is under legal obligation to prove that he needs the premises for such requirement. Expansion of existing business of a landlord run in a shop room adjacent to the shop room let out to a tenant involves element of must have and constitutes bonafide requirement. Thus, we do not find any reason to uphold the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge and accordingly, we set aside the same and restore those of the learned SCC Judge and Assistant Judge and decree the suit".</u>

20. Fact of the aforesaid case is that landlord instituted the SCC suit for eviction of the defendant from a shop room on the ground of his bonafide requirement. The prayer for ejectment was opposed by the tenant that he obtained the possession of the premises in suit upon making advance of Taka 55,000 and an agreement for lease was executed between him and the landlord fixing rent of the premises in suit at Taka 240 per month and the said rent was subsequently enhanced to Taka 375. The trial Court decreed the suit. As against that the tenant moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the finding that the trial Court while decreeing the suit did not arrive at the finding that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the tenant and that trial Court also did not arrive at the finding that there was a compelling necessity on the part of the landlord for bonafide use of the premises and that the landlord malafide picked up the tenant to evict with the intention to let out the premises in suit to others at enhanced salami where he had more shop rooms.

21. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted that since there was no clause in the agreement of tenancy for termination of the tenancy on the ground of bona fide requirement of the landlord and that as the landlord has some other shops in the same building and market other than the premises in suit and, as such, picking up the respondent on the ground of bona fide requirement is a malafide attempt on the part of the landlord to eject the defendant and that as possession of the premises in suit was made over to the respondent upon receiving a substantial amount and, as such, tenancy was not liable to be terminated on the ground of bonafide requirement of the landlord and consequently, tenant was not liable to be evicted. In the background of the discussions made herein-above the contentions, so made, in our view, are of no merit.

22. In view of the discussions made here in before, we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with costs.'

End.

lawyer:
Md Idrisur Rahman with Harun al Kaioum and Morsheda Parvin, Advocates—For the Petitioners 
Md Sultan Uddin, Advocate—For the Respondents Nos. 5 and 6.
parties:
Shefalika Khisa and others………..Petitioners
vs
Chairman, Land Appeal Board and others……..Respondents
full_judgment:
JBM Hassan J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 20-11-2004 (Annexure-G) passed by the Land Appeal Board (Full Board headed by the Chairman, respondent No.1) in Case No. 4-12/2004-Full Board (Rangamati) allowing the case and thereby setting aside the order dated 15-1-2003 of the Review Case No. 4-111/2002 (Rangamati) and the order dated 16-9-2002 of the Case No. 4-60/2000 Appeal (Rangamati) allowing the appeal case both passed by the Member-2 (respondent No.2) should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect And why the order dated 3-7-2000 (Annexure-B2) passed by the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong Division, Chittagong in Misc. Revision (Rangamati) Case No. 93 of 1999 allowing the revision and thereby setting aside the order dated 8-8-1999 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati in Misc. Case No. 141 of 1998 (Uttaradhikar) should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Relevant facts leading to issuance of the Rule Nisi are that the present petitioners filed an application before the Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati (the DC) for succession certification claiming legal heirs of deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa initiating Miscellaneous Case No. 141 of 1998 (Uttaradhikar). The DC directed the then Thana Nirbahi Officer (TNO), Sadar, Rangamati to submit a report in this regard and accordingly, a report was submitted by the TNO recommending the writ petitioners as successors of deceased. Meanwhile, the respondents Nos.5 and 6 also filed a representation before the DC claiming themselves as co-heirs of the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa. The DC again directed the then concerned TNO to hold a re-enquiry over the matter and accordingly, the TNO obtained report from the Chakma Raja and the Chairman of the Rangamati Pourashava and forwarded the same to the DC for his decision. In the aforesaid reports the Chairman of the Pourashava declined to give any opinion stating that he had no knowledge as to whether the respondent No.5 was a wife of the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa and on the other hand the Chakma Raja submitted report on 28-6-1998 recommending to include the respondents No.5 and 6 in the succession certificate of deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa along with the petitioners observing that late Shoibal Kanti Khisa married to the respondent No.5, Madhuri. Dewan on 10-7-1996 and out of their wedlock respondent No.6, namely, Joyjit Khisa was born. However, the DC after hearing both the parties passed order on 8-8-99 declaring the petitioners as successors of the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa and that the respondents Nos. 5 and 6 were not the successors of the said deceased.

3. Against the said order the respondents No.5 and 6 filed an application under section 17(2) of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 (the Regulations, 1900) being Miscellaneous Revision (Rangamati) Case No. 93 of 1999 before the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong. Ultimately, the revision was heard by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong and by his order dated 8-8-1999 the order of the DC passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 141 of 1998 (Uttaradhikar) was reversed and thereby the respondents Nos.5 and 6 were included in the successors' list of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa along with the petitioners. The petitioners again filed a review application before the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong and it was also rejected by order dated 30-10-2000.

4. Subsequently, the petitioners filed Appeal Case No.4-60/2000-Appeal (Rangamati) before the Land Appeal Board and after hearing the Member-2 of the Board by his order dated 16-9-2002 allowed the appeal setting aside the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner and thereby revived the order of the DC passed in favour of the writ petitioners. Although against the said order a review case being No. 4-111/2002 Review (Rangamati) was filed but after hearing it was also rejected by order dated 15-1-2003.

5. Challenging both the orders dated 16-9-2002 and 15-1-2003 of the Member-2 of the Board, the respondents No. 5 and 6 again filed appeal No. 4-12/2004 (Appeal) Rangamati before the Full Board for reviewing the orders of the Member-2 of the Board. After hearing, the Full Board by order dated 20-11-2004 allowed the review appeal and thereby set aside the earlier order of the Member-2 of the Board affirming the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner passed on 8-8-1999 and 30-10-2000. In this backdrop, challenging the order of the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board the petitioners filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule Nisi.

6. Appearing in the Rule Nisi, the respondents No. 5 and 6 have filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements of the writ petition. Contentions of these respondents, inter alia, are that the local Headman of the concerned area being acquainted with the tribe related personal laws i.e marriage, divorce and other connected materials, submitted a report acknowledging the respondents No. 5 and 6 as successors of the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa and that considering the said report, the Additional Divisional Commissioner passed order setting aside the order of the DC. Further contentions of these respondents are that the Land Appeal Board did not have the jurisdiction to entertain the appeal against the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner passed in relation to civil dispute under the Chittagong Hill Tracts area.

7. Mr Mohammad Idrisur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the DC on consideration of all factual aspects declared the petitioners only successors of deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa and also denied to declare the respondents Nos.5 and 6 as his successors but the Additional Divisional Commissioner on misconception of law reversed the said order on the basis of a biased report made by the Chakma Raja. He further submits that in view of section 66 of “রাঙ্গামাটি পার্বত্য জেলা পরিষদ আইন, ১৯৮৯”  (shortly, the Act, 1989) the local "কারবারি" or the Headman are the concerned authority for disposal of the disputes between the tribes of Rangamati Parbaytta District relating to their social, cultural and tribe concerned issues and that section 8 of the Regulations, 1900 has been changed by the amendment Act, 2003 ousting jurisdiction of the civil courts relating to family disputes inasmuch as relating to customary laws of the tribes the Headmen are well conversant and so, the present dispute ought to have been disposed of by the said authority. Although, Mr Rahman finds it difficult to deny the legal position as incorporated in section 17 of the Regulations, 1900 whereby jurisdiction of the Land Appeal Board has been ousted against revision of the Divisional Commissioner but he, however submits that since by the present Rule the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner has also been challenged, so instead of sending back the case to the Government in accordance with section 17, this Court can adjudicate the substantial issue as to determination of inheritance of deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa.

8. Mr Md Sultan Uddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents Nos.5 and 6 contends that the petitioners' learned Advocate admits that the concerned Headmen under the Chittagong Hill Tracts area are well acquainted relating to customary laws of the tribes and that the considering the same the DC himself required opinion from the headman of the concerned mouza who is also King of the Chakma (Chakma Raja) and pursuant to said report, the Additional Divisional Commissioner declared the respondents Nos.5 and 6 as legal heirs of the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa.

He further contends that in view of section 17(3) of the Regulations, 1900, the Land Appeal Board has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner relating to civil dispute between the tribes and considering this legal proposition, the Full Board set aside the earlier order of the Member-2 of the Land Appeal Board and so the impugned order does not suffer from any illegality. In this regard he refers to the case of Wagachara Tea Estate Ltd vs Md Abu Taher, reported in 69 DLR (AD) 381. He next contends that the petitioners themselves invoked the jurisdiction of the DC by initiating Miscellaneous Case No. 141 of 1998 before him seeking declaration of successors and therefore at this stage, they cannot deny the jurisdiction of the said DC referring to “রাঙ্গামাটি পার্বত্য জেলা পরিষদ আইন, ১৯৮৯” In support of his contention, Mr Md Sultan Uddin, refers to paragraph 56 of the aforementioned case reported in 69 DLR (AD) 381. He again contends that in all the laws the opinion of the Headman has been considered for settling the dispute of the tribes and here also the report was obtained from the concerned Headman pursuant to which the Additional Divisional Commissioner passed the judgment declaring the respondents Nos.5 and 6 as successors of the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa.

9. Relating to the marriage and divorce and other dispute of the tribes both the parties have referred to a book, namely, “চাকমা ব্যক্তিগত ও পারিবারিক আইন.” Referring to this book, Mr Mohammad Idrisur Rahman submits that it is an out put of a project, namely, “বৃহত্তর পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রামের ১১ টি আদিবাসী জনগোষ্ঠীর প্রচলিত প্রথা ও রীতিনীতির ভিত্তিতে বিশেষ অধিকারসমূহ সংরক্ষণ ও সচেতনতা উদ্বুদ্ধকরণ (পিপিআইআর) প্রকল্প মার্চ ২০০৫-মে ২০০৭”

10. We have gone through the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition jointly filed by the respondents Nos.5 and 6, the relevant laws, cited cases and other materials on records.

11. It appears that Shoibal Kanti Khisa died on 4-4-1998. After his death the petitioner No.2, namely, Riko Khisa initiated Miscellaneous Case No 141 of 1998 (Uttaradhikar) before the DC, Rangamati seeking succession certificate for himself as son and two others as wife and son respectively (the present petitioners). Pursuant to said application, the DC required enquiry report from the local TNO who submitted a report on 28-4-1998 mentioning the writ petitioners as successors of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa. In the meantime, the respondents Nos. 5 and 6 also filed an application in the said miscellaneous case to add them as successors of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa. In the circumstances, the DC again required a report from the local TNO and pursuant to the said order of the DC, the TNO procured two reports from the Chairman of the Rangamati Pourashava and the local Chakma Raja who was also Headman of the concerned mouza. Pursuant to the aforesaid reports, the DC after hearing both the parties, declared the petitioners as successors of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa and rejected the prayer of the respondents Nos.5 and 6 holding that the application of the respondents Nos.5 and 6 was filed at a belated stage beyond limitation period and that the respondent No.5 although was married to late Shoibal Kanti Khisa but after 21 days she was divorced and that four months seventeen days after the marriage the respondent No.6 was born which was unusual to acknowledging him as a son of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa.

12. Against the said order a revision was filed by the respondents Nos. 5 and 6 and in disposing of the said revision, the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong relied upon the report sent by the Chakma Raja and Headman of the concerned mouza and on the basis of his report, the Additional Divisional Commissioner reversed the order of the DC declaring the respondents Nos.5 and 6 as successors of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa along with the writ petitioners. Although, a member of the Land Appeal Board reversed the aforesaid order but finally the Full Board in a review application considered that the land Appeal Board has no jurisdiction to sit over the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner. This being the position let us first examine the relevant provisions of the section 17 of the Regulations, 1900 which runs as follows:

"Control and Revision 17. (1) All officers in the Chittagong Hill Tracts shall be subordinate to the [Deputy Commissioner], who may revise any order made by any such officer including [a Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector or a Sub-Deputy Magistrate and Sub-Deputy Collector] invested with any of the powers of the [Deputy Commissioner] under section 6. (2) The Commissioner may revise any order made under this Regulation by the [Deputy Commissioner] or by any other officer in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. (3) The [Government] may revise any order made under this Regulation"

13. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions, it is crystal clear that the Government can only revise the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner and thereby Land Appeal Board has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner relating to civil dispute of the tribes under the Regulations, 1900 and that this legal proposition has also been settled in the case of Wagachara Tea Estate Ltd vs Md Abu Taher reported in 69 DLR (AD) 381; wherein the apex Court held as under: "In the present case, the High Court Division rightly held that the language of the circular under memo dated 23rd May, 1989, does not show that the Land Appeal Board has been given power to hear appeal or revision in respect of matters arising out of civil suits disposed of by the Deputy Commissioner of CHT; that the Land Appeal Board Rules do not show that it has jurisdiction to hear appeal or revision in matters arising out of civil suit disposed of by the Deputy Commissioner of the Hill districts and that section 17(3) of the section of 1900 has not delegated the powers of the government to the Land Appeal Board. However, the observations that in Bikram Kishore Chakma (6 BLC 436), it was out of a dispute over "settlement of government khas land within Chittagong Hill District" meaning thereby that in case of disputes over settlement of land of the three hill districts, the Board has power to revise any decision given by the Commissioner is not a sound view in view of sub-section (3) of section 17 which clearly provides that the government may 'revise any order made under this sections. It is only the government which can revise any decision of the Commissioner made in exercise of power under Regulations, 1900. The Board has no power to decide any dispute from the decision of the Commissioner over the settlement of government khas land or any other matters relating to vested and Non-resident Property, Abandoned Property, Land Survey Record, Land Development Tax, Certificate Case, Waqf or Debuttor property or any other related matters which cover Regulations of 1900."

14. In view of the above ratio, we do not have any hesitation to hold that the order dated 15-1-2003 passed by the Member-2 of the Land Appeal Board reversing the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner was without jurisdiction and the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board by its order dated 20-11-2004 rightly determined this legal proposition by the impugned order and so it does not call for any interference by this Court.

15. In the above circumstances, the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner revives before us as a last forum in the line of dispute between the parties. In this context according to regulation 17(3) of the Regulations, 1900 the dispute can be sent to the Government who can only adjudicate the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner and that although there is no time limit to seek remedy before the Government despite in the meantime the parties in dispute have been languishing for more than 20 years since 1998. In this context, Mr Mohammad Idrisur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner has also been questioned in this Rule and that even the matter is sent back to the Government, ultimately it will again come back to this division for settling the issue finally as to determination of succession of the petitioners as well as the respondents Nos. 5 and 6 and at the same time, Md Sultan Uddin, the learned Advocate for the respondents Nos.5 and 6 also concedes to said submission for determining propriety of order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner.

16. In such situation, Mr Mohammad Idrisur Rahman, has again advanced his submission in that due to section 66 of the Act, 1989, the DC has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the issue of inheritance of late Shoibal Kanti Khisa and so the proceedings and order therein started from the DC to Additional Divisional Commissioner are all nullity and this dispute has to be sent back to the Headman for adjudicating the same in accordance with section 66 of the Act, 1989.

17. In reply, the learned Advocate for the respondents Nos.5 and 6 contends that the petitioner themselves filed the application for succession certificate invoking jurisdiction of the DC by initiating the Miscellaneous Case and now they cannot deny his jurisdiction.

18. To appreciate submissions of the contending parties, we have gone through the relevant provisions of the section 66 of the Act, 1989 which are as follows:

“৬৬। উপজাতীয় বিষয়ে বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত বিধান। (১) রাঙ্গামাটি পার্বত্য জেলার বাসিন্দা এমন উপজাতীয়গণের মধ্যে কোন সামাজিক, সাংস্কৃতিক বা উপজাতীয় বিষয়ে বিরোধ দেখা দিলে বিরোধটির নিষ্পত্তির জন্য স্থানীয় কারবারী বা হেডম্যানের নিকট উত্থাপন করিতে হইবে এবং তিনি সংশ্লিষ্ট উপজাতীয়গণের মধ্যে প্রচলিত রীতি-নীতি অনুযায়ী

বিরোধের নিষ্পত্তি করিবেন।

(২) কারবারী বা হেডম্যানের সিদ্ধান্তের বিরুদ্ধে রাঙ্গামাটি চাকমা চীফের নিকট আপীল করা যাইবে।

(৩) চাকমা চীফের আপীল নিষ্পত্তির ব্যাপারে দায়িত্ব পালনে সহায়তা করার জন্য একজন ত্রিপুরা এবং একজন মারমা

পরামর্শদাতা থাকিবেন এবং তাঁহারা সরকার কর্তৃক তিন বৎসরের জন্য মনোনীত হইবেন।

(৪) চাকমা চীফের সিদ্ধান্তের বিরুদ্ধে চট্টগ্রাম বিভাগের কমিশনারের নিকট আপীল করা যাইবে এবং তাঁহার সিদ্ধান্তই

চূড়ান্ত হইবে।

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, আপীল নিষ্পত্তির পূর্বে তিনি সংশ্লিষ্ট উপজাতি হইতে তৎকর্তৃক মনোনীত অন্যুন তিনজন উপজাতীয়

বিজ্ঞ ব্যক্তির সহিত পরামর্শ করিবেন ।

(৫) পরিষদ প্রবিধান দ্বারা এই ধারায় উল্লিখিত বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তির জন্য

(ক) বিচার পদ্ধতি;

(খ) বিচার প্রার্থী ও আপীলকারী কর্তৃক প্রদেয় ফিস নির্ধারণ করিতে পারিবেন;”

19. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions, we find that the disputes are classified in the following manner:

“উপজাতীয়গণের মধ্যে কোন সামাজিক, সাংস্কৃতিক বা উপজাতীয় বিষয়ে বিরোধ দেখা দিলে।”

20. Now the question to be answered whether these three words i.e সামাজিক, সাংস্কৃতিক বা উপজাতীয় বিষয়ে include the disputes between the parties as to determination of their succession for establishing civil right.

21. In this regard to understand the periphery of these three words, we have carefully examined the relevant provisions of Regulations, 1900 which are the fundamental laws of the tribes since long. Here, section 7 of the said Regulations of the prevailed at the relevant time are reproduced below (before amendment in 2003 as the dispute was initiated in 1998):—

"7. The Chittagong Hill Tracts shall constitute a district for the purpose of criminal and civil jurisdiction and for revenue and general purpose, the [Deputy Commissioner] shall be the District Magistrate and subject to any orders passed by the [Government] under section 6, the general administration of the said Tracts, in criminal, civil, revenue and all other matters shall be vested in the [Deputy Commissioner.]"

<u>22. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions, we find that the DC had the jurisdiction to adjudicate all the civil matters of the tribes of the Hill Tracts. Subsequently in 2003, the law has been amended establishing civil Courts for adjudicating certain disputes and section 7 has also been amended by reshuffling the jurisdiction of the DC ousting civil matters. At the same time inserting sub-sections (3)(4) and (5) of section 8, the civil matters have been brought under the jurisdiction of civil Courts wherein the family matters were split from civil matters and the same has been left with the Mouza Headmen and Circle chiefs. But the dispute between the present parties started and adjudicated under section 7 of the sections, 1990 before its amendment happened in 2003. Therefore, we are of the view that the dispute of determining successor involving civil rights was under the jurisdiction of the DC before amendment of Regulations, 1900 happened in 2003 and so, it does not come within the purview of section 66 of the Act, 1989 within the purview of the words   “সামাজিক, সাংস্কৃতিক বা উপজাতীয় বিষয়ে বিরোধ দেখা দিলে” which are not related to civil rights.</u>

23. Moreover, the petitioners themselves invoked jurisdiction of the DC by filing the miscellaneous case for succession certificate and now they cannot deny his jurisdiction for adjudicating the said issue. This view has been laid down in the "wagachara" case reported in 69 DLR (AD) 381 wherein the apex Court held as under:

"What's more, the appellant has surrendered to the jurisdiction of the Deputy Commissioner under the provisions of the Regulations of 1900. It cannot now say that this provision is not applicable. On the doctrine of approbation and reprobation, persons to the litigation cannot be permitted to take up inconsistent position. This principle has been argued by the Judicial Committee. A litigant who has all along maintained a position in support of one branch of his litigation cannot be permitted, when he fails upon this branch, to withdraw from the position and assert the contrary, more especially when he thereby places his opponent at a great disadvantage. To make the point more clear, a person or litigant cannot say at one time that a transaction is valid and thereby obtain some advantage to which he could only be entitled on the footing that it is valid and then turn round and say it is void for the purpose of securing some other advantage. It may accordingly be laid down as a broad proposition that one who, without mistake induced by the opposite party, has taken a particular position deliberately in the course of a litigation must act consistently with it, one cannot play fast and loose. It is well settled that party to this litigation cannot be permitted to assume inconsistent positions in court, to play List and loose, to blow hot and cold, to approbate and reprobate, to the detriment of the opponent; and that this wholesome doctrine applies not only to the successive stage of the same litigation, but also to another litigation other than the one in which the position was taken up, provided the second litigation grows out of the judgment in the first. Where a party invites the court to follow a procedure which is not contemplated by a particular law, say Code of Civil Procedure and is in fact a procedure extra cursum curie, he cannot turn round and say that the court is to blame for adopting the very same procedure which he invited the court to follow. The doctrine of estoppels would apply to a party who attempts to blow hot and cold."

24. Further, in section 66 of the Act, 1989 we find that the Headman is the authority to adjudicate the “সামাজিক, সাংস্কৃতিক বা উপজাতীয় বিষয়” and that against their decision Circle Chief will dispose of the appeal and then the Divisional Commissioner is the last appellate authority whose decision is final. In the same line, this matter has also been adjudicated initially giving opinion to the TNO by the Chakma Raja who is the concerned Headman as well as the Circle Chief and finally the Additional Divisional Commissioner adjudicated their decision in disposing of the appeal preferred against the appeal of the DC.

25. Therefore, in any view of the matter, we consider that the issue of deciding inheritance of the petitioners and the respondents Nos.5 and 6, have been adjudicated by the proper authority and therefore, the question of jurisdiction in disposing of this issue does not arise in this particular case in view of its own facts and circumstances as described above.

26. However, both the learned Advocates for the petitioners and the respondents have submitted that the substantive order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner have been questioned in this Rule and on this aspect, we have entered into the merit of the substantial issue to determine successors of Late Shoibal Kanti Khisa.

27. Undisputedly, it is on record that Late Shoibal Kanti Khisa married the respondent No.5 (Madhuri Dewan) on 10-7-1976. But referring to a unilateral declaration dated 1-8-1976 allegedly made by Late Shoibal Kanti Khisa on 1-8-1976, the DC considered their divorce and due to birth of respondents No. 6, 4 (four) months 17 (seventeen) days after the marriage, the DC disbelieved the birth of child under the legitimacy of Late Shoibal. However, facts remain that the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa married to the respondent No.5 and that respondent No.6 was born four months seventeen days after the marriage.

28. Therefore, two issues are involved here to be decided. Firstly, whether the divorce between Shoibal and respondent No. 5 took effect by the alleged declaration dated 1-8-1976 and that whether respondent No. 6 was their legitimate son.

29. Relating to first question, the petitioners' contention is that after 21 days of marriage, the deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa divorced the respondent No.5 by declaration (Talaknama) allegedly made on 1-8-1976. In this context, the Chakma Raja discussing their customary law in his opinion observed that the Talak did not take effect by the purported Talaknama having not been done on observance of their customary law relying on which the Additional Divisional Commissioner declared the respondent No.5 as widow of deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa considering continuation of wedlock. In this context, we have also gone through the book, namely, “চাকমা ব্যক্তিগত ও পারিবারিক আইন” as referred to by both the parties wherein chapter 4 incorporates the customs for making divorce in the Chakma tribes which are as follows:

“বিবাহ বিচ্ছেদ ছাড়াছাড়ি/সুরকাগজ

৪.১ বিবাহ বিচ্ছেদঃ চাকমা পরিবারে স্বামী ও স্ত্রীর বৈবাহিক সম্পর্ক ছিন্ন করাকে ছাড়াছাড়ি/সুরকাগজ দেনা বলা হয় ।

৪.২ বিবাহ বিচ্ছেদের বিভিন্ন পদ্ধতিঃ স্বামী কিংবা স্ত্রী যে কোন একজনের মৃত্যুতে চাকমা সমাজ একটি দাম্পত্য জীবন তথা

বিবাহিত জীবনের পরিসমান্তি ঘটে । তবে সমাজ ও আইন স্বীকৃত উপায়ে নিম্নবর্ণিত কারণে স্বামী ও স্ত্রীর মধ্যে জীবদ্দশায় বৈবাহিক সম্পর্কের পরিসমাপ্তি হতে বা ছাড়াছাড়ি/সুরকাগজ প্রদান হতে পারবেঃ-

ক) স্বামী-স্ত্রী উভয়ে স্বেচায় সামাজিক আদালতের দারস্থ হয়ে সিদ্ধান্তের মাধ্যমে একে অপরের সাথে বৈবাহিক

সম্পর্ক ছিন্ন করতে বা “সুরকাগজ' দিতে পারে ।

খ) সামাজিক আদালত বা বিচার বিভাগীয় কার্যক্রম দ্বারা“ছাড়াছাড়ি”হতে পারে ।

গ) ইদানিং শিক্ষিত সমাজে স্বামী বা স্ত্রী কর্তৃক বিজ্ঞ ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেট/নোটারি পাবলিক এর নিকট হলফনামা সম্পাদন মূলে “ছাড়াছাড়ি হতে বা “সুরকাগজ প্রদান করতে দেখা যায়। সেক্ষেত্রে সম্পাদিত হলফনামার কপি একপক্ষ তার নিযুক্ত আইনজীবীর মাধ্যমে অপরপক্ষকে প্রদান করে থাকে (যদিও তা সামাজিক প্রথাসিদ্ধ নয়) যা আধুনিক সংস্কার ।”

30. Keeping in mind the above customary law, the Chakama Raza (the Headman of the petitioners' mouza in his opinion made the following comment: "(ii) The Pronouncement of Divorce: "Under Chakma customary law, a divorce may only take place with mutual consent and the sanction of the karbari, headman or chief or by a judicial pronoun-cement from a competent court of law, including tribal courts and government courts. A unilateral pronoun-cement of divorce like a "talaknama" has no legal basis, unless acquiesced to or sanctioned by a competent court of law (including karbari, headman and chief). Therefore, the marriage would appear to be valid, in spite of the "talaknama"

31. In view of above comment of the concerned Headman (Chakma Raja) the Talaknama purported to have been executed on 1-8-1976, was a unilateral document having no judicial or social pronouncement as to their divorce and so, the divorce did not take effect and, as such, the respondent No.5 was the wife of deceased Shoibal Kanti Khisa until his death.

32. Since the respondent No.6 was born in the womb of respondent No.5 during subsistence of marriage with Late Shoibal Kanti Khisa, therefore he is a legitimate son of Late Shoibal Kanti Khisa. However, even for argument sake, if we accept the finding of the DC that he was born four months seventeen days after the marriage of the respondent No.5 and late Shoibal Kanti Khisa and in other words, respondent No. 5 conceived before marriage. In such situation their customary law accepts this child as legitimate. In this regard, chapter-3 of the referred Book, namely, “চাকমা ব্যক্তিগত ও পারিবারিক আইন” Provides as follows:

৩.১২ পলায়ন/অনিয়মিত (ধাবা ম্যানা) বিবাহের (পালিয়ে গিয়ে গোপনে বিয়ে করা) আইনগত ফলাফলঃ পলায়নের পর সামাজিক বিচারে জোর করে অপহরণ করার অভিযোগে পাত্রকে অপরাধী সাব্যস্ত করা না হলে এবং প্রেমিকার পিতা-মাতা সেই পাত্রের সাথে বিয়ে দিতে রাজি হলেও পলাতক অবস্থায় বিবাহ বহির্ভূতভাবে দৈহিক মিলনের অপরাধে সাজাভোগ করতে হবে। যেমনঃ শুকর, মোরগ, মদ ও নগদ টাকা জরিমানা প্রদান সাপেক্ষে তাদের মধ্যে বিয়ে হলে সমাজ কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত বলে গণ্য হবে। সমাজ কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত হলে পাত্র-পাত্রীর বিবাহ বহির্ভূত দৈহিক মিলনের দ্বারা জন্মগ্রহণকারী সেই সন্তানও বৈধ সন্তান হিসেবে গণ্য হয় এবং পিতা-মাতার উত্তরাধিকারী হয়ে পূর্ণ সামাজিক মর্যাদা ভোগ করবে।

প্রেমিক বা প্রেমিকার পিতা-মাতার অসম্মতির কারণে প্রেমিক যুগলের বিয়ে না হয়ে পলাতক অবস্থায় দৈহিক কারণে প্রেমিকা গর্ভবতী হলে সেই ভূমিষ্ট সন্তান সমাজের দৃষ্টিতে অবৈধ সন্তান হিসেবে গণ্য হবে। সন্তান যার ঔরসে জন্মলাভ করেছে । করবে সেই পিতার উত্তরাধিকারী এবং পিতার পারিবারিক মর্যাদারও অধিকারী হবেন না। তবে পরবতীতে সামাজিকভাবে উভয়ের  মধ্যে বিবাহ হলে অবৈধ সন্তান পিতার উত্তরাধিকার হবে ।”

33. Although, the petitioners allege that being born after four months seventeen days of marriage, it was indicated that at the time of marriage the respondent No.5 was conceived by somebody else and unusual birth of within four months seventeen days of the marriage, he cannot be a legitimate child. But fact remains that due to previous love affairs between the respondent No.5 and Shoibal Kanti Khisa, they were married and that knowing fully about the pregnancy of respondent No.5 Shoibal Kanti Khisa married her as he knew that the respondent No. 5 was conceived due to their cohabit before marriage and so after the marriage the born child is a legitimate child in accordance with the customary law of the Chakma tribes.

34. Therefore, in view of above discussions, we are of the view that the Additional Divisional Commissioner taking into consideration of the opinion of the concerned Headman (Chakma Raja) came to the decision declaring the respondents No. 5 and 6 as legal heirs of the deceased Shoibal Kanti and this opinion is supported by the tribes customary law as reflected in the petitioners, referred book, namely, “চাকমা ব্যক্তিগত ও পারিবারিক আইন” which is an outcome of a research of project, namely, “বৃহত্তর পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রামের ১১ টি আদিবাসী জনগোষ্ঠীর প্রচলিত প্রথা ও রীতিনীতির ভিত্তিতে বিশেষ অধিকারসমূহ সংরক্ষণ এবং সচেতনতা উদ্ধুদ্ধকরণ (পিপিআইআর)প্রকল্প মার্চ ২০০৫-মে ২০০৭।” and, as such, we do not find any illegality in his order for our judicial review.

35. Regard being had to the above, we do not find any merit in this Rule.

36. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as costs. Communicate a copy of this judgment and order to the respondents at once.

End.

full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman J: In this Rule Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order passed under Nothi No. 4/LTU/Mushak/Le:A:/04/ Dhaka Regency Ho:/One:/14/12390 dated 29-12-2014 by the respondent No. 4 making demand to pay Taka 14,55,66,579 as supplementary duty and VAT (Annexure-A) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 2. At the instance of the petitioner the impugned order dated 19-12-2014 (Annexure-A) was stayed by this Court for a prescribed period vide order dated 4-2-2015. 3. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the petitioner is a private limited company incorporated under the Company Act, 1994 and is engaged in the business of 5 (five) star Hotel and Restaurant under the name and style "Dhaka Regency Hotel & Resort Ltd." 4. However, the petitioner has obtained VAT registration from the concerned VAT office under the Value Added Tax Act, 1991 (in short, the Act) being registration No. 51010728847 under Service Code No. 5001.00 as "Hotel & Restaurant" for the purpose of payment of VAT and since then it has been paying VAT regularly. 5. During the course of business, an audit team of the respondent No. 1 in order to conduct audit of the petitioner's "Hotel and Restaurant" examined monthly returns (দাখিলকৃত) "Musuk-19" for the period of July 2009 to June 2012. After conducting audit it was detected that huge supplementary duty (in short, SD) and VAT evaded by the petitioner on its restaurant service. Accordingly, the VAT authority registered Oniom Case No. 01 of 2014 dated 1-1-2014. Pursuant thereto the Joint Commissioner, Large Tax Payer Unit on behalf of the respondent No. 4 issued a notice upon the petitioner vide Memo No.4 /LTU, Mushak/ Li:A:/04/Dhaka Regency hotel/Onee:Ma:/ 14/11050 dated 11-9-2014 (Annexure-D) demanding Taka 12,39,20,540 as SD, Taka 1,37,91,791 as VAT with interest at the rate of 2% at Taka 28,54,247 total Taka 14,55,66,579 for the period of July 2009 to June 2012 under sections 55(1) and 37(3) of the VAT Act 1991. Vide the said notice, the petitioner was asked to give reply within the period as prescribed therein. 6. In response thereto, however, the petitioner submitted a written reply stating, inter alia, that a writ petition was pending before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh on self-same matter; hence, requested to stay further proceeding of the notice till disposal of the writ petition, but there was no response thereto. Thereafter, the respondent No. 4 issued another notice on 21-10-2014 upon the petitioner with request to appear before him for personal hearing on 21-11-2014 (Annexure B). Upon hearing the parties and considering the facts and circumstances of the case the respondent No. 4 ultimately finalized the demand directing the petitioner to pay less paid SD and VAT amounting to Taka 1427,12332 during the period of July 2009 to June 2012 under section 55(3) and Taka 28,54,247 as interest under section 37(3) of the VAT Act, 1991. 7. By filing a supplementary affidavit, it has also been stated that Service Code of the petitioner is under S001.00 as such no SD can be imposed vide SRO No. 168/Ain/2013/672 MUSAH dated 6-6-2012 and SD was imposed on Hotel under service Code No. S001.10 and Restaurant under service Code No. S001.20. The petitioner's company being a hotel was exempted for payment of SD vide SRO No. 176/Ain/2011/590MUSUK dated 9-6-2011 and SRO No. 168/Ain/2013/672 MUSUK dated 6-6-2012. However, except drinks and floor show, if any. Vide the impugned notice the authority claimed SD over total value of service including VAT. 8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid demand notice the petitioner has preferred this application and obtained the Rule Nisi and subsequently, order of stay. 9. Mr Munshi Moniruzzaman along with Mrs. Saleha Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that vide the impugned order dated 29-12-2014 issued by the respondent No. 4 making demand to pay Taka 14,55,66,579 for alleged evasion of SD and VAT is illegal, unlawful and arbitrary, for the petitioner is carrying on the business of "Hotel and Restaurant Service" which is exempted for payment of SD under SRO No.134-Ain/2012/ 642-Mushak, dated 7-1-2012 and SRO No.152- Ain/2005/443-Mushak, dated 9-6-2015. He further goes to submit that the impugned demand has been made beyond the statutory period of 5 (five) years; hence, the same is barred by limitation under section 55 of the VAT Act, 1991 and hence, it is liable to be declared to have been issued without lawful authority. He also goes to argue that the SD and VAT was demanded under section 55 of the Act, 1991 and the petitioner is not liable to pay 2% interest under section 37(3) of the Act. As such, imposition of 2% additional taxes under section 37(3) of the Act, 1991 upon the petitioner is without jurisdiction. 10. On the other hand, Mr Samarendra Nath Biswas, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 4, the Commissioner, Large Taxpayer Unit, VAT, Dhaka without filing any affidavit-in-opposition submits that the instant Rule must fail as being not maintainable, for the petitioner had forum under section 42 of the Act, 1991 for challenging the order so has been impugned in the instant writ petition. 11. Heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Government, have perused the writ petition, relevant materials on record and the annexures so have been appended thereto. 12. In order to appreciate the respective arguments of both the parties, it is necessary to examine the demand cum show cause notice dated 11-9-2014 (Annexure-D), the very initiation of proceeding against the petitioner for realization of the less paid supplementary duty and VAT with interest under sections 55(1) and 37(3) of the Act. Relevant part of the said notice is quoted below; “…………. বিষয় ঢাকা রিজেন্সি হোটেল এন্ড রিসার্ট লিমিটেড এর জুলাই ২০০৯ থেকে জুন, ২০১২ খ্রিঃ পর্যান্ত কম পরিশোধিত রাজন্বের পরিমাণ (সম্পূরক শুল্ক ১২,৩৯,২০,৫৪০ + মূসক ১,৮৭,৯১,৭৯২) = ১৪,২৭,১২,৩৩২ (চৌদ্দ কোটি সাতাইশ লক্ষ বার হাজার তিনশত বত্রিশ) টকা এবং মূসক আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ৩৭(৩) অনুযায়ী ২% হারে সুদ বাবদ ২৮,৫৪,২৪৭ টাকাসহ সর্বমোট (১৪,২৭,১২,৩৩২ + ২৮,৫৪,২৪৭) = ১৪,৫৫,৬৬,৫৭৯ (চৌদ্দ কোটি পঞ্চান্ন লক্ষ ছেষট্টি হাজার পাঁচশত উনআশি) পরিশোধের লক্ষ্যে মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫(১) অনুযায়ী দাবিনামা জারি। সূত্রঃ অনিয়ম মামলা নং ০১/২০১৪, তারিখঃ ১-১-২০১৪। ২। ঢাকা রিজেন্সি হোটেল এন্ড রিসোর্ট লিঃ, বৃহৎ করদাতা ইউনিট, মূল্য সংযোজন কর এর আওতাভুক্ত একটি সেবা মূলক প্রতিষ্ঠান। মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ অনুযায়ী সেবা কোড এস-০০১.০০ এর আওতায় আবাসিক হোটেল রেস্তোরা যাহার মধ্যে আবাসন, খাবার, ও পানীয় সরবরাহ কালে হোটেল বা রেস্তোরায় মদ জাতীয় পানীয় সরবরাহ করা হয় বা যে কোন ধরনের ফ্লোর শো এর আয়োজন করা হয় (বৎসর এক দিনের জন্য করা হলেও) তহালে বিক্রিত সেবা মূল্যের উপর ১০% হারে সম্পূরক শুল্ক প্রযোজ্য । ৩। ঢাকা রিজেন্সি হোটেল এন্ড রিসোর্টস লিঃ নামক প্রতিষ্ঠানটির জুলাই, ২০০৯ থেকে জুন; ২০১২ খ্রিঃ সময়ের মাসিক দাখিলপত্র পরীক্ষা করে দেখা যায় যে, রেস্তোরা সেবার বিপরীতে প্রাপ্ত বিলের-উপর ষথাযথ মূসক পরিশোধ করা হয়নি। প্রতিষ্ঠানটির দাখিলকৃত (মূসক-১৯) অনুযায়ী বর্ণিত সময়ে মোট বিক্রিত সেবা মূল্য, এর উপর ১০% হার প্রদেয় সম্পূরক শুল্ক, মূসক আরোপযোগ্য মূল্য, পরিশোধিত সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসকের পরিমাণ এবং কম পরিশোধিত/ফাঁকিকৃত সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসকের তথ্যাদি নিন্নবর্ণিত ছকের মাধ্যমে নিম্নে দেখানো হলোঃ

It appears from the demand cum show cause notice dated 11-9-2014 that the respondent No. 4 had initiated proceeding against the petitioner towards realization of less paid SD and VAT from its Restaurant service amounting to Taka 14,27,12332 under section 55(1) of the Act and Taka 28,54,247 as interest under section 37(3) of the said Act during the period of July 2009 to June 2012. 14. Upon hearing the parties, the respondent No. 4 had finalized said demand cum show cause notice vide impugned order dated 29-12-2014 (Annexure-A) under section 55(3) of the Act, 1991 observing, inter alia, “সার্বিক পর্যালোচনায় প্রতিদিত হয়েছে যে, আইনের সুস্পষ্ট বিধান থাকা সত্ত্বেও প্রতিষ্ঠানটি যথানিয়মে সম্পূরক শুল্ক পরিশোধ করেনি। এ কারণে সরকার তার প্রাপ্য রাজস্ব থেকে বঞ্চিত হয়েছে। শুনানিকালে প্রতিষ্ঠানের পক্ষ হতে হাইকোর্টের দায়েরকৃত মামলা এবং অব্যাহতির জন্য চেয়ারম্যান, জানাবো ও বেসামরিক বিমান চলাচল ও পর্যটন মন্ত্রণালয়ের মাননীয় মন্ত্রির সাথে আলোচনার বিষয়টি উল্লেখ করেন। মামলার রায় তাদের বিরুদ্ধে হলে তারা মেনে নিবেন মর্মে অপপটে স্বীকার করেন। কাজেই প্রতিষ্ঠানের উপর আনীত অভিযোগ সন্দেহাতীতভাবে প্রমাণিত হওয়ায় সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসক বাবদ (১৪,২৪,১২,৩৩২ + ২৮,৫৪,২৪৭) = ১৪,৫৫,৬৬, ৫৭৯ (চৌদ্দ কোটি পঞ্চান্ন লক্ষ ছেষট্টি হাজার পাঁচশত উনআশি) টাকা সরকারী পাওনা টাকা রিজেন্সি হোটেল এন্ড রিসার্ট লিমিটেড এর নিকট হতে আদায়যোগ্য। কাজেই মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫(৩) অনুযায়ী ফাঁকি প্রদত্ত রাজস্ব আদায়ের লক্ষ্যে চূড়ান্ত দাবিনামা জারি করা হলো ।” 15. In view of the above, 1st issue requires determination in the instant Rule is that whether the petitioner is liable to pay SD for its "Hotel and Restaurant" business; 16. Admittedly, the petitioner obtained a VAT registration certificate from the concerned VAT authority under Service Code No. S001.00 as "Hotel and Restaurant" and since registration it has been providing combined "Hotel and Restaurant" service in its premises. In this regard, the petitioner categorically stated in paragraph No. 9 of the writ petition that: "The petitioner carries on a business of hotel under the name and style Dhaka Regency Hotel & Resort (the said hotel). The petitioner lets rooms to public at large to stay temporarily. And there is arrangement for catering and selling wine and alcohol to its permitted customers. The petitioner carries on its business of hotel and resort, which ranked as five-star hotel. The said hotel is a hotel as complete package. Its nature as a hotel is combined with all activities including but not limited to health club, swimming pool, bar, restaurant etc. It does not carry on its activities as bar, restaurant etc. as different entities than that of its hotel business. Foreigners and tourists while they visit this country stay in this hotel. So for the purpose of providing food and wine of different culture and society to the tourists from different countries, separate arrangement is made and food and wine of different countries are served in different places within the single premises of the hotel. There is no separate restaurant. The hotel itself provides catering and other service for serving food, wine and alcohol" 17. Section 7 of the VAT Act, 1991 provides imposition of SD. Section 7 is quoted below for ready reference: ৭। সম্পূরক শুল্ক আরোপ ।-(১) বিলাস পণ্য, অত্যাবশ্যক নহে এবং সামাজিভাবে অনভিপ্রেত এবং অন্যান্য পণ্য ও সেবা যাহার ওপর জনস্বার্থে সম্পূরক শুল্ক আরোপ করা যুক্তিযুক্ত তৃতীয় তফসিল উল্লিখিত এমন পণ্য ও সেবা যাহা বাংলাদেশে সরবরাহকৃত, আমদানিকৃত বা প্রদত্ত হয় উহার ওপর উক্ত তফসিলে উল্লিখিত হাঁরে সম্পূরক আরোপিত হইবে। (২) সম্পূরক শুল্ক আরোপের উদ্দেশ্যে পণ্য বা সেবার মূল্য হইবে, (ক) আমদানিকৃত পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে, আমদানি শুল্ক আরোপের লক্ষ্যে Customs Act এর section 25 অধীন আমদানি শুল্ক আরোপণীয় মূল্যের সহিত আমদানি শুল্ক যোগ করিয়া যে মূল্যে হয় যেই মূল্য (খ) বাংলাদেশে প্রস্তুতকৃত বা উৎপাদিত পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে, প্রস্তুতকারক বা উৎপাদিক কর্তৃক এবং করযোগ্য অন্যান্য পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে ব্যবসায়ী কর্তৃক উক্ত পণ্যের ক্রেতার নিকট হইতে প্রাপ্য পণ্য যাহাতে মূল্য সংযোজন কর ও সম্পূরক শুল্ক অন্তর্ভুক্ত থাকিবে না (গ) বাংলাদেশে প্রদত্ত সেবার ক্ষেত্রে, সেবা প্রদান বাবদ সর্বমোট প্রাপ্তি যাহাতে মুল্য সংযোজন কর ও সম্পূরক শুল্ক অন্তর্ভূক্ত থাকিবে না এবং (ঘ) যে পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে খুচরা মূল্যের ভিত্তিতে মূল্য সংযোজন কর আরোপিত হইবে সেই পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে সম্পূরক শুল্ক আরোপের উদ্দেশ্য এই আইনের ধারা ৫(৩) এ বর্ণিত খুচরা মূল্য উক্ত পণ্যের মূল্য বলিয়া বিবেচিত হইবে৷ (৩) মূল্য সংযোজন কর যে সময় ও পদ্ধতিতে প্রদান করা হয় সেই একই সময় ও পদ্ধতিতে সম্পূরক শুল্ক প্রদেয় হইবে ।” 18. 19. The petitioner assertion is that the Government has exempted paying SD on Hotel service under SRO No. 152-Law/2005/443-Mushak dated 9-6-2015 and SRO No. 134-Ain/2012/642 Mushak dated 7-12012. It is true that the Government is exercising power conferred under section 14 of the Act, 1991 was given exempted for payment SD on "Hotel Service" under Service Code No. S001.10 vide the above SROs. But, the service on Restaurant was not allowed such exemption by the said SROs. So, the petitioner was liable to pay SD in its "Restaurant service" provided in the same premises. The issue of payment SD on "Hotel and Restaurant" service has been resolved by this Division in the case of Westin vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Dhaka, reported in 21 BLC 314, it has been observed, inter alia— "Now, coming back to our cases we have found that exemption of paying supplementary duty was there on the hotel but no exemption was given upon the service Code S001.20 which the 'restaurant'. This goes without saying as on the basis of ratio decidendi of the 32 DLR and 64 DLR as referred to above that the restaurants inside the hotels having different service Code are separate entity rendering different services altogether upon which there was no exemption of supplementary duty whatsoever. Section 7 of the Act enjoins supplementary duty to be paid referring third schedule of the Act and we have made elaborate discussion on those aspects already. It has been rightly observed in 32 DLR (AD) that— In a fiscal or taxing statute one has to look merely at what is clearly said therein, for there is no room for any intendment, nor for any equity or for any presumption. In case of unresolved ambiguity, it may be interpreted favorably to the citizen but nothing more. The attempt of the Court in case of ambiguity is to be guided by the principle of justice and fairness and to try to arrive at a true meaning of word. 20. Further, it has been observed: We have found no ambiguity of any kind to hold that the restaurants inside the hotels in question at the relevant time were not exempted from paying supplementary duty. The exemption of supplementary duty upon 'Hotel' and 'Restaurant' was given under section 14 of the VAT Act by SRO No. 338 dated 3-12-2003. In the year 2004 SRO No. 166 dated 10-06-2004 repealed the earlier SRO-338 which exempted supplementary duty only upon the hotel but restaurant was not allowed such exemption. Now by any legal fiction or by bringing any analogy it cannot be inferred since the hotels under service Code No. S001.10 were given exemption from paying supplementary duty time to time, the restaurants inside those hotels were also given the same exemption. Law does not allow something to archive indirectly which cannot be achieved directly. Nothing short of waiver exemption or by operation of law that can be done. There is no gain saying the fact that the 'Restaurant' under service Code No. S001.20 was never given any exemption under section 14 of VAT Act1991 from paying supplementary duty. All the submissions to justify the same fall apart being fallacious having no substance." 21. It is also admitted that the petitioner in its respective premises has provided "Hotel and Restaurant" service together and it did not pay any SD on its restaurant service. However, the payment of SD on restaurant service was not exempted by the operation of law or SRO and hence, the petitioner cannot be said at this stage that it is not liable to pay SD in its Restaurant service. 22. Another issue involves in the instant Rule is that whether the impugned demand notice is barred by limitation under section 55 (1) of the Act, 1991 and also whether the VAT authority can claim 2% interest in the proceeding initiated under section 55 of the Act without initiation proceeding independently under section 37 of the Act 1991. 23. It appears from the notice dated 11-9-2014 (Annexure -D to the writ petition) that the respondent No.4 made a demand cum show cause notice upon the petitioner for payment of less paid SD and VAT along with interest under section 55(1) of the VAT during period of July 2009 to June 2012. Section 55(1) of the VAT Act provides that; “সেক্ষেত্রে উক্ত ব্যক্তিকে তাহার উপর যে তারিখে উক্ত মূল্য সংযোজন কর বা, ক্ষেত্রমত, মূল্য সংযোজন কর ও সম্পূরক শুল্ক প্রদেয় হইয়াছিল বা প্রত্যর্পণ বা ফেরত প্রদান বা সমন্বয় করা হইয়াছিল সেই তারিখ পাঁচ (৫) বৎসরের মধ্যে সংশ্লিষ্ট মূল্য সংযোজন কর কর্মকর্তা নোটিশ ছারা, নোটিশ উল্লিখিত শুল্ক বা মূল্য সংযোজন কর দাবি করিয়া, উহাতে উল্লিখিত সময়সীমার মধ্যে উক্ত শুল্ক বা মূল্য সংযোজন কর পরিশোধের জন্য কারন দর্শানো নোটিশ জারি, করিবেন ।” 24. From perusal of the aforesaid provisions of law it is apparent that a demand can only be made in respect of the period 5(five)-years, not beyond. In the instant case, the respondent concern while issuing the demand notice dated 11-9-2014 made a claim for unpaid SD and VAT during period of July 2009-June 2012. In view of statutory provision contained in section 55(1) of the Act, 1991 the respondent concern could only demand for the period of 5 (five) years i.e. 11-9-2009-June 2012. Consequently, the claim in respect of July 2009 to 10-9-2009 is suffering from legal infirmity i.e., it is barred by limitation under section 55(1) of the VAT Act, 1991. However, the demand so far it relates to 10-9-209 to June 2012 is covered under the said provision of law. 25. Evidently, the show cause notice dated 11-9-2014 and the subsequent final demand notice dated 29-12-2014 were made by the respondent concerned under section 55 of the Act, 1991. As has already been observed earlier that the petitioner is liable to pay SD &VAT on its Restaurant service. However, the respondent concern without initiation any proceeding under section 37 of the Act, 1991 claimed interest simultaneously by the impugned demand, which is not permissible under the Act, 1991. Said findings of our's final support in the case of Provati Insurance Company Ltd. vs Commissioner of Customs Excise and VAT, reported in 17 BLC 450, where it has been observed as under:— "In absence of compliance with the requirements of section 55(1) of the Act, thereafter of demands made twice as required under section 37(2)(Kaka), the penalties under section 37(2) and 37(3) have been illegally imposed." 26. Also, in the case of M/s Hotel Zakaria International (Pvt) Limited vs Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal passed in writ petition No. 3605 of 2002 observing that; "However though the petitioner evaded VAT/Supplementary duty but the VAT authority issued demand VAT notice/letter under section 55 of the VAT Act clamming the unpaid amount of VAT from the petitioner. As the demand notice was issued under section 55 of the VAT Act demanding unpaid VAT/Supplementary duty taxes etc. there was no scope to impose 2% additional taxes under section 37(3) of the VAT Act." 27. In view of the discussion made herein above, the claim of 2% interest to the tune of Taka 28,54,247 vide the impugned demand notice is absolutely without jurisdiction. In other words, the petitioner is not liable to pay the said amount of interest. However, the respondent concern is at liberty to realize the said amount of interest with due process of section 37 of the Act, 1991. 28. With regard to the maintainability of the Rule as to having alternative forum to appeal against the impugned order under the VAT Act, 1991. We find many decisions of this Court where it has been categorically observed that when an illegality is apparent on face of record and the respondents performing the function of the Republic have acted totally without jurisdiction, invoking forum as provided under Article 102 of the Constitution is not a bar. 29. In this regard, in the case of Messrs Chemico Laboratories Ltd. vs Secretary, Ministry of Finance Internal Resources Division, reported in 11 MLR (AD) 192 it has been held that; "It is not disputed that the order of the adjudication officer that is Commissioner of Excise, Customs and VAT, Rajshahi directing the petitioner to pay Taka 67,59,921.15 as VAT which the petitioner did not pay is an appealable order and the petitioner did not prefer any appeal before the proper forum. Mr Mahmud tried to argue that since the Rule has been issued in respect of the one portion of the order the other portion of the same order may also be examined by the High Court Division. Since the other portion of the order that is payment of VAT which the petitioner avoided to pay is an appealable order in our view, the High Court Division rightly refused to issue the Rule." 30. For the reason as discussed herein above we find that the writ petition is maintainable so far it relates to demand which have been made by the respondent concern beyond the period of 5(five) years i.e July 2009 to 10-9-2009 under section 55 of the Act, 1991 and the demand of interest 2% amounting to tune of Taka 28,54,247 under section 37(3) of the Act, 1991 being passed without jurisdiction. 31. However, we find no legal infirmity in the impugned demand order for payment of unpaid SD and VAT under section 55(3) of the Act, 1991, so far as it relates to the period of 11-9-2009 to June 2012. 32. In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case and visa-vis the law we find merit of the Rule, though in part. 33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part. 34. The impugned demand order dated 29-12-2014 bearing Nothi 4/ LTU/Musuk/ Le:/ 04/Dhaka Regency Ho: /One: /14/12390 issued by the respondent No. 4 (Annexure-A) so far it relates to period of July 2009-10-9-2009 and 2% interest at Taka 28,54,247 is hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect. 35. The respondent No. 4, the Commission, Large Tax payer unit, Value Added Tax is hereby directed to calculate the balance amount of SD and VAT excluding the period of July 2009 to 10-9-2009 and interest so far it relates to the impugned order (Annexure A to the writ petition) within 3 (three) weeks from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment and order and to inform it to the petitioner with due process of law. 36. However, the petitioner is directed to pay the balance amount of SD and VAT within 30 (thirty) days from the date of communication thereof by the concerned respondents failing which the concerned VAT authority is at liberty to realize long outstanding Government revenue in due process of law. 37. There will be no order as to costs. Communicate the judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith. End.
