Mosharraf Hossain Chowdhury and others -------- Appellant
Vs. 
 Md Jahurul Islam Chowdhury and others -------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated August 10,1997 passed by the  High Court Division in Second Appeal No.162 of 1975.)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: The appeal, by leave, at the instance of the defendants is against the judgment dated August 10,1997 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 162 of 1975 dismissing the same upon affirming the judgment and decree dated April 20, 1974 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Rangpur in Other Appeal No. 175 of 1970 allowing the same upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated June 23, 1970 of the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Rangpur in Other Suit No. 45 of 1968 so far the same relates to the land described in schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' of the plaint. The aforementioned suit was filed seeking declaration of title in respect of the land of schedule 'Ka' of Mouza Son a-tala and as regard the land of schedule 'Kha and 'Ga' of Mouza Sandalpur.

2. The trial Court decreed the suit in respect of the land of 'Ka' schedule and dismissed the suit as regard the claim of the plaintiffs in respect of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule. The plaintiffs took appeal as against the judgment and decree of the trial Court so far the same related to the land of schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga', The appellate Court allowed the appeal and thereby decreed plaintiffs' suit and consequent thereupon the plaintiffs' suit stood decreed in respect of the land of all the 3 schedules. As against the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court the appellants herein took second appeal before the High Court Division but without any success.

<u>3. The suit was filed stating, infer alia, that land of 'Ka' schedule belonged to Tasaruddin who died leaving a son by name Tofazzal Hossain, a daughter by name Amena Khatun and a widow Jamila, that after death of Tasaruddin the land of 'Ka' schedule was put to rent sale in execution of rent decree and the land of 'Ka' schedule was purchased by Khatemon, wife of Tofazzal on May 14, 1946 and since the purchase Khatemon, plaintiff No. 2 is possessing the land of 'Ka' schedule on payment of rent, that land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule of mouza Sandalpur belonged to Izzatullah Chowdhury who had no issue and said Izzatullah Chowdhury brought up his relation's son Tofazzal as his foster son and Izzatullah Chowdhury got Tofazzal married with Khatemon in Baishakh, l346 BS, that Izzatullah Chowdhury sold the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule to Tofazzal by the registered kabala dated 25th, Falgoon, 1345 BS corresponding to March 9, 1939, that Tofazzal and his wife were living in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that since transfer Tofazzal Hossain had been in possession of the land of schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' till his death in 1353 BS and after his death Khatemon used to possess the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule through bargaders, that after the death of Tofazzal his wife Khatemon was Jiving in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury as his daughter-in-law, that Izzatullah Chowdhury died in Magh, 1366 BS, that a year before the death of Izzatullah Chowdhury, plaintiff No. 2 i.e. Khatemon was driven out from the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury by the defendant No.4 claiming himself to be the Ammoktar of lzzatullah Chowdhury, that having been driven out plaintiff No. 2 took shelter in the house of her father and started a criminal case against the defendant No. 4 and some others and they were convicted, but were acquitted by the appellate Court and at that stage trouble arose between the parties over the possession of the land of schedule 'Ka', 'Kha' and 'Ga', that at the instance of plaintiff No. 2 a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was stated but later on same was converted into a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the properties of the aforementioned three schedules were attached and management thereof was given to the receiver appointed by the Court. In the aforesaid circumstance plaintiffs who are the heirs of Tofazzal filed the suit seeking relief as stated hereinbefore.</u>

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 4, 11, 12 and 13 by filing joint written statement stating, inter alia, that Izzatullah Chowdhury purchased the land of 'Ka' schedule in a rent sale in the benami of plaintiff No. 2, wife of Tofazzal Hossain (since deceased) who was foster son of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that lzzatullah Chowdhury was the real owner of the property, described in schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' and he created a benami deed in respect of the land of said 2 schedules in the name of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain in fear of Marwari creditors, that the sale in favour of Tofazzal Hossain in respect of the land of 'Kha' and Ga' schedule was never acted upon, nor it was treated as a deed of transfer by any of the parties to the deed, that Izzatullah Chowdhury during his lifetime was in possession of all the disputed property through bargaders, that plaintiff No. 2 while staying in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury as widow of his foster son, Tofazzal Hossain, fraudulently obtained possession of some original documents including the deed dated 25 Falgoon, 1345 BS, and transferred those documents to her father's house, that Izzatullah Chowdhury having had come to know of the said fact drove away Khatemon from his house about a year before his death.

<u>5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record relating to 'Ka' schedule land i.e. plaintiffs' case of purchasing the land of said schedule by plaintiff No. 2 and the case of the contesting defendants as to purchasing the 'Ka' schedule by Izzatullah Chowdhury in the benami of plaintiff No.2 held that plaintiff No.2 is the real owner of the land in 'Ka' schedule. The trial Court while considering the case of the plaintiffs and the defendants as regard the land of' Kha' and 'Ga' schedule observed that question of possession of the property will not be of very much help to ascertain the real title of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule. In the background of the admitted circumstances that Tofazzal Hossain till his death in 1353 BS with his wife Khatemon lived in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury and after death of Tofazzal his wife Khatemon lived in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury with children and, as such, "it is very difficult to distinguish the possession of Khatemon from that of Izzatullah Chowdhury", that question of inadequate consideration will not be a sufficient ground for taking the view that the transaction was a benami transfer since the transfer in question by Exhibit-l was made by a foster father in favour of his foster son, that passing of consideration as deposed by the scribe of Exhibit-1 in the proceeding under section 145 CrPC being of a professional deed writer in the absence of other independent witness cannot be relied upon safely and, as such, the matter or passing of consideration "does not help us much in determining the real dispute as to title", that the question of custody of the original document with plaintiff No.2 "does not help me very much in determining the real title" since from the evidence on record it is seen that PW 2's position in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury "was that of a mistress" so long she was there and in that state of the matter it is quite probable that she took Exhibit-l in her custody and for which trouble started between her and lzzatullah Chowdhury and finally, she was driven out with her children from the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that the motive for making benami transaction by Exhibit-1 could not be established since lzzatullah Chowdhury "had no substantial debt to justify a Benami transaction for fear of any Marwari creditor", that in the background of dealing with the property of Exhibit-l i.e. property of khatian Nos. 28 and 47, by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit- A dated 13-1-1944 and dealing with the property that Tofazzal's sister Amena Khatun got from lzzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A and dealing with the said property as reflected by Exhibit-A(1) and Exhibit-A(2) clearly indicates that IzzatuJlah Chowdhury "did never intend to make any bonafide transfer by the earlier kabala Exhibitl in favour of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain", that the subsequent transfers by the kabalas Exhibits A(1) and A (2) are bonafide trans- fers, that Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred the land of khatian Nos. 28 and 47 by Exhibit-A to Tofazzal's sister Amena to his knowledge and that transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury to Tofazzal's sister Amena was a bonafide transfer, that from the rent decree Exhibit- 3(b) it cannot be said that the said rent suit was in respect of the land of khatian No. 31, that there is gulf of difference between the rent decree (Exhibit- 3(b) and the transfer made by the kabala Exhibit-A, that the Exhibit-A reveals the con-duct of Izzatullah Chowdhury and Tofazzal Hossain who are parties to the kabala, Exhibit-l but the Exhibit-3 reveals the conduct of the heirs of Tofazzal Hossain after his death and that it is also not known what was the nature of the ex parte rent decree, that discrepancies in the body of the kabala and the schedule thereof (Exhibit-1) sufficiently indicates that lzzatullah Chowdhury "made no bonafide transfer by the kabala Exhibit-1 ", since a vendor always takes reasonable care as regard the land he transferred when the same is a real one, that Exhibit-B series dakhilas as regard the land of Sandalpur, the lands in dispute are in the name of Izzatullah Chowdhury and the same are "more dependable than the dakhilas produced by the plaintiffs in their names", that in the facts and circumstances of the case it can reasonably be held that Izzatullah Chowdhury never intended to make "any bonafide and real transfer by the kabala Exhibit-1 in favour of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain." On the aforesaid findings and decisions the trial Court held that "neither Tofazzal nor the plaintiffs acquired any bonafide title in the disputed lands of Kha and Ga Schedule." As stated hereinbefore the trial Court decreed the suit in respect of the land of 'Ka' schedule but dismissed the suit in respect of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule.</u>

6. The plaintiffs as against the part of the judgment and decree of the trial Court i.e. dismissing the plaintiffs' suit in respect of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule, went on appeal. From the defendants' side there was no appeal as against the judgment and decree of the trial Court decreeing the suit in respect of the land of Ka' schedule. The appellate Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court so far the same related to the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule on the findings that in the background of the materials on record, particularly evidence as to payment of consideration by Tofazzal Hossain in connection with Exhibit-1, the trial Court should have held that Exhibit-l is a valid document and the same was duly acted upon, that the trial Court, upon taking into consideration transaction made by Exhibit A, was in error in holding that Exhibit-I was not a bonafide deed of transfer and that it was not acted upon, that taking into consideration the fact that Exhibit-I was registered on 25th Falgoon, 1345 BS and Tofazzal Hossain married PW 2 in Baishakh, 1346 BS the contention of the plaintiffs that Exhibit- 1 was made for making provision for the future of TofazzaI cannot be lightly brushed aside, since in the background of the admitted position that Tofazzal Hossain and his wife, plaintiff No.2 stayed in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that plaintiffs having had established by oral and documentary evidence that Tofazzal Hossain and after his death his heirs possessed the land of Exhibit-1 and the said fact clearly established the fact that by Exhibit-1 Tofazzal acquired title in the land of schedule 'Kha'' and 'Ga', that Exhibit-3(a), the certified copy of the rent decree, also shows that Tofazzal Hossain exercised his right and title in respect of the land of khatian No. 28 i.e. land of the 'Kha' schedule, that evidence of DW 2 proves the possession of the land in suit by the plaintiffs through bargader, that plaintiffs have succeeded in establishing that Tofazzal Hossain exclusively possessed the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule and the fact of possession of the land goes long way in determining the real nature of Exhibit-1, that because of the relationship between the vendor and vendee low price, as in the case of Exhibit-I cannot be the ground for holding that the transaction was a benami one, that payment of consideration money as regard the transaction made by the Exhibit-I has been proved by Exhibit- 8, the deposition of the scribe, that the trial Court was not well founded to discard the evidence of the scribe on the view that evidence of the scribe of Exhibit-I was of a professional deed writer since "deed writers under all circumstances do not depose falsely", that contention of the defendants that plaintiff No. 2 for illegal gain took away the Exhibit-l is nothing but a device "to nullify the effect of evidentiary value regarding custody of original document", that from the evidence of DWs it is seen that Izzatullah Chowdhury had no substantial debt upon borrowing from Marwari and, as such, the contention of the defendants that to put away the property or Exhibit-1 from the clutch of the creditor Izzatullah Chowdhury made Exhibit-1 is of no merit, that taking into consideration the fact of payment of consideration money by Tofazzal for the transaction evidenced by Exhibit-1 and possession of the land of Exhibit-1 by Tofazzal Hossain and after him his heirs and payment of rent to the Zamindar as well as to the Government by Tofazzal Hossain and his heirs and failure on the part of the defendants to prove that Exhibit-1 is a benami document, the only conclusion is that "kabala (Exhibit-1) is a bonafide, valid and active document. In fact, it operated to pass title in favour of Tofazzal," that presence of Tofazzal Hossain in the office of sub-Registrar on the date when by Exhibit-A, Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred 2.40½ acres of land of Exhibit-1 to. Tofazzal's sister, Arnena and by Exhibit-1 (a) Amena transferred land to her brother Tofazzal does not saddle Tofazzal Hossain with the knowledge of the transfer of land of Exhibit-1 by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain, that the transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A and the transaction made by Amena by Exhibit-A(1) did not affect the validity of Exhibit-1 since the same has been found "a valid and bonafide document and title of the disputed land passed by it", that Exhibit-A executed by Izzatullah Chowdhury as regard the land of khatian Nos. 28 and 47 i.e. land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule, "cannot nullify the effect of Exhibit-1 ", that there is nothing on the record to show what prompted Izzatullah Chowdhury to make sham transaction by Exhibit-1 , that when motive for making benami transaction by Exhibit-1 could not be proved by the defendants and it having been established that Izzatullah Chowdhury for the future provision of Tofazzal Hossain made Exhibit-1, as such "it can be reasonably presumed that transaction witnessed by Exhibit-1 is a bonafide and real one", that the conclusion so made gets supported from the subsequent transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury to plaintiff No. 2's son, plaintiff No. 4 by Exhibit-4, that in the context of the fact on record it cannot be said that Exhibit-I was not acted upon, that in the background of the consideration of the facts and the circumstance, only conclusion that can be derived is Exhibit-1" is a valid and active document and Tofazzal acquired valid title to the land of schedule Kha and Ga by virtue of that deed" and, as such, plaintiffs have right, title and possession in the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule.

7. As against the judgment of the appellate Court decreeing the plaintiffs' suit in respect of the land of 'Kha ' and 'Ga' schedule, defendants moved the High Court Division in appeal, Second Appeal No. 162 of 1975. The High Court Division dismissed the appeal primarily taking into consideration the custody of the Exhibit-1 and production thereof by the plaintiffs and possession of the land of the 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule by the plaintiffs. The High Court Division while dismissing the appeal held that defendants failed to prove that the Exhibit-I was a benami deed, that the transferees defendant Nos. 12 and 13 from Amena cannot get benefit of the provision of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, since they failed to establish the ingredients of the said provision of Law, that defendants failed to prove motive of bringing into existence Exhibit-I by Izzatullah Chowdhury as they failed to establish that Izzatullah Chowdhury had debt to Marwari and the same having had remained outstanding and for that to save his property from the clutch of the Marwari lzzatullah Chowdhury created the alleged benarni deed Exhibit-1 in favour of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain, that the fact of transfer of homestead by Izzatullah Chowdhury to plaintiff No.1, son of late Tofazzal Hossain and transfer of some other land by Izzatullah Chowdhury to Tofazzal established the fact that by Exhibit-I Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule, that payment of rent by the plaintiffs to the Zamindar and the Government established the fact that they on the basis of the Exhibit-I and other kabalas upon assertion of their right possessed the land in question that preparation of the RS record in the name of the plaintiffs and payment of rent by the plaintiffs established the fact of possession of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule by the plaintiffs, that defendants could not prove that Exhibit-A was executed and registered by Izzatullah Chowdhury and, as such, by Exhibit-A ownership of Tofazzal Hossain in the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule was not affected, that question of benami is essentially a question of fact and that the lower appellate Court as the last Court of fact on consideration of the evidence on record and upon cogent and legal reasoning has made the decision that the Exhibit-I is not a benami deed.

8. Leave was obtained for consideration of the contentions that the subsequent conduct of the parties to the document Exhibit-I being material in deciding the question of benami the lower appellate Court was in error in leaving the subsequent conduct of the parties to the said document out of consideration upon a wrong view that Exhibit-1 being a valid document the subsequent documents being Exhibit- A series and Exhibit-B series in derogation of the right created by Exhibit-1 cannot nullify the effect of Exhibit-1 and the High Court Division was wrong in not taking into consideration the error of law com- mitted by the lower appellate Court.

9. The learned Counsel has submitted that High Court Division did not apply its mind to the point raised in the Second Appeal i.e. the lower appellate Court reversed the finding of the trial Court without adverting to the reasons assigned for said finding and the lower appellate Court was in error in not considering the Exhibit-A, the document by which Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred land of Exhibit-1 to Amena, the sister of Tofazzal Hossain, Exhibit- A(1) kabala by which Amena transferred her land to defendant No. 12 and Exhibit-A(2) kabala by which Amena transferred land to defendant No. 3 and the rent receipts Exhibit-B series showing payment of rent by the transferees from Amena and the evidence of DWs 1,3 and 4 relating to dealing with the property of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule by Izzatullah Chowdhury and Tofazzal Hossain subsequent to execution of Exhibit-1 and the lower appellate Court was in error in leaving out of consideration the aforesaid evidence led from the side of the defendants on the erroneous view that Exhibit-l being valid deed and bonafide document the effect thereof was not affected by Exhibit-A and the subsequent dealing with the property in respect whereof benami transaction was contended from the side of the defendants being an important test in determining the question of benami, the lower appellate Court was in error in holding Exhibit-l as a real and not a benami deed without taking into consideration the evidence regarding the dealing with the property in question by Izzatullah Chowdhury and Tofazzal Hossain subsequent to the execution of Exhibit-1.

10. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellants that Exhibits A, A(1) A and (2) are inconsistent with the plaintiffs case of denial of benami since those documents show that Izzatullah Chowdhury did not intend to transfer the property of the 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule by Exhibit-1 to Tofazzal Hossain and the said important aspect of the matter was skipped by the High Court Division as well as by the lower appellate Court on a view that Exhibit-1 is a valid and bonafide document, that the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court did not consider Exhibit-B series, particularly Exhibits B(1), B(2) and B(3), rent receipts showing payment of rent by the recipients of the Kabalas Exhibit-A(1) and A(2) executed by Amena who acquired the land so transferred by Exhibit-A (the land of Exhibit-A was very much the land of schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga) from Izzatullah Chowdhury and that there is absence of finding as to genuineness or otherwise of the said exhibits in the judgment of the lower appellate Court and in the judgment of the High Court Division. The learned Counsel has also submitted that the nature and character of the transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibitor, in other words, transfer made by Exhibit-1 was not a real one i.e. benami is reflected in the transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A i.e. transferring the land by Exhibit-A subsequent to the Exhibit-l which was made on March 9, 1939 and had Izzatullah Chowdhury in reality transferred the land of schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' to Tofazzal Hossain by Exhibit-1 then transfer by Exhibit-A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain would not have been made by lzzatullah Chowdhury within the knowledge of Tofazzal Hossain since he was very much present, as seen from the evidence on record, in the office of the Sub-Registrar on the date Exhibit-A was made.

<u>11. The learned Counsel continues that in the facts and circumstances of the case question of possession of the land of'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule for discarding the case of benami claimed by the defendants is not material since evidence is there that Tofazzal Hossain was the foster son of Izzatullah Chowdhury and after marriage Tofazzal Hossain stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury and that after death of Tofazzal Hossain his wife and the children stayed in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that the evidence as to payment of consideration as regard the transaction by Exhibit-1 or, in other words, about the source of consideration relating to transaction as evidenced by Exhibit-1 is of doubtful nature since evidence relied upon by the lower appellate Court about the payment of consideration as regard the transaction made by Exhibit-1 was of the person i.e. deed writer, about the fact which took place more than 22 years ago and in the usual and normal course of the profession in which the said person was engaged he was not supposed to be aware of the transaction which took place so long ago. It may be mentioned the evidence relating to source of consideration money as regard the transaction made by Exhibit-1 was certified copy of the deposition (Exhibit-8) made in a proceeding initiated under section 145, CrPC. From the plaintiffs side except the certified copy of the deposition of the deed writer made in the proceeding initiated as per provision of section 145 there was no other independent and corroborative evidence.</u>

12. The learned Counsel of the plaintiff-respondents submitted that the lower appellate Court on detailed discussions of the materials on record arrived at the finding that the document, Exhibit-I was genuine and bonafide and the said finding of the lower appellate Court having been upheld by the High Court Division, the said finding of fact sparingly interfered by the superior Court unless the finding is against the materials on record or in arriving at the said finding there was procedural error of law or that the finding arrived at was based on misconstruction of a document and misreading of the materials on record. The learned Counsel also submitted that none of the aforesaid situations being not present in respect of the finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court and affirmed by the High Court Division there is no occasion for interfering with the judgment under appeal. It has further been submitted by the learned Counsel since the Exhibit- 1 is a genuine and bonafide document and there being no provision in the same for revocation on the intervention of certain factor and, as such, even if there had been transfer by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A for that there was no revocation of Exhibit-1 and, as such, the right, title and interest of Tofazzal Hossain having not been affected by the act of Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A, the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs is very much in the land in suit as being the heirs of Tofazzal Hossain in whose favour right and title in the land in suit accrued on the basis of Exhibit-1.

13. The learned Counsel continued that, upon taking into consideration Exhibit-A and the transactions of the land acquired by Exhibit-A by recipient of Exhibit-A there cannot be a conclusion that document Exhibit-1 was a benami transaction, that transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A was hit by the provision of section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act (the Act) as well as by the provision of section 42 of the Act and that there has been an attempt on the part of Izzatullah Chowdhury to defraud Tofazzal Hossain by the Exhibit-A, that lower appellate Court as well as High Court Division having had considered all the accepted ingredients of benami transaction and' having .had found absent in respect of the transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-1 the finding of the said Courts that the transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-1 to Tofazzal Hossain was an out and out sale and that was not a benami transfer and as there has been no error of law by the lower appellate Court as well as by the High Court Division in arriving at the aforesaid finding i.e. the Exhibit-1 is a complete sale deed and thereby created right in respect of the land so transferred in favour of Tofazzal Hossain, no interference is called for with judgment of the High Court Division. The learned Counsel in continuation of the submission that Exhibit I is not a benami transaction has referred to the finding of the lower appellate Court that consideration money in respect of the transaction took place by Exhibit-1 was paid by Tofazzal Hossain that, the Exhibit-1 has been produced from the custody of plaintiff No. 2, that land transferred by the Exhibit-1 was possessed by Tofazzal Hossain in exercise of his independent right in presence of Izzatullah Chowdhury and rent was paid by Tofazzal Hossain and after his death his heirs and thus taking the aforesaid facts along with the fact that the defendants failed to prove that Exhibit-l was a benami document, there could be only one conclusion that Exhibit-A is a bonafide, valid and active document and that by the same title passed to Tofazzal Hossain. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondents since Exhibit-1 is a valid and bona- fide document and the title passed by the said document the subsequent transfer by Exhibit-A of the land of Exhibit-1 did not affect the validity of the Exhibit-1.

14. It may be mentioned at no stage of the suit or the appeals i.e. appeal before the lower appellate Court and the High Court Division it was never the case of the plaintiffs that transaction by Exhibit-A by Izzatullah Chowdhury was an attempt on his part to defraud Tofazzal Hossain. No material was brought on record that at the relevant time i.e. on January 13, 1944 there was any occasion on the part Of Izzatullah Chowdhury to defraud his foster son by making transfer by Exhibit-A in favour of Tofazzal's sister. lzzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit- A transferred 1.31 acres of land from khatian No. 28 and 1.9'/2 acres from khatian No. 47. No evidence has also been brought on record that relation between Izzatullah Chowdhury and his foster son had for any reason become sour or there had been misunderstanding or that there had been any incident whereby Tofazzal Hossain incurred displeasure of his foster father Izzatullah Chowdhury and that prompted lzzatullah Chowdhury to defraud Tofazzal Hossain by making transaction by the Exhibit-A. In that view of the matter we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Counsel for the plaintiff respondents that transaction by Exhibit-A by lzzatullah Chowdhury was an attempt to defraud Tofazzal Hossain. The other submission was that transfer made by lzzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit- A was hit by the provision of section 53 of the Act. The said submission is also of no merit since no situation as contemplates by the provision of section 53 of the Act was present in respect of the transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A in favour of Amena, the sister of Tofazzal Hossain.

15. It may also be mentioned no such case was pleaded from the side of the plaintiffs at any point of time except in the course of hearing of the present appeal. It may be mentioned that on the day transaction by Exhibit-A was made by lzzatullah Chowdhury his foster son Tofazzal Hossain was very much present in the office of the Sub-Registrar. The lower appellate Court has observed that because of presence of Izzatullah Chowdhury on the date Exhibit-A was registered he cannot be fastened with the knowledge of transfer of the land of khatian Nos. 28 and 47 to his sister Amena by Exthibit A. In our opinion, the view so taken by the lower appellate Court appears to be not correct if considered in the context of normal course of business, in that there is no material on record to show that Tofazzal Hossain was in the office of the Sub-Registrar for some other business and that his presence in the office of the Sub-Registrar on the date in question i.e. when transfer was made by Exhibit-A, was a coincidence since he had been in the office of Sub-Registrar for some other business other than the business that was transacted by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A. It may be mentioned Exhibit-I was executed and registered on March 9, 1939 and the Exhibit-A was registered on January 13, 1944. So it is seen that the transfer by Exhibit-A was made by lzzatullah Chowdhury about 5 years after the Exhibit-1. As stated hereinbefore no material was brought on record to establish the contention that by Exhibit-A Izzatullah Chowdhury tried to defraud Tofazzal Hossain. It may be mentioned lower appellate Court as well as the High Court Division while arriving at the finding that transfer by Exhibit-I was not a benami transaction took into consideration the motive, custody of the document, possession of the land as in Exhibit-1 and payment of rent to the Zamindar and the Government.

16. The undisputed position is that Tofazzal Hossain was reared/fostered by Izzatullah Chowdhury as foster son some time before the Exhibit-1 was executed and registered in Falgoon 13, 1345 BS and that Tofazzal Hossain after his marriage in the year 1346 BS stayed with lzzatullah Chowdhury and he died in 1353 BS and after the death of Tofazzal Hossain his wife and children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury till he drove away Tofazzal's wife in the month of Kartik, 1366 BS for the activities which were not liked by him and one of such activities was taking valuable documents from the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury by the plaintiff No. 2 to her parents' house. It may be mentioned Izzatullah Chowdhury died in the month of Magh, 1366 BS. It is on record that till the date plaintiff No. 2 was driven away by Izzatullah Chowdhury, she was the mistress of the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury and in that state of the matter it is quite probable that she had control over the management of the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury and also had access to the households of Izzatullah Chowdhury and, as such, it was quite possible for her to take Exhibit-1 in her control beyond knowledge of Izzatullah Chowdhury. This being the position the production of the Exhibit-I from the possession of plaintiff No.2 as was correctly considered by the trial Court cannot be considered the factor in the determination of the character of the Exhibit-1 i.e. whether the document Exhibit-1 was a benami or a sale deed.

17. The lower appellate Court as well as High Court Division while considering the nature and character of the Exhibit-1 took into consideration the question of passing of consideration in respect of the transaction took place by Exhibit-I and upon placing reliance on the deposition of Rahmatullah (Exhibit-8) in the proceeding initiated under the provision of section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but later on converted into a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It appears from Exhibit-8 that immediately after the death of Izzatullah Chowdhury in Magh, 1366 BS or, in other words, it can be said when he died in October/ November, 1959, the criminal proceeding under the aforesaid provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure was initiated in 1960 over the possession of the land in suit. The trial Court upon assigning reason discarded the deposition of Rahmatullah, claimed to be scribe of Exhibit- 1 who deposed in the criminal proceeding and the appellate Court upon discarding the reason assigned by the trial Court placed reliance on the evidence of the scribe that he has no reason not to tell the truth about the transaction. In our view, in a contentious matter it is hazardous to place reliance on the deposition of a single witness who has deposed about a matter of long past and in the normal course of business or trade of such person it is unusual for him to remember the fact he deposed. In that state of the matter we are of the view in the absence of corroboration of the deposition of the scribe, the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court were in error in arriving at the finding as to the nature of the Exhibit-1 i.e. that the said document was a sale deed and that same was not a benami deed. The High Court Division and the lower appellate Court in determining nature of the transaction made by Exhibit-1 considered the question of possession of the land of Exhibit-1 and for making decision as regard possession placed reliance on the evidence of PWs 3-5 and the documentary evidence, Exhibits. 2-2(d) as well as the Exhibit-2(J)-2(L). In our view, in the context of the facts and circumstances of he instant case the question of possession of the land in suit can in no way be made basis in making decision regarding nature and character of deed, Exhibit-1, i.e. whether the same is a sale deed or benami deed as because the undefined position is that prior to the execution of Exhibit-I.

18. Tofazzal Hossain was fostered by Izzatullah Chowdhury and after Marriage in the year 1346 BS TofazzaI Hossain till his death in 1353 BS with his wife stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury and after Tofazzal's death, his wife stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury upto Kartick, 1366 BS. In that state of the matter we are of the view the evidence of PWs 3-5 as to cultivating the land as bargader and delivering produce of the land to Tofazzal Hossain or to his wife or to his son cannot be the basis for coming to decision as to possession of land of Exhibit-1 by Tofazzal Hossain or his heirs because of the fact that after the death of Tofazzal Hossain his wife and children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury upto Kartick, 1366 BS and three months thereafter Izzatullah Chowdhury died in the month of Magh, 1366 BS.

<u>19. The payment of rent as claimed by plaintiffs on the aforesaid ground cannot be made basis for arriving at a finding about the nature of the Exhibit-1. It may be mentioned Exhibits 2(m) to 2(q) are not relevant for the present appeal since those exhibits (rent receipts) relate to the land of 'Ka' schedule. About the decree passed in respect thereof the present appellants have not taken any appeal. The lower appellate Court while considering the nature of the Exhibit-1 took into consideration the Exhibit-4 (the heba deed) by which Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred certain land to Tofazzal's son and also took into consideration the document by which Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred some agricultural land to Tofazzal Hossain's wife. The view as to the nature and character of the Exhibit-1 taken by the lower appellate Court placing reliance on the Exhibit-4 and another document, in our view, is not legally well founded since had Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred the land by Exhibit-1 to Tofazzal in that case almost after 4 years i.e. in 1944 he would not have transferred land of the Exhibit-I to Amena, the sister of Tofazzal Hossain. It may be mentioned the said transfer was made, in the background of the materials on record, within the knowledge of Tofazzal. It may be mentioned that whatever land Amena got by Exhibit-A i.e. the kabala made by lzzatullah Chowdhury in favour of Amena, she transferred the land of Exhibit-A on 2 occasions by the Exhibits A(l) and A(2) and the said transferees are in possession of the said land.</u>

<u>20. The learned Counsel for the appellant in support of his contention that Exhibit-1 was a benami document emphasised the subsequent conduct of the maker of the document i.e. Izzatullah Chowdhury, as demonstrated by Exhibit-A and in support of the aforesaid contention, i.e. subsequent conduct of the maker of the document which is being claimed as benami document, is material in determining the nature and character of the said document, has referred to the case of Nurjahan Begum vs Mahmudur Rahman Mallick reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 506 (same case has also been reported in 34 DLR (AD) 61). Therein it has been observed "but their subsequent conduct including their dealings and the enjoyment of the property become relevant factors for consideration". In the aforesaid case, it has also been observed : "In a benami transaction source of purchase money is an important criteria but it is not conclusive …..Source of consideration money though an important criteria in a benami transaction, but in the absence of an unambiguous ownership consideration of other relevant circumstances become important in a case where ownership is disputed. The disputed question of benami cannot be determined only on the consideration of source of consideration money, and it becomes incumbent for the court to fall back upon the surrounding circumstances of the transaction, the position of the parties and the relationship to each other". The learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court in determining the nature of Exhibit-l in the negative or, in other words, Exhibit-l is not a benami document but sale deed, did not at all give any importance relating to the subsequent conduct of the parties i.e. transfer of the property of Exhibit-1 by Izzatullah Chowdhury in the year 1944 by Exhibit-A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain. The learned Counsel as regard the matter of intention of the parties to the document Exhibit-1, upon emphasising the fact of transfer made by lzzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A. submitted had Izzatullah Chowdhury intended to transfer title of the property as are "in Exhibit-I to Tofazzal Hossain in that case he would not have dealt with the property later on by Exhibit-A. The learned Counsel also referred to case of Bhim Singh (dead) by LRs vs Kan Singh reported in AIR 1980 (SC) 727 wherein following observation has been made: "The second case which is loosely termed as a benami transaction is a case whether a person who is the owner of the property executes a conveyance in favour of another without the intention of transferring the title to the property there under. In this case, the transferor continues to be the real owner". It is the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellants since the Exhibit-A clearly demonstrates that Izzatullah Chowdhury had never intended to transfer the land as are in Exhibit-l to Tofazzal Hossain and, as such, the High Court Division as well as the Court of appeal below were in serious error in holding that by Exhibit-1 Tofazzal acquired title without taking into consideration the material fact as demonstrated by Exhibit-A that Izzatullah Chowdhury never intended to transfer title of the land as in Exhibit-l to Tofazzal Hossain.</u>

<u>21. In deciding question of benami in respect of a transaction matters of factors generally taken into consideration are, source of the purchase money, custody of the deed, possession of the property, motive for benami transaction, subsequent conduct of the person said to have made the benami transaction and the intention of the person as regard the transfer claimed to be benami and subsequent dealing with the property by the person who is claiming transaction as benami. In the instant case much emphasis has been given by the appellate Court and the High Court Division in arriving at the decision that the transaction made by Exhibit-I was a sale on the question of payment of money, claimed to have been paid by Tofazzal Hossain, upon placing reliance on Exhibit-8 i.e. deposition of the scribe of the deed Exhibit-1, in the proceeding as regard the property of Exhibit-I initiated under section 145, Code of Criminal Procedure. It has already been mentioned that except the evidence of the scribe (Exhibit-8), who deposed sufficiently long time after the transaction in 196 I on a matter that took place in 1939, there is no corroboration of the evidence of the scribe. It may be mentioned Tofazzal Hossain was the foster son of IzzatuIlah Chowdhury. There is no evidence on record that at the relevant time i.e. March 9, 1939 Tofazzal Hossain had any source of income of his own and out of which he had capacity of making payment of the amount about which the scribe of the Exhibit-1 deposed. It may also be mentioned it was the contention of the plaintiffs that Izzatullah Chowdhury for future provision of Tofazzal Hossain made the transfer by Exhibit-I. If that be so then the claim of passing consideration as deposed by the scribe of the deed does in no way fit in with the case of the plaintiffs that transaction by Exhibit-1 was made for the future provision of Tofazzal Hossain. We have noticed that after marriage in Baishakh, 1346 BS Tofazzal and his wife stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury and that after death of Tofazzal Hossain in 1353 BS Tofazzal's wife stayed in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury and it is on record that as Tofazzal's wife stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury she was in full control of the management of the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, in that state of the matter, she had access to every comer of the house. It is on record that Izzatullah Chowdhury having noticed that Tofazzl's wife was not faithful to the trust deposed by Izzatullah Chowdhury in her, he drove away Tofazzal's wife in Kartick, 1366 BS. In the afore state of the matter, it cannot altogether be ruled out as contended by the defendants that Tofazal's wife taking advantage of the trust deposed in her by Izzatullah Chowdhury she removed the Exhibit-1 and in the said state of the matter, she having taken control of the Exhibit-I came out with the claim over the property as in Exhibit-1. In the background of the facts and circumstances of the case, the probability of the custody of the Exhibit-1 as contended by the defendants with Tofazzal's wife cannot be considered of no basis. In that view of the matter we are of the view trial Court was quite correct in holding that custody of the Exhibit-1 is not of so much help in determining the real nature of the Exhibit-1. The other factor, as is taken into consideration to determine the particular transaction is benami of not, is possession of the property. The property as in Exhibit-l admittedly was of lzzatullah Chowdhury. Tofazzal Hossain was the foster son of Izzatullah Chowdhury and after his marriage he and his wife as well as children stayed with lzzatullah Chowdhury. In that state of the matter it can definitely be not said that possession of the land of Exhibit-1 was exclusively with Tofazzal. The plaintiffs tried to prove their claim of possession of the land of Exhibit-l through the evidence of PWs 3-5 but in the background of the facts as stated hereinbefore their evidence cannot be made basis for arriving at the decision that Exhibit-1 is not a benami deed.</u>

<u>22. Though amongst other circumstances possession of the property, which is claimed to have been acquired in a benami transaction or that the transaction which is claimed to be benami, is considered important and also relevant, but in the instant case in the background of the fact i.e. Tofazzal Hossain had no separate identity being foster son of Izzatullah Chowdhury and after marriage Tofazzal Hossain and his wife and their children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury and after death of Tofazzal Hossain in 1353 BS his wife and children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury upto Kartick, 1366 BS when Tofazzal's wife and children were driven away by Izzatullah Chowdhury. As it is the undenied position that Tofazzal's wife and his children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury till they were driven out from the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, it, with certainty and definiteness, cannot be said that possession of the property of Exhibit-1 by Tofazzal Hossain and after him by his wife and children was distinguishable from the possession which Izzatullah Chowdhury had in the property in question as well as other property. In deciding the question of benami amongst other circumstances the fact of subsequent dealing with the property of the transaction which is being claimed to be benami is also considered important. In the instant case it is seen that after execution and registration of Exhibit-1 by Izzatullah Chowdhury in 1939 in favour of Tofazzal Hossain in the year 1944 some property of the said Exhibit-1 was transferred by Izzatullah Chowdhury in favour of Tofazzal's sister and this shows the intention of Izzatullah Chowdhury as regard the transaction made by Exhibit-L Had Izzatullah Chowdhury in, fact transferred the property vesting title in Tofazzal Hossain by Exhibit-I then certainly he would not have gone for dealing with the property of Exhibit- 1 subsequently by alienation by Exhibit- A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain. It may also be mentioned whatever property was acquired by Amena by Exhibit-A, she transferred some thereof  by Exhibits A(1) and A(2). The transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A clearly shows that he never intended to vest any title of the property of Exhibit-I with Tofazzal Hossain. It may be mentioned that on the date of transaction by Exhibit-A by Izzatullah Chowdhury, Tofazzal Hossain was very much in the office of Sub-Registrar and this shows that transaction by Exhibit-A was made to the knowledge of Tofazzal Hossain and thus conclusion can logically be derived that Tofazzal Hossain was quite certain that by Exhibit-1 no title was vested in him in respect of the property of the said document. In deciding the question of benami intention of the owner of the property executing a conveyance in favour of another whether intended to transfer the title to the property thereby is considered a factor. It has already been seen that subsequent dealing with the property by the Exhibit- A by Izzatullah Chowdhury clearly establishes the fact that he never intended to transfer the title as regard the property of Exhibit-I to Tofazzal. In the background of the afore state of the matter, it can be said that transaction that was made by Exhibit-1 was a benami transaction.</u>

23. In the background of the discussion made hereinabove we find merit in the appeal.

24. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment of the High Court Division dated August 10, 1997 in Second Appeal No. 162 of 1975 upholding the judgment and decree dated April 20, 1974 in Other Appeal No. 175 of 1970 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Rangpur is set aside and thereupon judgment and decree dated June 23 of 1970 in Other Class Suit No. 45 of 1968 of the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) is restored.

<u>The Receiver is directed to hand over the property of schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' to the appellants i.e. the contesting defendants.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Dr. M Zahir with AY Masihuzzaman, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner 
M Nurullah with Kamal-ul Alam and AQM Shafiullah, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Nur Mohammad ------ Petitioner 
vs.
Agrani Flour Mills Ltd and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This is an application by the petitioner Mr. Nur Mohammad under section 38 of the Companies Act, 1913 for rectification of share register of respondent No. 1, namely, Agrani Flour Mills Ltd. hereinafter referred to as the Company.

2. The case of the petitioner, in brief, is as follows: The Company is a private limited company which was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 with 4 subscribers, namely: (i) Mr. Abu Taher, (ii) Mrs. Abu Taher (Rokeya Begum), (iii) Mr. Mostafa Kamal and (iv) Mr. Nur Mohammad the petitioner. It is alleged that the Managing Director of the Company respondent No. 2 Mr. Abu Taher persuaded the petitioner for better management of the company to sign some blank letterheads of the petitioner's trading company. After obtaining signatures on blank papers from different share-holders of the company respondent No. 2 and respondent No. 3 started acting arbitrarily in violation of the Articles of Association of the Company. It is stated that respondent No. 2 submitted "E" form of the company to the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies on 30th September, 1983 showing, inter alia, that respondent No. 3 Mr. Mostafa Kamal had transferred his 10 shares to the respondent No. 2 of the Company on 4.5.83 following which the said Mr. Mustafa Kamal lost his directorship of the Company. This transfer of share without first offering the same to the petitioner was illegal, null and void. It was alleged to be a sham transaction. The respondent No. 2 by submitting another "E" form in 1988 showed that the petitioner had transferred his 10 shares in the company to respondent No. 2 although the petitioner never transferred his shares in the company to anybody. The alleged transfer by Mr. Mostafa Kamal (respondent No. 5) of his 10 shares in favour of respondent No. 2 not being in accordance with the Articles of Association and law, and the petitioner not having transferred his 10 shares in the company to respondent No. 2, the petitioner by this application seeks rectification of the share register under section 38 of the Companies Act.

3. I will first take up the question of transfer of 10 shares by respondent No. 5 Mr. Mustafa Kamal in favour of the respondent No. 2 Mr. Abu Taher, the Managing Director of the Company. It has been argued by the learned Advocates for the petitioner that the shares of Mr. Mostafa Kamal were transferred to Mr. Abu Taher respondent No.2 in violation of the Article of Association. It is submitted that the transfer could not have taken place without first offering the shares to be transferred to all the existing share-holders including the petitioner. In this connection he has referred to Article 18 of the Association of the Company. He has further argued that he was a share-holder at the time when the said transfer took place and this is apparent from the Board's resolution dated 21st March, 1983 as shown in Annexures 4 which recorded in the minutes that the petitioner having informed that he would not be share-holder of the company and had offered to sell his own shares, it was presumed that he would not be interested to purchase the shares of Mr. Mostafa Kamal. It was also false that the petitioner had offered to sell his shares. Keeping these submissions made by Dr. M. Zahir in mind it may be convenient to refer to the relevant article of the association of the Company relating to the transfer and transmission of the shares in the Company. Article 16 of the Articles of Association of the Company provides:

"16. Shares may be transferred at any time by a member to his or her wife, husband, children or in the case of male shareholder to his mother, brother or brothers, sister or sisters only. Transfer to any other person other than those mentioned shall have to be made or registered by prior sanction of the Board of Directors only.

Article 18 of the Association reads as follows:

"18. No transfer of any share or debenture of the company shall be made so long any member is willing to purchase the same. The transfer or shall give one month's notice in writing to the Company and ascertain whether any member is willing to purchase the shares or the debentures."

It is clear from Article 16 that a member at any time may transfer his shares to any of his close relatives who is mentioned in the Article and no prior permission is required from the Board of Directors nor is necessary in such case to offer the share to any existing member. On the other hand, Article 18 of the Association provides that no transfer of any share or debenture of the Company will be made so long any member is willing to purchase the same. Article 18 of the Association, in my opinion, means that other than transfers made to close relatives as mentioned in Article 16 no share or debentures of the Company can be transferred to an outsider that is, who is not a member, so long as any member of the company is willing to purchase the same. In the instant case, Mr. Mostafa Kamal transferred his 10 shares to respondent No. 2 Mr. Abu Taher who is a share-holder of the Company.

4. Dr. M. Zahir has argued as the petitioner was a shareholder and stood pari pasu with Mr. Abu Taher, the shares of Mostafa Kamal under Article 18 ought to have been offered to him. I am unable to accept this interpretation of the learned Advocate, as such an interpretation could result in a dead-lock where the number of shares intended to be transferred by an existing share-holder was less than the number of share-holders of the Company and all the existing share-holders were willing to purchase the shares. So it is my opinion that there is no restriction under Article 18 of the Company to transfer share to any existing share-holder and the restriction relates only to a transfer to an outsider. In the light of my observations, I do not find that the transfer of 10 shares by Mr. Mostafa Kamal respondent No.5 in favour of respondent No. 2 Mr. Abu Taher was in violation of any law or Article 18 of the Articles of Association of the Company. So even if the observation of the Board of Directors in its meeting held on 21st March, 1983 that the petitioner had offered to sell his shares and had resigned from the Board and so it was to be presumed that he would not be interested to purchase the shares of Mr. Mostafa Kamal, was incorrect and false, it did not affect the transfer of Mostafa Kamal's shares in favour of Mr. Abu Taher.

5. I will now take up the question of the alleged sale and transfer of the 10 shares by the petitioner in favour of respondent No.2 Mr. Abu Taher. The petitioner has categorically stated that he did not transfer any share to the respondent No.2 Mr. Abu Taher. It is submitted that the petitioner has given lacs of takas to the company and he could not have transferred his 10 shares in the Company for a paltry sum of Taka 1,000.00. The respondent Company, on the other hand, has annexed certain documents to show that the petitioner had offered to sell his 10 shares in the Company and intended to resign from the directorship of the Company. Annexure-"X" is a letter written on a letterhead of Nur Hossain & Company signed by the petitioner Nur Mohammad as proprietor of the said Company on 26th July, 1979. By the said letter, the petitioner is alleged to have offered to resign from the directorship and to transfer his 10 shares in the Company. Pursuant to that letter a meeting of the Board of Directors was held on 28th August, 1979 whereby the resignation of the petitioner from the Board was accepted with effect from the date of the meeting. Annexure 4 to the affidavit-in-opposition is the minutes of the meeting of the Board of Directors of the Company held on 21st March, 1983 whereby it was, inter alia, resolved that whereas the petitioner Nur Mohammad, a share-holder of the Company had already offered to sell his shares in the Company, Mr. Abu Taher, respondent No. 2 shareholder of the Company shall purchase the shares of the petitioner. It was further resolved that Mr. Nur Mohammad, the petitioner be requested to execute the instrument of the transfer of shares and that the same be submitted to the Company for approval of the transfer. It is the case of the respondent company that the said Mr. Abu Taher, respondent No.2 had deposited Taka 1,000.00 as consideration for the transfer of 10 shares in the bank account of the petitioner which had been accepted and withdrawn by the petitioner from his account. The petitioner, in his affidavit-in-reply, had denied the receipt of any consideration money for his alleged transfer as he never agreed to transfer his shares. Annexure-"X", it appears, is a letterhead of Nur Hossain & Company and it has been signed by the petitioner as its proprietor. The signature of Nur Mohammad appearing on the annexure has not been denied. Prima facie it therefore appears from this annexure that the petitioner offered to transfer his 10 shares in the Company and resign from the Board although the letter is written on the business letterhead of a company whose proprietor is the petitioner Nur Mohammad. Nothing was done in respect of the transfer until the meeting of the Board of Directors was held on 21st March, 1983, (Annexure-4) i.e., almost 4 years after the alleged offer to sell the shares was made. It does not appear, however, that a cheque was issued on account of TS Corporation in favour of the petitioner's account which was deposited in the account of the petitioner which is alleged to have been withdrawn by him. It is, therefore, argued that the petitioner having accepted the consideration money, the shares of the petitioner stood transferred to respondent No. 2 and the petitioner, therefore, could not apply for rectification of the share register in respect of his shares. One thing that transpires is that there is no receipt showing acknowledgement of Taka 1,000.00 by the petitioner for his 10 shares. It is also not absolutely clear that Taka 1000.00 paid from the account of TS Corporation in favour of the petitioner's account was connected with the transfer of his shares although it may appear to be so from the circumstances. Now the question is, even if the position is accepted that the petitioner had received Taka 1,000.00 from the respondent No. 2 for the transfer of his 10 shares, whether such a transaction could in law complete the transfer of shares and the respondent No. 2 be accepted as owner of those shares. It has been argued on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner neither executed any instrument of transfer of shares in favour of respondent No. 2 nor he handed over possession of the share certificate to respondent No. 2 or to the Company.

6. With regard to transfer and transmission of shares Article 14 of the Association of the Company provides as follows:

"14. Subject to the restrictions of these Articles, shares shall be transferable, but every transfer must be in writing in any usual or common form or in such other form as the Board shall from time to time approve and must be left at the office accompanied by the certificate of the shares to be transferred and such other evidence (if any) as the Board may require to prove the title of the intending transferor"

There is nothing on record to show that the transfer of the 10 shares belonging to the petitioner was made in writing in any usual or common form. Sub-section 3 of section 34 of the Companies Act, 1913 provides for the transfer of the shares and reads as follows:

"34(3) It shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares in or debentures of the company unless the proper instrument of transfer has been duly stamped and executed by the transferor and the share certificate has been delivered to the Company along with the scrip:

It will thus appear from the sub-section that there are two things required for registration of the transfer of shares. One is the instrument of the transfer signed by both the transferor and the transferee, and the other is the delivery of share certificate itself. It has been argued that no instrument of transfer was executed by the transfer or and the transferee and, as admitted by the respondents in its Board meeting (Annexure-4), the share certificate was not handed over by the petitioner. In such circumstances, it is not lawful to register the name of the respondent No. 2 as the owner of 10 shares belonging to the petitioner. I find that there is nothing on record to show that an instrument of transfer was executed by the transferor. With regard to the share certificate I find that the Board in its meeting held on 21st March, 1983 (Annexure-4) admitted that the petitioner had not submitted his share certificate and therefore, resolved that the petitioner be requested to submit the same for approval of the transfer. There is also nothing on record to show that the share certificate of the petitioner was ever handed over to the company. Dr. Zahir has referred to Matter No. 37 of 1984 relating to Ulka Flour Mills Ltd. (a certified photo copy of affidavit-in-reply of the petitioner was submitted) where Mr. Abu Taher, respondent No. 2 as one of the petitioners, stated on oath that they (petitioners in the said matter) were the only share-holders of Agrani Flour Mills Ltd. and that the respondent No. 2 (the present petitioner) was one of its directors and he resigned on 26th July, 1979 due to his financial difficulties which was duly accepted by the Board of Directors but the present petitioner intentionally did not surrender the share certificate though he received Taka 1,000.00. This statement was made by an affidavit on 5.3.1986 and filed in the court on 3.5.89. Although the share certificate of the petitioner was shown to me by the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent there is no statement by the respondent that the certificate had been handed over by the petitioner. In the absence of any definite statement from the respondent about the delivery of the share certificate, and in view of the documents on record admitting that the share certificate was not delivered to the company or to the respondent No. 2 it cannot be accepted that the share certificate was in fact handed over to the company or respondent No. 2.

7. The question, therefore arises whether in the absence of instrument of transfer of shares it was lawful to register the transfer of the petitioner's 10 shares in favour of respondent No. 2.

<u>8. Mr. M. Nurullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 1 has referred to the case of Maheshwari Khetan Sugar Mills (P) Ltd and others vs. lshwari Khetan Sugar Mills and others reported in AIR 1985 (All) 135 where it was held that the procedure laid down for the transfer of shares in a company under section 108 was directory and not mandatory. I may quote section 108 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956 for convenience which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"108(1). A company shall not register a transfer of shares in or debentures of, the company unless a proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed by or on behalf of the transferor and by or on behalf of the transferee and specifying the name, address and occupation, if any, of the transferee, has been delivered to the company along with the certificate relating to the shares of debentures, or if no such certificate is in existence, along with the letter of allotment of the shares of debentures......................”</u>

<u>While considering this section, Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the above said case held: "When enacting section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 Parliament has not followed the wording of section 75 of the English Companies Act, 1948, and has departed from section 34(3), the corresponding provision of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended under the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1936, Parliament can therefore be deemed to have had in mind not to declare the non-compliance of section 108 as unlawful and illegal. As the law does not prescribe the consequences or does not lay down penalty for non-compliance of section 108 the provision can be considered to be directory and not mandatory. It is true that there has to be substantial compliance of a provision which is merely directory, but in cases not strictly covered by the provision the authority can deviate from that rule and take a decision which is equitable and fair to both the parties".</u>

<u>9. It was argued therefore that the law relating to transfer was merely directory. In the present case since the contract of transfer had been substantially performed the company rightly transferred the petitioner's share to respondent No. 2 and corrected the share register accordingly. Dr. M Zahir, on the other hand, has submitted that this decision of the Allahabad High Court in fact shows that although the transfer under section 108, the Indian Companies Act 1956 was directory as it did not make transfer unlawful in the absence of instrument of transfer, it would be unlawful under sub-section 3 of section 34 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 which is applicable in the present case. In other words, the provision of sub-section 3 section 34 makes it mandatory for a transfer to be accompanied by an instrument of transfer of shares. Dr. Zahir has gone further in showing that execution of instrument of transfer by the transferor or the transferee is mandatory even under section 108 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956. In this connection he has referred to the decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Mannalal Kheren vs. Kedar Nath Khetan and others reported in Company Case (In the Supreme Court of India) Volume 47, page 185 where it was held that the provision contained in section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956, that a company shall not register a transfer of shares in the company unless a proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed has been delivered to the company is mandatory in character. The provision of section 108 is emphasized by the negative language used in the section. The relevant portion of the judgment of the Supreme Court of India reads as follows:</u>

<u>"The provision contained in section 108 of the Act states that, "a company shall not register a transfer of shares.......................anless a proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed by or on behalf of the transferor and by or on behalf of the transferee.....................has been delivered to the company along with the certificate relating to the shares or debentures...................or, if no such certificate is in existence, along with the letter of allotment of the shares". There are two provisions to section 108 of the Act. We are not concerned with the first proviso in these appeals. The second proviso states that nothing in this section shall prejudice any power of the company to register as shareholder or debenture-holder any person to whom the right to any shares in, or debentures of, the company has been trasmitted by operation of law. The words "shall not register" are mandatory in character. The mandatory character is strengthened by the negative form of the language. The prohibition against transfer without complying with the provisions of the Act is emphasised by the negative language. Negative language is worded to emphasise the insistence of compliance with the provisions of that Act.................negative words are clearly prohibitory and are ordinarily used as a legislative device to make a statutory provision imperative."</u>

<u>In the instant case, sub-section (3) of section 34 is applicable which in clear terms provides that "it shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of Shares in or debentures of the company unless the proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed by the transferor and the transferee has been delivered to the company along with the scrip". The procedure laid down by the sub-section is clearly mandatory and not directory as suggested by the learned Advocate for the respondent. I have already said that there is nothing on record that an instrument of transfer was executed either by the transferor or the transferee for the transfer of the petitioner's shares in favour of respondent No. 2 and in the absence of such instrument, it is unlawful to register the transfer of shares by the petitioner in favour of respondent No. 2.</u>

10. Dr. Nurullah had referred to section 27 of the sale of Goods Act that the share being a moveable property, share stood transferred with the delivery of share certificate to the respondent. As I have already said that it has not been stated anywhere in the affidavit by the respondent that the share certificate had been handed over to the respondent or the company, and in the absence of such statement and the specific provision of sub-section (3) of section 34 of the Companies Act it cannot be held that share stood transferred by delivery of the share certificate to the respondent

11. In the light of the above observations and discussions, the registration of the transfer of 10 shares of the petitioner in the company to the respondent No. 2 Mr. Abu Taher calls for rectification.

12. In the result, the application for rectification of the share register in respect of 10 shares transferred by Mr. Mostafa Kamal, respondent No. 5 in favour of Mr. Abu Taher, respondent No. 2 is rejected. However, the application for rectification of share register in respect of sale and transfer of 10 shares of the petitioner in favour of respondent No. 2 Mr. Abu Taher is allowed. The company is directed to rectify its share register and register the names of the petitioner Nur Mohammad as owner of 10 shares of the company.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.
