parties:
Taferuddin Pramanik ------ Petitioner.
Vs. 
Tahmina Khatun and ors ----- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Kushtia, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 106 of 1968 affirming those passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Kushtia, in Miscellaneous Case No. 234 of 1966 and arises out of a proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenanacy Act.

2. The case of the pre-emptors in Miscellaneous Case No. 234 of 1966 was that they were owner of the land contiguous to the land under pre-emption. The same was sold by the opposite party No. 5 of that proceeding opposite party No., 1, the petitioner before this Court on 5-6-1965 for Rs. 2,000/-. The opposiie party No. 1, according to the appellant, was neither a cosharer nor a contiguous land-owner but was a stranger purchaser. The applicants came to know of the transfer on 24-8-1966. As such they have applied for pre-emption within the time prescribed, making the necessary deposit.

3. The transferee did not contest the case but filed an application to be added as a co-applicant paying for pre-emption. His case was that he was also the owner of the land contiguous to the land transferred and has homestead there. As such he is entitled to pre-emption in preference to the applicants. The applicants contested the claim of the transferee and contended that the transferee was not the owner of land contiguous to the land transferred and that this application is not maintainable in law and is barred by limitation.

4. The learned Munsif rejected the claim of the transferee holding that section 96(4) of the Act gives the right only to those transferees who are co-sharer-tenants to be added as co-applicants and not to those transferees who are owners of the land contiguous to the land transferred. On appeal by the transferee, the learned Subordinate Judge upheld the judgment and order of the learned Munsif, Hence this present Rule.

Mr. Md. Abdul Haque, the learned Advocate, appeared in support of the Rule and Mr. M. Behter Ali appeared on behalf of the oppossite party.

Since the matter involved an important question of law, Mr. M. H. Khondkar, the learned Advocate, was requested to assist this Court on the point as amicus curiae. Mr. Birendra Nath Chowdhury and Mr. Mahmudul Islam also appeared and placed their interpretations on the question at issue.

5. Section 96(i) of the Act gives a co-sharer of a holding or a contiguous landholder the right to apply for pre-emption. Such person has to file application for pre-emption within four months of the service of notice upon him and if no notice has been served upon him, within four months of the knowledge of the sale. Section 96(4) deals with the right of the remaining co-sharer tenants or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred to join the application for pre-emption within the period mentioned in, sub-section (1) or within two months of the date of service of notice of the application under clause (b) of sub-section (3), whichever is earlier. It is also laid down in the said sub-section (4) that any cosharer tenant or tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred who has not applied either under section 96(1) or under section 96(4) shall have no further right to pre-emption under section 96. Sub-section (1) of section 96 lays down that section 96, amongst others, shall not apply to a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by a purchase. In that view of the matter only transfer to a co-sharer by purchase or to a stranger falls within the purview of section 96.

6. Section 96(4) of the Act gives right to two categories of persons to join the application for pre-emption, (1) remaining co-sharer tenant including the transferee, if one of them, and (2) the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred. It has been argued on behalf of the opposite party that the legislature having specifically included the transferee co-sharer tenant in the category of remaining co-sharer tenants and omitting to include the transferee contiguous landholder from the category of tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, by application of the maxim of "expresslo unius est exclusio alterlus", it must be held that the legislature intended not to confer the right to join application for pre-emption as co-applicant to the transferee contiguous landholder, otherwise, after using the words "including the transferee, if one of them" in the first category, the legislature had no difficulty in using the said words in the second category. On the other hand, two-fold argument has been advanced from the bar in support of the contention that the transferee contiguous landholder will also have the right to apply under section 96(4) of the Act; (1) the use of the words "remaining co-sharer tenants" in the first category might have led to confusion as to whether a transferee co-sharer comes within the description of 'remaining co-sharer tenants' and as such the legislature expressly mentioned that the transferee co-sharer tenant will be included within the term 'remaining co-sharer tenants'. But as the words "tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred" normally include the contiguous landholder who happens to have purchased the land sought to be pre-empted the legislature did not feel the necessity of repeating the words 'including the transferee' in the second category;

(2) the aforesaid, maxim is not an absolute rule of interpretation and it cannot be applied when it works injustice or produces absurd result or when the omission is the result of inadvertence or accident. In this connection a passage from Maxwell's Interpretation of Statues (12th Edn.) at page 295 has been cited. The passage runs thus—

"But this rule, expressio unius, may not always provide the answer to the problem of construction. "It is said Lopez, L. J. "often a valuable servant, but a dangerous master to follow in the construction of statutes or documents. The exclusion is often the result of inadvertence or of accident, and the maxim ought not to be applied, when the application having regard to the subject-matter to which it is to be applied leads to inconsistency or injustice."

<u>7. It may be mentioned here that the language of section 96(4) of the Act is the same as the language of section 26F (4) (a) of the B. T. Act with an addition in respect of contiguous landholders and while enacting the provision of section 96 (4) of the Act the legislature adopted the language of section 26F(4) (a) of the P. T. Act which runs as follows:—</u>

<u>" When an application has been made under sub-section (1), any of the remaining co-sharer tenants, including the transferee, if one of them, may within the period referred to in that sub-section or within one month of the date of the application, whichever is later, apply to join in the said application;</u>

<u>It is quite possible that while adopting the language of section 26F(4) (a) of the B. T. Act, the legislature did not give sufficient attention while making the provision in respect of the contiguous landholders and the omission of the words "including the transferee" in the second category may well have been inadvertent and unintentional. Section 96 of the Act itself carries intrinsic evidence of such inadvertent omission. Section 96(5) (a) deals with the priority of right of different persons entitled to apply for pre-emption, but the legislature omitted to mention in the list of priority, the position of a co-sharer whose interest accrued by virtue of gift of exchange though such co-sharer has a right to apply for pre-emption. Furthermore, I do not find any logical reason for the legislature to exclude the transferee contiguous landholder from the category of contiguous landholder in section 96(4). The legislature does not deprive a co-sharer-tenant who happens to have purchased the land sought to be pre-empted from the right of applying under section 96(4) of the Act. The question of joining the application for pre-emption by a contiguous landholder arises only when the application under section 96(1) has been filed by a contiguous landholder. When the right to join an for application pre-emption has been given to contiguous landholder, it is illogical and hard to exclude the transfefee contiguous landholder from the category of contiguous landholder in section 96(4) only for the reasons that he has gone ahead of the other contiguous landlords in purchasing the land in question. The legislature can-not be ascertained as intention to produce an illogical or unjust result. A transferee contiguous landholder remains a contiguons landholder even which he he has purchased the land in respect of which application for pre-emption has been filed and in my opinion the transferee landlord cannot be taken to have been excluded from the category of contiguous landholder in section 96(4) simply because the legislature has not used the words "including the transferee" in describing the category of contiguous landholders I, therefore, hold that transferee contiguous land-holder is included in the category of "tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred" and he can maintain an application under section 96(4) of the Act.</u>

8. In the result, this Rule is made absolute. The Judgments and orders passed by the Courts below are hereby set aside and the case is sent back to the learned Munsif for deciding the same in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made above. In the facts and circumstances of the case I make no order as to costs. Let the records for the sent down expeditiously.

End.

parties:
Mosaddeque Hossain ------ Appellant
VS.
Dr. Esmat Mirza and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 3-2-97 passed by the High Court Division in FMA No. 199 of 1996),
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J : This appeal following leave by the preempted-appellant is from the judgment and order dated 3-2-97 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 199 of 1996, allowing the appeal and remanding the case for trial to the trial Court.

2. Zobaida Mirza, mother of the respondents, took lease of a plot of one bigha land being plot No. 555, Road No. 15(old), Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka from the then Government of East Bengal. She gifted the said plot to her husband Mirza Abdus Sattar on whose death the said plot devolved upon his heirs, the respondents, who amicably partitioned the same. 6.43 kathas out of one bighas fell to the saham of respondent No. 4. He sold this 6.43 kathas of land to the appellant by a registered deed of conveyance dated 18-3-96. Respondent Nos. 1-3 then filed a petition under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, shortly the NAT Act, for pre-emption of 6.43 kathas of land under transfer in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1996.

3. The pre-emptiee-appellant contended in his written objection that the Dhanmondi land being held by the tenant-respondents directly under the Government and section 85 (2) of the NAT Act having provided that "Nothing in this Act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government", the case under section 24 of the NAT Act is not maintainable. The trial Court took up this contention as an issue of law under Order 14 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the appellant and after hearing the parties by its order dated 6-11-96 dismissed the Miscellaneous Case as not maintainable upholding the contention of the appellant. Respondent Nos. 1-3 took an appeal against the said order, FMA No. 199 of 1996 to the High Court Division and a Division Bench by the impugned judgment and order set aside the order of the trial Court holding that section 24 of the NAT Act is applicable and remanded the case to the trial Court for disposal of the other issues in accordance with law. The pre-emptee is the appellant before us.

4. It was argued by the pre-emptor-respondents in the High Court Division, as the Division Bench noted, that the trial Court misunderstood section 85(2) of the NAT Act and failed to notice that a Full Bench of the then Dhaka High Court held in the case of Haji Aktaruzzaman vs. Jadunath Pal and another, 17 DLR 384, that the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the NAT Act has not been taken away by section 85(2). The High Court Division also noted the submission of the appellant, namely, that a plain reading of section 85(2) shows that the legislature meant to exclude land held by a tenant directly under the Government from the operation of the NAT Act. The appellant relied upon the cases of Munshi Golam Hossain Haji vs. Mohammad Abdul Hafez, 7 DLR 116, and Abdur Rahim vs. Sayeed Miah, 33 DLR 10. The appellant further submitted that if section 85(2) is read along with section 81A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the SAT Act, then it will be clear that the provisions of the NAT Act are not applicable to a non-agricultural tenant who has not become a tenant under the Government due to acquisition of rent-receiving interest of his landlord.

5. After noticing the aforesaid arguments of the appellant and the respondents the High Court Division proceeded to pronounce as follows:

"We have given our anxious thoughts on the submissions of the learned Advocates. We have read the decisions cited by them and the two sections quoted above several times. Thank God, we have been able to realise where lies the riddle. We are faced with an interesting, but simple question and not a tricky one as appears at the first impression.

The puzzle word is "tenant". What section 85(2) means by the word "tenant" contained in it? "Tenant" ordinarily means an occupier of immovable property, paying rent to a person who is generally called "landlord". This definition is not sufficient. There are two categories of tenant. One has the full ownership in the land ie it is transferable and heritable and the other has not. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was enacted for the first category and not for the second category. Section 85(2) speaks about the second category. If this section wanted to mean the first category, then it would have used the expression "non-agricultural tenant" instead of the word "tenant".

It is absurd to think that the tenants under the Government in the land within Dhanmondi Residential Area have got no right of pre-emption, but the tenants under the Government in the land on the other side of the Green Road have such right. Since the leasehold right in the land within Dhanmondi R/A is transferable and heritable and yearly rent is payable to the Government, its owner thereof is a non-agricultural tenant and not a "tenant" as maintained in section 85(2)."

6. The High Court Division then held that an application under section 24 of the NAT Act for pre-emption in respect of a land situated within Dhanmondi Residential Area is maintainable. The decision in the case of Abdur Rahim vs. Sayeed Miah, 33 DLR 10, was held not to be a correct decision and was overruled.

7. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission that the interpretation of section 85(2) of the NAT Act given by the High Court Division was wrong as it was based on conjecture and surmise, not on consideration of the scheme and objectives of the NAT Act and that such an interpretation is without any support either in logic or in the text of the Act. Leave was also granted to consider the appellant's submission that the appeal involves an important question of law of great public importance, namely, whether in the face of section 81 A of the SAT Act, the provisions of the NAT Act will be applicable in the case of tenants holding non-agricultural lands directly under the Government.

8. At the hearing of the appeal Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel appeared for the appellant as he did for the appellant before the High Court Division. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel appeared for the respondents, as he did for the respondents in the High Court Division. It is a common grievance of both the learned Counsels that the interpretation of the word "tenant" in section 85(2) of the NAT Act given by the High Court Division was not advanced by either side and the learned Judges also did not invite the attention of the learned Counsels as to their own discovery on the subject. Surprise was their common feeling when they received the judgment. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed even went to the extent of saying that the only pleasure he obtained from the judgment appealed against is that the appeal was allowed. The reasonings were not his and he would not support the judgment on the reasoning’s given by the learned Judges. He regretted that his submissions were not fully reflected in the judgment.

9. Here, therefore, is a case where the loser is aggrieved because he lost on a reasoning which was never brought to his notice in the Court and the winner is also aggrieved because he never wanted to win on the reasoning of the learned Judges.

10. Before we proceed to set down the respective arguments of both sides, it will be profitable to quote section 81A of the SAT Act which is as follows:

"81A. Rights and liabilities of non-Agricultural Tenants (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Part, the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act, shall, where the revisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, (EB Act XXIII of 1949) applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act.

(2) The rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants shall, except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Act IV of 1882)."

11. Section 85(2) of the NAT Act provides as follows:

"85(2). Nothing in this Act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government:

Provided that the right vested in a tenant by the provisions of this Act shall not be divested by the acquisition of the superior right only in the land by the Government."

12. It may also be convenient to notice the definition of the word "tenant" in section 3(2) of the NAT Act which is as follows:

"3(2). "Tenant" means a person who has acquired from a proprietor or a tenure-holder a right to hold non-agricultural land for any of the purposes provided in this Act, and includes also the successors-in-interest of persons who have acquired such a right."

13. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that the word "tenant" used in section 85(2) cannot be meant to refer to the definition of the word "tenant" in section 3(2) of the NAT Act, for section 3(1) provides that there shall before the purposes of this Act" two classes of non-agricultural tenants, namely, tenants and under-tenants. Hence the word "tenant" has been used for the purposes of the Act itself. Section 85 of the Act is with regard to bar to application of the Act to certain lands and to certain cases. Therefore the word "tenant" used in section 85 should not be understood in the sense in which it has been used in the definition of that word in section 3(2). The High Court Division has drawn, in his submission, an artificial, imaginary and untenable distinction between two categories of tenants under section 85(2), namely, one who has the full ownership in the land which will be transferable and heritable and the other not. The High Court Division has also held on surmise that the NAT Act was enacted for the first category and not for the second category and that section 85(2) speaks about the second category. The legislature having used in section 85(2) the expression "any non-agricultural land held by a tenant" the High Court Division was wrong, he submits, in holding that the word "tenant" in section 85(2) refers to a tenant of non-transferable and non-heritable land and not to a non-agricultural tenant holding non-agricultural land directly under the Government. Such an interpretation renders the proviso to section 85(2) totally unnecessary and a mere surplus age, he submits. It may also lead to an anomalous situation, namely, that the rights and liabilities of the tenants of premises belonging to persons other than the Government will be regulated and governed by the provisions of the NAT Act to the exclusion of the Premises Rent Control law. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that section 81A of the SAT Act being a later law and stipulating otherwise shall prevail over the provisions of section 85(2) of the NAT Act which shall be deemed to have been impliedly repealed.

14. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that it was his submission before the High Court Division which was not noticed and it is also his submission now that the first thing to notice is the definition of "tenant" under section 3(2) of the NAT Act which was enacted in 1949. Since in 1949 the Government was neither a proprietor nor a tenure-holder the definition of "tenant" in section 3(2) does not in terms apply to the word "tenant" used in section 85(2) of the Act. He submits that the word "tenant" has been used in section 85 (2) of the Act to mean a tenant of premises under the Government. It is his submission that section 81A(2) of the SAT Act by providing that except some matters that rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants other than those who have become a tenant under the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior right will be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, does not alter the position as under section 71 of the NAT Act the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act shall continue to apply to all tenancies to which the provisions of the NAT Act apply. His submission is that a land is held under the Government in various capacities but section 85(2) restricts the word "tenant" to only premises held under the Government.

<u>15. Having heard both sides in details, we find considerable force in the submission of Mr. Mahmudul Islam that the High Court Division has made an artificial and imaginary division between two kinds of tenants under section 85(2) of the NAT Act and has unnecessarily applied the word "tenant" to an imaginary second category. This interpretation cannot be supported by either tracing the history or the scheme of the Act itself. Nor do we find any reason from the scheme of the Act to apply the word "tenant" to tenant of premises under the Government, as Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has argued. Both the interpretations appear to us to be superficial and imaginary.</u>

16. Mr. Mahmudul Islam has produced before us a copy of the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1948 and informs us from the commentary thereof that before the partition of Bengal a comprehensive Bill regulating the rights of landlords and tenants in respect of non-agricultural lands was introduced and in the last Session of the Bengal Legislative Assembly the Bill was passed by it after referring it to a Select Committee. But it could not become law as it was not considered and passed by the Bengal Legislative Council. The same Bill containing the same provisions as in the previously-passed Bill by the Bengal Legislative Assembly with some minor changes was passed by the West Bengal Legislative Assemble on the 22nd March, 1948. It will be noticed that the same Bill was passed by the East Bengal Legislative Assembly in March-April, 1949 without any amendment in the Bill originally passed by the Bengal Legislative Assembly. But the West Bengal Legislative Assembly by the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1948 introduced a deviation in the definition of the word "tenant" in section 3(2) as follows:

"3(2). "Tenant" means a person who has acquired [a right to hold non-agricultural land directly under the State] for any of the purposes provided in this Act, and includes also the successors in interest of persons who have acquired such a right."

[The words in parenthesis are a departure from the originally-passed Bill].

17. It will be noticed that in our NAT Act, 1949 tenant means a person who acquires a right to hold non-agricultural land "from a proprietor or a tenure-holder", whereas in the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a tenant means a person who acquires a right to hold non-agricultural land directly under the State. The West Bengal deviation from the original Bill (which has been retained in our legislation) makes the scope and purpose of the two legislations diametrically opposite. Moreover, the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1948 has been made non-applicable under section 85(a)(c) thereof to various kinds of land "while such land remains the property of Government". In other words, once a land is leased out by the Government and the Government parts with its ownership, the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act comes into operation, but our NAT Act will not apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government. The distinction is very marked and obvious. In our country the Government obviously wanted to retain the right to control and supervise its tenants through the provisions of lease-deeds and Transfer of Property Act unencumbered by the provisions of NAT Act, whereas in West Bengal the scheme was to deliver the land to the arms of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as soon as the land ceases to remain the property of Government, as for example, by giving a 99-years'' lease as in the present case. The same Bill has taken two different turns in two adjoining areas.

<u>18. We asked the learned Counsels to enlighten us on what benefits or disadvantages will accrue to the Government lessees of Dhanmondi Residential Area if the entire Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is made applicable to them. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed made a thorough investigation into the entire Act and found to his dismay that but for the right of pre-emption under section 24, the conditions of lease under which Dhanmondi lands are held by the lessees will come into direct conflict with some of the provisions of the NAT Act which may adversely affect the lease itself. This exercise re-enforces Mr. Mahmudul Islam's view, which we endorse, that the object of section 85(2) of the Act was to retain control over non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government unencumbered by the provisions of the NAT Act. Section 81A(2) stated positively how the rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants other than those who have become tenants under the Government by virtue of compulsory acquisition of land shall be determined. The NAT Act has not been mentioned to be a governing law in respect of such tenants of non-agricultural land under the Government. Hence, on both accounts, under section 85(2) of the NAT Act and section 81A(2) of the SAT Act, the ouster of NAT Act from the categories mentioned therein are complete. Section 24 of the NAT Act has no manner of application to lands of Dhanmondi Residential Area.</u>

19.For all the above reasons we disapprove of the view taken by the High Court Division in the matter.

The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.
