full_judgment:
This Application as filed in 1994 under section 38 of the Companies Act, 1913 for a rectification of share register has finally come to be disposed of fourteen years later by this Court under circumstances where it now falls under the purview of section 43 of the Companies Act, 1994 ("the Act").

2. This Matter arises in the context of facts and issues pertaining to the respondent No.1 MM Ispahani Ltd. ("the Company") that straddle several decades of corporate history that follows a historical timeline beginning from the second decade of the 20th century to the present date. It is also simultaneously a case of the fluctuating fortunes of a corporate entity that has had to face the exigencies of sub-continental politics and state formation as evident in the Partition of the Sub-Continent in 1947 and the emergence of Bangladesh in 1971. It is evident that the vicissitudes of Pakistan's internal politics, the independence of Bangladesh in 1971 and the Bangladeshi political scenario up until at least the late-1980s has come to bear upon the Company and its promoters by sheer reason of their ethnic heritage. That factor has had a considerable role to play in the facts of this case.

3. It is in the above context that this Court now embarks upon considering this Matter as begins with the entrepreneurship of three brothers, namely (1) Mirza Ahmed Ispahani, (2) Mirza Mahmood Ispahani and (3) Mirza Abol Hassan Ispahani (hereinafter referred to as "MAI", "MMI" and "MAHI" respectively and the "Three Patriarchs" collectively). These three siblings, who carried on a successful trading business as a partnership concern in Calcutta in the 1920s and 1930s, transformed that partnership concern into a company limited by shares, i.e., the Company, as both incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 in 1934 wherein MAI had 32 old paisa share equivalent to about 50%, MAHI had 17 old paisa share equivalent to about 26% and MMI had 15 old paisa share equivalent to about 24% in the share structure of the Company. The growing fortunes of the Company led to it emerging as the parent company to a progressively expanding group of companies engaged in the commercial and industrial sectors all over British India. The Company is said to have been converted from a private to a public limited company on. 10-7-1947 with the majority of the shareholding still remaining with the families of the Three Patriarchs. It is shown that notwithstanding such transformation, the Company never actually shed its private character as a quasi-partnership entity and, in fact, has till today never made any offer of shares to the public.

4. The petitioner No.1 is the son of MMI and the petitioner Nos.2 and 3 are the wife and son respectively of the petitioner No.1. The petitioner No.1 has also a daughter named Mariam Ispahani who is, however, not a party to this case.

5. This Court deems it prudent to begin with events internal to the Company that took place in October 1971, ostensibly in Karachi, at a point in time when the War of Independence was raging in East Pakistan where the Company had established its principal place of business. It is the petitioners' case that the petitioner No.1, Mariam Ispahani and Ghamar Ispahani (wife of MAHI) came to be the beneficiaries of 2,000, 3,000 and 12,184 ordinary shares respectively constituting a total of 17,184 ordinary shares in the Company as evident by various share transfer forms executed by MAHI (Exhibit 5 series'). It is stated that these share transfer forms were originally submitted to the Company in November 1971 for the purpose of registration of share transfer by the Company, but to no avail. It is asserted that MAI, who was the Chief Executive of the Company in the mid 1970s, on the excuse of the political condition prevailing at the time explained the Company's failure to register the said share transfers assuring nevertheless, that he would attend to this personally at a more propitious time. The share transfer forms having accordingly, been returned to the petitioner No.1, he is stated to have thereafter reminded MAI on several occasions as to the outstanding process of registration only to be requested by MAI to be patient. In keeping with the prevalent corporate culture in the Company that allowed for the venerable Three patriarchs reigning supreme, and given that MAI, in particular, being the most senior of the Three Patriarchs in whom the family and others reposed absolute trust and who commanded obedience, the petitioner No.1 accordingly, showed great deference to MAI's requests.

6. In the meantime, and while the registration of the above share transfers remained outstanding, the emergence of Bangladesh in December 1971 led to the Company and most of its sister companies to be taken over by the Government of Bangladesh as abandoned properties in early 1972 under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It is noted that the Company itself was released from its abandoned status in 1974. It is shown that in the second-half of 1972 the Three Patriarchs the petitioner No.1 and the respondent No. 2 Mirza Mehdy Ispahani, son of MAI, assembled at a meeting in London where the respondent No. 2 is stated to have regretted his failure to correct an outstanding "imbalance" in the shareholdings of the family members in the said Company. The respondent No.2 is stated to have assured the petitioner No.1 and others present at the meeting that such imbalance in the shareholding would be corrected as soon as favourable circumstances made this possible. By way of a further assurance, the respondent No.2 is shown to have given an undertaking in writing duly signed by him assuring that the group shares would be corrected so as to reflect the following percentage of shares among the founder directors' families, namely, MAI 50%, MMI 25% and MAHI 25% of the shares of the Company (Exhibit '6'). Acknowledging that MAI was greatly instrumental in releasing the Company and most of its sister companies from their abandoned status after 1974, it is stated in the Application that as these were restored to private ownership between 1974 and 1986 MAI emerged as the new Chief Execute 2 Officer of the Company. It is also asserted that notwithstanding the above interlude of the Company's abandoned status, the essential character of the Company as a family business was never disturbed and that, in fact, between 1975 and 1986 no changes occurred in the shareholders' position in the Company with the exceptions of the transfer of qualification shares from MAI to one Mr SM Huq and another Mr EA Siddiqui so as to enable these two individuals to become directors of the Company. The year 1986 is of some significance in this case given that this was the year that MAI passed away. It is stated that so long as MAI was alive the members of the family felt assured that their interests were well protected. It is further stated that several times after the meeting in London in 1972 the respondent No.2 was approached by the petitioner No.1 but the former procrastinated on one excuse or the other in carrying out his commitments regarding ensuring a mole equitable representation of all three main branches of the family in the Company's share structure. It is contended that upon MAI's death the affairs of the Company came to be gradually taken over by the sons of respondent No.2, that is, the respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 in particular, who began to wield considerable authority. It is to be noted that of the other two patriarchs, MAHI had passed away earlier in 1981 and MMI later on 1-9-1991.

7. It is noted that while the MAI-branch of the family was predominantly resident in Bangladesh after 1971, the families of MAHI and MMI for the most part continued thereafter to be resident in Pakistan. The petitioner No.1 however, remained a director of the Company from 1971 to 1977. Thereafter, up until 1991 the peripatetic petitioner No.1 acted in an advisory capacity to the Company during the entire length of which period, as is evident from his deposition as PW 1, he divided his time between Bangladesh, Pakistan, Iran and the United Kingdom. It is stated that only after the petitioner No.1 returned to Bangladesh from Karachi in September 1991 upon his father's death on 1-9-1991 did he sense a notable shift in the power structure having already taken place within the Company with the Bangladesh-based MAI-branch of the family holding the reins of power and authority. It is at this point in time that the petitioner No.1 decided to take up again the matter of the imbalance in the share structure of the Company as was attempted to be addressed in London in 1972 with the respondent No. 2, but to no avail. The best that the petitioner No.1 appears to have extracted from the Company after some effort were lists of shareholders evident in various Forms-'E' Summary of Share Capital and Lists of Share-holders for the years 1970, 1987, 1989, 1990 and 1991 (Exhibit '4 series'). It is here that yet another development within the Company comes to light by reason that at this juncture on 2-8-1992 the petitioner No.1 addressed a letter to the Company putting it on notice of his right to some 14,283 shares of his late father MMI by way of transmission, given that the other five surviving legal heirs of MMI had relinquished their rights to these shares in favour of the petitioner No.1 (Annexure 'E'). That notification from the petitioner No.1 elicited a reply from' the Company on 1-9-1992 (Exhibit '25'), the con-tents of which are reproduced in their entirety herein below:

"Dated : 1-9-1992

Mr MMA Ispahani

Flat Nos. 3 & 4

Mansion Building Ispahani Park Moghbazar, Dhaka.

Dear Sir,

Please refer to your letter dated 2-8-1992.

We are surprised to read the contents of your letter mentioned above, as within your knowledge all the shares held by your father Late Mr Mirza Mahmood Ispahani in M/s MM Ispahani Ltd were duly transfer-red to Hussainia Trust on 15th February, 1989.

Thanking you.

Yours faithfully,

(NUM Humayun)

Company Secretary

MM Ispahani Ltd."

It is here that this Court is introduced to the Hussainia Trust (hereinafter referred to as the "Trust" as necessary), the revelation of the transfer of late MMI's shares to which is stated by the petitioner No.1 to have been a bolt from the blue at the time. This is because it was always the understanding of the petitioner No.1, and as substantiated by information received by him from the Company only a year earlier, that pursuant to the normal practice of share scripts belonging to the family members being retained by the Company for safe custody MMI's shares scripts together with other shares belonging to other members of the family including the petitioner No.1 were indeed, being so retained by the Company. In this regard, the petitioner No.1 has produced a letter dated 19-9-1991 addressed by the Dhaka Office of the Company to its Chief Accountant in Chittagong, and as copied, amongst others, to the petitioner No.1, as attesting to the currency of that situation at the time (Exhibit '20'). Copies of the Company's records as made available to the petitioner No.1 upon his request now revealed in particular that on 15-2-1989 the Company approved the transfer of a substantial share interest in the Company to the Hussainia Trust. In this regard, the petitioner No.1 was intrigued in particular to note that this and several other transactions as to shares by and within the Company were sought to be effected after the demise of the two founder directors, namely MAHI in 1981 and MAI in 1986.

8. It is pointed out that upon an examination in particular of the Form "E" Summary of Share Capital made up to 27-9-1989 (Exhibit 14(2)') it is evident that a large number of share-holders of the Company purportedly transferred their shares to the Hussainia Trust, a public trust created by a Trust Deed registered on 27-3-1964. It is shown that the objective of the Trust was subsequently modified by the respondent No.2 in 1986 mainly to benefit the Shia community in Bangladesh. The petitioners have found it curious to note that among the large number of transferors who are purported to have transferred their shares on 15-2-1989 to the Trust, there are those belonging to diverse faiths, namely, Hinduism, Christianity. Judaism and the Muslim Sunni sect while the respondent Nos. 2 to 6 who are Shia Trustees of the Hussainia Trust as well as major shareholders in the Company, remained apparently uninspired to similarly make any similar generous transfers of shares in favour of the Hussainia Trust. It is contended that this effectively bulk transfer to the Hussainia Trust on 15-2-1989 was but a device that had the intended effect of 98% of the shares of the Company being effectively controlled by the members of the family of the respondent No. 2 contrary to the understanding arrived at in London in 1972, thereby, disproportionately and drastically altering and reducing the extent of the share-holding interests of the other two branches of the family to a paltry collective 1.57%. It is now contended by the petitioner No. 1 that the fact of these transfers were, in fact, unknown to him at the time in his capacity both as a trustee of the Hussainia Trust and an adviser to the Ispahani Group of Companies by reason that these developments were deliberately hidden from him. In this factual milieu the petitioner No. 1 once again on 20-4-1993 (Exhibit 'D') formally submitted to the Company his request for a registration of the October 1971 share transfers, recounting the circumstances in which, given MAI's requests and assurances for such registration to be attended to personally by him at a more convenient and appropriate time, the said registrations had for long been held in abeyance. Given that a considerable time had elapsed since 1971 and also that MAI had passed way in 1986 the petitioner No. 1 now requested for prompt action and on his part assured the production of the original share transfer forms against receipt by him of the relevant share scripts held by the Company. The response elicited from the Company came in the form of a letter dated 17-6-1993 simply communicating, without further explanation, the directors' refusal to register the transfers (Exhibit '24'). In such a state of affairs the petitioners contend that the transfer of MAHI's shares in particular to the Hussainia Trust on 15-2-1989 (Exhibit '9' series), these being a total of 17,184 ordinary shares (pre-bonus shares) inclusive of the 2,000 shares transferred to the petitioner No. 1 and 3,000 shares transferred to his daughter in 1971, was done fraudulently. Given that the respondent Nos. 2 to 6 at the time of the making of this request were the members of the Board of Directors of the Hussainia Trust and also members of the Board of Directors of the Company they, thereby, secured to themselves the absolute control and management of the two entities for their own benefit notwithstanding the existence of the share transfer instruments of October 1971 in favour of the petitioner No. 1 and his daughter.

9. While on the issue of the Hussainia Trust, it is pertinent to note that approximately four years into the filing of this Application a development of some consequence to the petitioners' interests as arose in this Application took place within the said Trust. This is evident from the filing of the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition on behalf of the respondents dated 6-8-2000. The Company and the Hussainia Trust having at some point in time woken up to the legal bar against the Trust operating as a shareholder in a public limited company, addressed a letter to the petitioner on 12-5-1998 regarding the decision of the Hussainia Trust to return MMI's shares to his legal heirs as were otherwise stated to have been "donated" by him to the Trust (Exhibit 'A'). This process of the return of the shares of MMI to the petitioner No. 1 is shown to have finally been effected on 27-10-1999 (Exhibit 'C'). However, of greater relevance to the petitioner's claim is the manner in which the Hussainia Trust effected a transfer of the 17,184 shares belonging to MAHI. By a Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition on behalf of the respondents dated 10-4-2002 it is shown that by a series of transfers effected by the respondent No. 10 Hussainia Trust, and approved by the Board of Directors of the Company on 30-6-1998, the Hussainia Trust transferred the entire 17,184 shares of MAHI, inclusive of the 2,000 and 3,000 shares earlier transferred in October 1971 to the petitioner No. 1 and his daughter respectively, to the respondent No. 8 Mirza Iraj Ispahani, MAHI's grandson during the pendency of this Matter (Exhibit '11'). The petitioners contend that such transfer to the respondent No. 8, at least to the extent of a total of 5,000 shares otherwise claimed by the petitioner No. 1 and his daughter, is illegal and mala fide.

10. The petitioner No. 2 Ameneh Ispahani, wife of the petitioner No. 1, was also the beneficiary of a share transfer exercise in October 1971 in that 1,923 shares were transferred to her by the respondent No. 9 Mirza Zia Ispahani (Exhibit '5(4)') who is also a son of MAHI. It appears that these shares were somehow spared the share transfer exercise in favour of the Hussainia Trust that took place in 1989. The petitioner No. 2 is, however, aggrieved by the fact that in the following year, that is in 1990, the respondent No. 9 effected a transfer of the said shares to the respondent No. 6 Mirza Shaker Ispahani, a son of the now deceased respondent No. 2 (Exhibits '14' and '15'). The said transfers to the respondent No. 6 appear to have been approved by the Company on 30-7-1990.

11. The interest of the petitioner No. 3 Emaad Ispahani comes to be considered in this Matter by reason of his sister Mariam Ispahani in 1989 having transferred to him by way of an oral gift her 3,000 ordinary shares received in October 1971 from MAHI. Thereafter, the petitioner No. 3 presented the required documents including an affidavit dated 16-8-2004 sworn by Mariam Ispahani confirming the oral gift, in respect of the aforesaid 3,000 shares, on 2-10-2004 as were duly received by the Company (Annexures-'X' and 'X-1' to the Supplementary Affidavit on behalf of the respondents dated 12-11-2008). It is now asserted that till date the Company has neither entered the name of the petitioner No. 3 in its share register nor communicated any response to the request received in that regard from the said petitioner. It is also submitted that the cause of action as to these 3,000 shares also arose when the Company allowed the transfers of MAHI's entire share-holding of 17,184 shares by the Hussainia Trust in favour of the respondent No. 8 on 30-6-1998.

12. It is in the light of all these facts and issues leading to the filing of this Application in 1994, and the considerable developments thereafter, that this Court has now to consider the claim of the petitioners that, collectively and in its entirety, has come finally, and by way of an amendment of the Application (as reflected in the amended Paragraph No.29 of the Application) to be enumerated thus :

"(i) 2.215 preference shares (at the rate of 100 per share) inherited from MMI by the petitioner No.1

(ii) 14,283 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) 35,707 ordinary shares (post-bonus) inherited from MMI by the petitioner No.1 having succeeded hereto in accordance with the laws of inheritance.

(iii) 1,572 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) i.e. 3,930 ordinary shares (post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.3 from Mrs Fatima Sultan.

(iv) 29,435 ordinary shares (post-bonus) being the short fall (between 82,031 and the already recorded shares) to achieve 25% of the total paid up capital pursuant to the undertaking of the respondent No.2.

(v) 2,000 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) i.e. 5000 ordinary shares (post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.1 from MAHI in October 1971.

(vi) 1,923 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) i.e. 4,807 ordinary shares (post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.2 from the respondent No.9-Mirza Zia Ispahani.

(vii) 3,000 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) i.e. 7,500 ordinary (post bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.3 from his sister, Mariam Ispahani (who had acquired in October, 1971)."

These amendments, amongst others, were allowed by this Court's Order dated 4-12-2004.

13. The respondents have predicated their response to this Application on the general assertion that there is nothing on record to show that the shareholding of the Company shall be held by and be confined to the members of the Ispahani family or that indeed, the percentages of the holding of such shares by the three main branches of the family should correspond to the figures above as claimed by the petitioners. Asserting that there is no law or practice that the shareholding in any company must remain constant, the respondents submit that any change effected over the years in the Company's shareholding structure and ratio has been done in accordance with law. The respondents categorically deny the veracity of the petitioner's assertion that the petitioner No.1 Mariam Ispahani and Ghamar Ispahani (wife of MAHI) are the beneficiaries of 2,000, 3,000 and 12,134 ordinary shares respectively in the Company by virtue of share transfer forms executed by MAHI in October 1971 or that these transfer forms were originally submitted to the Company in November 1971 or that in the mid 1970's MAI informed the petitioner No.1 that due to prevailing circumstances the transfers would best be registered at a more opportune time in the future. In this regard, it is stated that the respondents have nothing to do on this aspect of the petitioner's claim given that this constitutes an affair exclusively between the transferor and the respective transferees. The 1972 London Agreement is also denied its legal efficacy by the respondents by submitting that any alleged assurance and commitment as may be read into either text of the alleged pact (Exhibits '6' and '6-1') are in any case meaningless and unenforceable in law. In this regard, the respondents consider as misconceived the petitioners' assertion that in his communication to the petitioner No. 1 of 2-1-1973 (Exhibit '21') the now deceased respondent No.2 gave an under-taking in writing that the gross shareholdings should be so corrected as to reflect MAI's 50% shareholding, MMI's 25% shareholding and MAHI's 25% shareholding in the Company. Thus, what the petitioners interpret as having spelt out the mode of implementation of the 1972 London Agreement is discordantly interpreted by the respondents as highlighting the impracticability of implementing that 1972 Agreement given the realities on the ground. Asserting also that the Company is run and guided by its Memorandum and Articles of Association, the respondents submit by that reason that it would be impossible for any particular branch of the family to assume control over the affairs of the Company. The entire rationale behind the 1989 bulk transfers of shares to the Hussainia Trust as well as the reversal of that process in 1998 is deducible, from the respondents' point of view from the Affidavit-in-Opposition on behalf of the Added respondent No. 10 Hussainia Trust dated 3-1-2005 focusing on the circumstances of the transfer to it of MAHI's shares. MAHI is depicted as an individual who had been residing outside Bangladesh prior to 1971 and who, seeing no prospect of his return to this country in the post-1971 period, is said to have gifted all his shares prior to 1971 to the Hussainia Trust. To that end MAHI is said to have handed over all his shares scripts to MAI who was both a founder trustee of the Hussaina Trust and a founder director of the Company. These transfers having eventually been registered in 1989 were subsequently undone when the Hussainaia Trust came to realise that it could not under the law retain any share-holding in the Company. That was the context in which the Trust by its letter dated 12-5-1998 informed the family members of then recently deceased MAHI of that state of affairs. In reply, MAHI's widow, son and daughter vide letters, all dated 3-6-1998, informed of the decision of all of MAHI's heirs to relinquish their interest in all of MAHI's shares with a view to facilitating these being transferred to and held by MAHI's grandson the respondent No. 8 Mirza Iraj Ispahani at the earliest (Annexures 'X-3' and 'X-4' of the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition by the respondents dated 10-4-2002). Accordingly, the Hussainia Trust is said to have transferred all of late MAHI's shares to the respondent No. 8 and handed over all the share scripts, the receipt of which was acknowledged by him on 18-2-1999.

14. A similar position is adopted by the Hussainia Trust regarding MMI, father of the petitioner No.1, who being in a similar position as his brother MAHI and of equal mind not to return to Bangladesh, is said to have similarly "donated" all his shares in the Company to the Hussainia Trust through the agency of his elder brother MAI (Exhibit 'A'). It is stated that when the time came for the Trust to undo the effects of the 1989 transfers vis-a-vis MMI's shares, the Hussainia Trust on 12-5-1998 addressed the Exhibit 'A' letter to the petitioner No.1 informing him of the legal bar as operated in the Trust's shareholding interest in the Company and consequentially of its decision to return MMI's shares to his legal heirs. It is shown that upon information sought of the petitioner No.1 regarding MMI's legal heirs and those provided by the petitioner No.1, including the fact of relinquishment of interests in his favour by all the heirs of his deceased father on 12-10-1999 (Exhibits 'B' and 'B-)1'), the shares were eventually dispatched to him on 27-10-1999 (Exhibit 'C'). Additionally, on information provided by the petitioner No.1 in Exhibits 'B' and 'B 1' regarding his mother Fatima Sultan's transfer of her 3,930 ordinary shares to her grandson, the petitioner No.3, these were also returned to the petitioner No.3 by the Company on 27-10-1999 (Exhibit 'C'). Care, however, is taken by the respondents to establish in this regard that the 1989 bulk transfer and the reversal of that transfer process in 1998 are predicated particularly on the fact that so far as MAHI is concerned none of his shares were ever transferred either to the petitioner No.1 or his daughter Mariam Ispahani and do not constitute any recognition of the petitioners' claims to such of MAHI's shares as they contend were transferred to them in 1971.

15. Based on the above, it is evident to this Court that in view of the return of MMI's shares to the petitioner No.1 by the Hussainia Trust, and as accepted by him in October 1999, the claims enumerated in the Application as referred to above, i.e. (i) 2,215 preference shares (at the rate of 100 per share) and (ii) 14,283 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) and 35,707 ordinary shares (post-bonus) inherited from MMI by the petitioner No.1, and (iii) 1,572 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) i.e., 3,930 ordinary shares (post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.3 from Mrs. Fatima Sultan, are redundant as having already been satisfied and, therefore, do not now fall to be considered by this Court. It is with the remaining claims as above referred that this Court is now concerned.

16. Heard the learned Advocates, perused all averments and documents brought on record and the depositions of all witnesses.

17. At the very outset this Court has had to consider the submission on behalf of the petitioners as to the propriety and the standing of the respondent No.3 in his capacity as Vice-Chairman and the General Manager (Finance)-cum-Company Secretary Mr NUM Humayun to swear certain of the affidavits on behalf of the respondents. The learned Advocate for the petitioners Mr Akhtar Imam has referred in this regard to Article 140 of the Company's Articles of Association ("Articles") (Annexure 'A') which he submits is in evidence of the fact that the general, powers of management of the Company as vest in the directors are generally to be exercised collectively and that this read with Article 141(7) includes the collegiate power and authority to institute, conduct and defend legal proceedings by or against the Company. Indeed, the Articles allow for directors' powers to be delegated or for powers of attorney to be given for the exercise of such authority. Mr Imam has cited Article 146 in explaining that the directors may similarly entrust and confer upon the Company's Managing Director such of the powers as are exercisable by them under the Articles as they may think fit. Given these requirements, Mr Imam submits that the respondent No.3 in deposing as the DW 1 surprisingly appeared unaware of any authority that he may have had from the Company for either swearing affidavits or deposing on behalf of the Company. It is asserted that indeed, no such authority was ever granted him by the Company. That being the case, it is submitted that neither a Vice-Chairman nor a General Manager has any authority under the Act or the Articles to swear affidavits or depose on behalf of the Company as both Mr M Ali Behrouze Ispahani and Mr NUM Humayun respectively have attempted to do. The DW 1 having upon re-examination on this aspect on 15-4-2008 deposed for the Company as Vice-Chairman and later as Chairman that he and Mr Humayun in his capacity as the Company Secretary had inherent powers to represent the Company, it is submitted by Mr Imam that there is in law no such inherent powers recognised as exercisable by such functionaries. Therefore, there being an absence of any express delegation of authority to these two functionaries by Powers of Attorney and/or a resolution of the directors collectively operating as the Board of Directors in this case, the respondent No.3 and the General Manager (Finance)-cum-Company Secretary are contended to have consequentially so acted without any lawful authority as to lead to the unavoidable legal consequence of the failure of the defence case. Consequentially, Mr Imam submits that the petitioners' case sup-ported by the deposition of the PW 1 and as substantiated by the various Exhibits must be found to have succeeded in all material particulars. The learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1 to 6 Dr M Zahir has in response drawn this Court's attention to the provisions of Order XXIX, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("Code") in particular as allows for any pleading in any suit by or against a corporation to be signed and verified on behalf of the corporation by the secretary or by any director or other principal officer of the corporation who is able to depose the facts of the case. Dr Zahir submits that these provisions sufficiently explain and amplify the reference to inherent powers by the DW 1 in his deposition. In this regard, Dr Zahir has referred to the judgment in Ms Nibro Limited vs National Insurance Co Ltd reported in AIR 1991 Delhi, 25 as authority for the interpretation that Order XXIX, rule 1 as distinct from authorising persons mentioned therein to institute suits on behalf of a corporation merely authorises them to sign and verify the pleadings on behalf of the corporation. He submits that in this regard the respondent No.3 and the General Manager (Finance) cum-Company Secretary are in the clear by virtue of being such of the several functionaries contemplated under Order XXIX, rule 1 as having the authority to sign and verify pleadings as they have indeed done. Given such submissions, it does appear to this Court that the argument as to the ostensible lack of the authority of the above two individuals to so act is without merit. Further, for a proper understanding of the provisions of Order XXIX, rule 1 this Court has deemed it pertinent to probe into those of Order VI, rule 14 as require the signing of pleadings by a party and its pleader, if any. In the event of such a party being a juristic entity as a company it is inevitable that the pleadings shall have to be signed by some person or the other on behalf of the company. Order XXIX, rule 1, it is found, is intended to meet that contingency and its provisions as referred to above aptly facilitate that process. This Court, in this regard, has taken note of the Indian Supreme Court's judgment in United Bank of India vs Naresh Kumar and others reported in AIR 1997 (SC), 3 as upholds that interpretation and reading of Order VI, rule 14 together with order XXIX, rule 1 of the Code. The Indian Supreme Court in that regard observed thus in elaboration of such interpretation in paragraph 10 at pages 5 and 6:

"Reading Order VI, rule 14 together with Order XXIX, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure it would appear that even in the absence of any formal letter of authority or power of attorney having been executed a person referred to in rule 1 of Order XXIX can, by virtue of the office which he holds, sign and verify the pleadings on behalf of the corporation."

In this regard, it is found that the offices of Vice-Chairman/Chairman and General Manager (Finance)-cum-Company Secretary are sufficiently enabling to clothe such office-holders with the authority as enunciated above and consequently are declaratory of the absence of any infirmity attaching to these office-holders to sign and verify pleadings on behalf of the Company. In dwelling further on this aspect vis-a-vis the respondent No. 3 specifically, the significance of the respondent No. 3 being identified in the Application itself as a shareholder-director has not been lost on this Court. Equally significant is the fact that the petitioners do not dispute the status of the respondent No. 3 as either the Vice-Chairman or later the Chairman of the Company. That being the case, and there being nothing on record to show otherwise, the actions of the respondent No. 3 albeit with regard to the swearing of the affidavits and the making of depositions on behalf of the Company may safely be assumed to be authorised by the Company, thereby, consequentially binding the Company. This Court finds no reason why that assumption as endorsed in Freeman vs Buckhurst Park Properties reported in [1964] 1 All ER 630 should not be of application in these facts and circumstances. Given such circumstances, it does appear that the argument as to the ostensible lack of authority to so act of the respondent No. 3 is without merit. As a last resort, as Dr Zahir submits, it can always be satisfactorily argued that the respondent No. 3 in particular in his primary and basic capacity as a party in this Matter is sufficiently equipped to swear affidavits and to depose in this Matter as he has indeed done. With this aspect of this Matter out of the way, this Court now proceeds to consider the more substantive and contentious issues pertaining to the petitioners' claims as already identified above.

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioners Mr Akhtar Imam has impressed upon this Court that the claims and disputes in this case have necessarily to be examined in the context of the Company's distinctive corporate culture. According to Mr Imam, the Company is the product of business conducted by three generations of Ispahanis in accordance with standards established by the family elders being the Three Patriarchs who are MAI, MAHI and MMI. The history of the Company's evolution since the 1920s from a partnership to a private and, eventually, a public limited company is marked by the constant factor of family values reigning supreme in its internal administration. The centrality of this aspect within the Company's management culture is evident, for example, in the fact that even when the Company was converted to a public limited company on 10-7-1947, and since that date, it has, in fact, never gone for a public offer of its shares. It is also noted that mutual faith and trust predicated on a deference to hierarchical authority was always intended to be central to the Company's existence. This unique feature of the Company's internal makeup, Mr Imam submits, requires an appreciation of the fact that a company as the respondent No. 1 "is more then a mere legal entity, with a personality in law of its own". Referring to Ebrahimi vs Westbourne Galleries Ltd reported in [1973] AC 360 and [1972] 2 All ER 492, Mr Imam argues that in a case as this, this Court must allow, as the House of Lords found in the Ebrahimi Case, for a recognition of the fact that within a company there are "individuals, with rights, expectations and obligations inter se which are not necessarily submerged in the company structure." The House of Lords in the Ebrahimi Case recognised that in many cases, of which this Matter appears to be one, a company must necessarily be seen as something more than a purely commercial entity. A perusal of Lord Wilberforce's judgment in the Ebrahimi Case in this regard reveals that a Court may legitimately probe into the fact of a company being formed or continued on the basis of a personal relationship involving mutual confidence, an element that is found particularly in cases where an erstwhile partnership, like the respondent No. 1 Company, has been converted into a limited company. Accordingly, this Court deems it prudent to examine the petitioners' outstanding claims in the context of that corporate culture of mutual trust and confidence as generated by the authority wielded by the Three Patriarchs during their lifetime. In the facts and circumstances of this case, that enquiry must began with the 1972 London Agreement apparently entered into by or on behalf of the Three Patriarchs on 22-9-1972 to address an outstanding problem of an imbalance between the shareholdings of MAI, MAHI and MMI (Exhibits '6' and '6-1'). The contention of the petitioners regarding the London Agreement is that it reflects an assurance by the now deceased respondent No. 2, in particular, to attend to the rectification of then prevailing imbalance as to the shareholdings of the Three Patriarchs to the effect that eventually MAI's shareholding would stand at 50%, MAHI's at 25% and MMI's at 25% as well. The petitioner No. 1 as PW 1 has deposed that the imbalance so sought to be corrected was, in fact, created during the respondent No. 2's stewardship of the Company and that the respondent No. 2 in 1972 took the initiative to address the same with the consent and approval of the Three Patriarchs as soon as favourable circumstances permitted the same. Though the parties to this ostensible agreement may be read to have been alerted to the fact of meeting the exigencies of the time and securing their interests prospectively given that on that date the Company stood listed as an abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972 and there may have been a hope to see to a possible implementation of that agreement once the Company was released from its abandoned status, it is equally evident and, as Dr Zahir has argued, on that date as the Company suffered from an abandoned status it was not for any of the signatories to that ostensible agreement to deal with the shares of the Company as they proposed to do. Second, it is evident upon a perusal of the Exhibits '6' and 6'-1 that of the three family elders MAI appears not to have been a signatory to that agreement. It is probable that the compulsion at the time was for addressing the imbalance at a more propitious time either when the Company became de-listed as an abandoned property (as occurred in 1974) and/or upon securing MAI's express approval to the same. It appears that even before those eventualities materialised paving the way for an implementation of a finalised agreement, certain impracticalities appear to have been identified by the respondent No. 2 and as were communicated by him to the petitioner No. 1 by a letter dated 2-1-1973 (Exhibit '21'). Referring to the London Agreement, that letter expresses a need to further explore the feasibility of implementing the percentages of shareholdings as discussed the previous year in London given that certain confusion as to the exact share holdings of the Three Patriarchs needed to be worked out by reference specifically to various other companies and entities comprising the Ispahani Group of Companies and the extent to which any of these in turn would or would not fall within the purview of the London Agreement. Significant also is the fact that the letter declares MAI's displeasure with the terms on which the London Agreement appears to have been framed. It is in this context of the contents of the said letter that Dr Zahir has argued that the 1972 London Agreement having not been predicated on a clear understanding of which corporate entities would fall under its purview and having also ignored the interests of share-holders other than the Three Patriarchs and their immediate family members was per se unworkable. According to Dr Zahir, the 1973 communication to the petitioner No. 1 was merely an assertion as to probing further into the feasibility of such agreement at all materialising and no more. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary appearing on record, it does indeed, appear to this Court that no serious endeavour was made beyond 1973 to address and resolve the outstanding problems identified by the respondent No. 2 and that, in fact, the 1972 London Agreement was never implemented.

19. More fundamental has been the thrust of Dr Zahir's arguments that in these circumstances the 1972 London Agreement can only be viewed as the family elders ventilating their thoughts as part of their reaction to many of their business concerns, including the respondent No. 1 Company, having been declared abandoned by the Government of Bangladesh earlier that year. That argument, this Court opines, is of considerable significance to the other claims of the petitioners based upon the transfers of shares made by MAHI in favour of the petitioner No. 1, and his daughter in particular, as early as in October 1971. To the extent that MAHI is shown in Exhibit '6' as an active participant in the dialogue that took place in London a year later, Dr Zahir submits that from MAHI's point of view his participation in the dialogue was declaratory of his intention to forsake the transfer exercise that he may have initiated earlier in favour of the petitioner No. 1 and his daughter in 1971 and that the petitioner No. 1 shall by that reason be estopped from denying that inevitable consequence of the 1972 London Agreement. In other words, this Court is asked by the respondents to consider the 1972 London Agreement only to the extent that it reflects an expression of intent by MAHI to give the 1971 transfers of shares a go-by. Mr Akhtar Imam, for his part, has argued that the 1972 London Agreement rather than reflecting the initiation of a dialogue that may or may not have materialised eventually into a binding workable agreement, capable of being enforced by the petitioner No. 1 in particular, must instead be read as a mere confirmation of a previous set of oral agreements, such confirmation being evident in the signatures appended to the agreement by those concerned including the respondent No. 2. In this regard, Mr Imam has highlighted the fact that respondent No. 2 having himself signed the London Agreement, the terms of which, in fact, poorly reflect on his stewardship of the Company, amongst others, that by itself shows that the respondent No. 2 was earnest in implementing this genuinely entered into agreement.

20. Upon a consideration of the above, this Court has taken particular note of the contents of the Exhibit '21' letter of 2-1-1973 that belies Mr Imam's argument that the 1972 London Agreement was a final pact agreed and entered into by all concerned but possibly held in abeyance until implemented at a more propitious time. The weight of evidence on record and of the submissions above of Dr Zahir further exposes the weakness of Mr Imam's submission in this regard. By that reason this Court finds that the so-called 1972 London Agreement was, in fact, never fully executed or implemented, but rather in its exhibited form reflects a mere response amongst many of the family elders to meet certain exigencies and contingencies. That being the case, the said exhibited documents of 1972 cannot be said to have legally generated any rights and obligations that can be enforceable through the agency of this Application. By that reason, the petitioners' claim as found enumerated in the amended Application and as quoted above pertaining to a claim to 29,435 ordinary shares to achieve 25% of the total paid-up capital of the Company must fail. This Court will now consider with reference to the 1971 transfers of shares the residual effect, if at all, of the 1972 London Agreement to negate the 1971 share transfer process of its efficacy.

21. This Court takes pause here to note that this case is replete with currents and cross-currents of conflicting dealings in the shares as were the subject-matter of the transfers of shares in October 1971 against the backdrop of a fairly unsettled political scenario evidenced in 1971 and directly affecting the petitioners and the respondents albeit under a facade of trust and goodwill as well as deference to the wishes and actions of the Three Patriarchs during their lifetime. It is evident that with the death of the last of the patriarchs, that is, MMI in 1991, that facade crumbles.

22. A perusal of the Exhibit '5 series' in evidence of the transfers of shares as took place in October 1971 reveals that MAHI in addition to transferring the bulk of his shareholding of 17,184 ordinary shares to his wife Ghamar Ispahani (Exhibits '5' and '5-1'), transferred 2,000 ordinary shares to the petitioner No. 1 for a consideration of Rs. 2,00,000 (Exhibit '5-2') and to Mariam Ispahani for a consideration of Rs. 3,00,000 (Exhibit '5-3'). The latter two transfers appear to have been witnessed by the respondent No. 9 Mirza Zia Ispahani. For his part, the said respondent No. 9, also in October 1971, transferred 1,923 shares to the petitioner No. 2 for a consideration of Rs. 1,92,300 (Exhibit '5-4'). As noted above, Dr Zahir has argued that the 1972 London Agreement though not materialising into anything concrete had eventually nevertheless, operated to nullify the share transfers of October 1971. Mr Akhtar Imam has countered that argument by submitting that MAHI could validly enter into the 1972 London Agreement as his shares in the Company on that date still legally remained his to deal with and represent without at the same time taking away from the efficacy of the October 1971 share transfers.

23. Mr Imam has gone on to explain further the legal basis of his arguments to this effect which, in the view of this Court, has had far reaching consequences with regard to the continued availability of the benefits of the transfers to this date as claimed by the petitioners. At the very outset the relationship of the transferors and transferees appear to be bound by the very receipt of consideration money for effecting such transfers not only on the part of MAHI but also the respondent No. 9. It is this Court's finding that the spate of transfers in October 1971 witnessed both MAHI and the respondent No. 9 quite unwittingly setting in motion a process that bound the transferors and the transferees in an equitable relationship of trustees and 'ces tui que trust' respectively that would now be illegal and unconscionable for anyone to deny.

24. As enunciated by the Indian Supreme Court in R Mathalone vs Bombay Life Assurance Co. Ltd reported in AIR 1953 (SC), 385 the relation of a trustee and a 'ces tui que trust' is established on the transfer of shares whereby the transferee becomes the sole beneficial owner of those shares sold by the transferor in whom the legal title remains vested. It is the crux of such relationship that the transferor holds the shares for the benefit of the transferee. It was also found in that case by the Indian Supreme Court that within this relation-ship "equity clothes the transferor with the status of a constructive trustee and this obliges him to transfer all the benefits of property rights annexed to the sold shares of the 'ces tui que trust'." In the facts and circumstances of that case the Indian Supreme Court deemed it necessary to qualify the beneficial aspect of such relationship as accrues to the transferee 'ces tui que trust' by holding that the principle of equity as enunciated above cannot, however, extend to cases where the transferee has not taken active steps to get his name registered as a member on the register of the company with due diligence should in the meantime certain other privileges or opportunities arise like, for example, for a purchase of new shares in consequence of the ownership of the shares already acquired. The fact that in many instances even blank transfers of shares would not deter equity from recognising the beneficial owner-ship of shares of a transferee is recognised, for example, in the judgment in Ms Howrah Trading Co. Ltd vs Commissioner of Income-Tax, Central Calcutta reported in AIR 1959 (SC), 775 where it was held that even on the execution and handing over of a blank transfer certain equities arise between the transferor and the transferee pending a registration of such transfer with the company. Among those equities, the Court held, would be the right of the transferee to claim, for example, the dividend declared and paid to the transferor who is treated as a trustee on behalf of the transferee. It is interesting to note, and as appears in the opinion of this Court, to bear upon the facts and circumstances of this case, that the equitable relationship as above explained by the Indian Supreme Court was recognised in particular in the R Mathalone Case as being spawned of the principle of the general law of trust that a trustee must act in a manner most beneficial to the 'ces tui que trust' and he can retain no benefit to himself from the corpus of the trust estate or from anything that accrues to that estate subsequently. It was also recognised that the relationship between a constructive trustee and the transferee 'ces tui que trust' shall generally last until such time as the shares sold could not be registered in the name of the transferee.

25. Confining this Court's attention for the time being to the impact that the 1972 London Agreement may have had, as argued by Dr Zahir, to adversely operate to any of the petitioners' beneficial interests in the shares sold by MAHI and the respondent No. 9 in October 1971, it is not readily understood by this Court as to how that dialogue of 1972, as did not, in the view of this Court, ever materialise into anything concrete giving rise thereby to substantive rights and obligations, could nevertheless easily dislodge the equitable relationship created by the share transfer process in October 1971 between the transferors and the transferees. It is, therefore, this Court's finding that at least until September, 1972 MAHI, in particular, continued on that date to be the constructive trustee of the shares he sold to the petitioner No. 1 nothing MAHI may have done or executed pertaining to those very shares can be interpreted as otherwise than attempting at doing all that was beneficial for the petitioner No. 1 transferee 'ces tuique trust.' That principle would equally inure to the benefit of Mariam Ispahani as the transferee of 3,000 ordinary shares from MAHI. The question that now remains is, whether in the facts and circumstances of this case in general, and what has been termed by Dr Zahir as indolence on the part of the petitioners to secure the registration of the said transfers, such "indolence" operated at any material time to cause that equitable relationship to have dissolved or evaporated. Indeed, much has been submitted on the issue of delay on the part of the petitioners to even attempt at securing the registration of the transfers, the admitted date of any such attempt being 204-1993. Much will bear on this Court's construction of what may or may not be considered as indolence or unreasonable delay in this case, not the least of which would be this Court's appreciation as earlier noted of the corporate culture unique to the Company permitting of analogies to be drawn, as above explained, to the Ebraltimi vs Westbourne Galleries Ltd scenario but also significantly, of the Company's subsequent dealings in these disputed shares from the late-1980s onwards in the form of transfers to the Hussainia Trust. An ideal example of what this Court has earlier found to be this certain conflicting, yet almost contemporaneous, dealings in the disputed shares, arises in the context of certain oral gifts of shares both by MAHI and MMI made purportedly prior to the liberation of Bangladesh, that is in 1970 and attested to both by the respondent No. 8 Mirza Iraj Ispahani and the respondent No. 10 Hussainia Trust in their respective Affidavits-in-Opposition.

26. Much has been submitted by Mr Akhter Imam as to what the Hussainia Trust was intended to achieve by the bulk transfer of shares on 15-2-1989 and the fact that this was but a device for the respondents to secure to one branch of the family permanently resident in Bangladesh, that is the MAI branch, virtually absolute control of the Company by marginalising the other two branches of the family. It is also evident as earlier noted that four years into the filing of this Application the Trust divested itself of its shareholding in the Company. This Court is now concerned with the trajectory of events that led to the transfers, amongst others, of the disputed shares to the Hussainia Trust and the mechanism selected by the Trust, with at least the tacit approval of the Company, to secure a reversion of the shareholding interests in 1998. If the affidavits of the respondent Nos. 8 and 10 are anything to go by, it becomes clear that for a period of approximately eighteen years the shares, as ostensibly gifted by MAHI and MMI to the Trust, and pending the registration of transfers to the Trust were left with MAI for safe-keeping. Two factors become very important in this regard. First, that during that long period of time MAI passed away in 1986 and, more significantly, MAHI passed away in 1981. The other more significant feature, and as submitted by Mr Akhtar Imam, is indeed, the issue of the protracted process by which the oral gifts matured into actual transfers of shares in 1989. Circumstances in which the petitioners are now found to have been during that period attest, in the view of this Court, to their general regard to the wishes and requests of the family elders, as well as the petitioner No. 1 in particular, being gradually marginalised in the administration not only of the Company but of the Hussainia Trust, of which he at all material times was a trustee, and paint a picture of a state of disempowerment that cannot be ignored by this Court in finding on the element of purported indolence on the petitioners' part to register the share transfers of 1971. With regard to the latter aspect, this Court notes that the petitioner No. 1 in challenging his removal from the Hussainia Trust for lack of co-operation and as effected on 4-6-1992 has already filed a declaratory suit being Title Suit No. 266 of 1994 which is currently awaiting disposal at the appropriate forum. With regard to the former aspect, the situation prevailing in the Company as bore upon the petitioner No. 1, an intermittent resident of Bangladesh and a director and adviser to the Company with a large section of his immediate family being non-resident, comes across sufficiently clearly from the contents of his letter dated 20-4-1993 (Exhibit 'D'). This Court deems it prudent to reproduce below the

contents of that letter in their entirety:

Declaratory of the peremptory decision of the directors declining to register the transfer of shares as requested by the petitioner No. 1, this Court is in agreement with Mr Imam's submissions that it runs contrary to the provisions of Article 46 of the Company's Articles implicit in which is a requirement in the facts and circumstances for reasons to be clearly given to justify a refusal to register transfers of shares. More significantly, it is noted that at the time of the issuance of the letter on 17-6-1993 the Company remained silent as to any objection it may have had pertaining to the delayed presentation of the application for registration, a ground that has in these hearings emerged as a focal point of the respondent's case. Indeed, as Dr Zahir has submitted upon a query by this Court that even if legal presumptions can be said to attach to the transfer processes of 1971, those would stand rebutted by reason of delay and acquiescence as ruled upon by the Appellate Division in Tamizul Haque vs Shamsul Haque reported in 43 DLR (AD) 34. This Court notes that in that case the Appellate Division held that an application for rectification of a share register, being one not governed by any provision of the Limitation Act, 1908, fell to be governed by the general principle that it shall be filed within a reasonable time and not after an inordinate delay with the important qualification that what is or is not reasonable shall always depend on the facts and circumstances of a particular case.

<u>27. The Hussainia Trust appears, with hindsight, to have been a misadventure, but an important interlude nevertheless, by which the Company appears to have unilaterally decided upon by a process of selection as to who are the rightful owners of MAHI's shares. Interestingly, that selection came with the Hussainia Trust finding itself in a legal quandary as to the holding of such of MAHI's shares and good sense prevailing as to their due return to their owners, but curiously so, four years after the filing of this Application. Aside from the fact that MAHI and his descendants/successors-in-interest, for the most part, were non-resident at all material times, a fact as both instigated the oral gifts prior to 1971 and prevented for those being claimed even after MAHI's demise in 1981 by his successors-in-interests, no satisfactory explanation has been forthcoming either as to the actual existence of such gifts or, in the alternative, as to why upon MAHI's death in 1981 his shares, as were ostensibly being held by way of safe-keeping by MAI, did not go to his heirs by way of transmission between 1981 and 1989. Equally, there is found nothing on record to show that the Company followed objective standards and principles of law in addressing this problem of transmission by only in 1998 securing the return of MAHI's shares to the respondent No. 8 Mirza Iraj Ispahani with great deference to the communications and declarations received from Iran Rahim, MM Isky Ispahani and Ghamar Ispahani on 3-6-1998 (Exhibits '16', '16(1)' and 'C' respectively) that basically and collectively prayed for all of MAHI's shares then reverting from the Trust to be transferred to the respondent No. 8 Mirza Iraj Ispahani. This exercise of reversion faces the same legal difficulty as the 1972 London Agreement in that this reflects an arbitrary selection process not benefiting in any way from any express intent or declaration ever made by MAHI to the derogation of the interests of the petitioner No. 1 and his daughter Mariam Ispahani to readily dislodge the equitable relationship of transferor-trustee and the transferee 'ces tui que trust' that continued, in the opinion of this Court unabated even given the intervening circumstances of MAHIs demise in 1981. In this regard, this Court, also finds it difficult to find legally sup-portable the position adopted by the respondent No. 8 with the assistance of his immediate family members that he should be the ultimate beneficiary of the reversion process initiated by the Hussainia Trust in 1998 when prior to 1989 he and his immediate family were caught napping as to ascertaining their now much touted interests in the disputed shares. This Court has in this regard taken particular note of the inconsistency with which his paternal grandmother Ghamar Ispahani has come to his rescue several years into the filing of this Application as evident in her Exhibit 'C' letter of 3-6-1998 which in its tenor and purpose runs inexplicably discordant to her communication of 30-4-1994, and an affidavit dated 20-7-1995 confirming her individual status as a 1971 transferee 'cestuique trust' vis-a-vis MAHI and also regarding her objection at the time to these shares being subjected to a transfer to the Hussainia Trust in 1989 giving rise to a conundrum as to her true intentions that have not been sufficiently explained in this case. It is also this Court's finding that if, and as appears from the conduct of the respondents, the 15-2-1989 transfers to the Hussainia Trust were revoked as being void under the law, there is no reason why given the lack of any earlier and prompt action on their part with regard to the said shares prior to 1998, MAHI's descendants can suddenly rely on the said transfers of 1989 to have had a beneficial effect in the long run for them giving them an opportunity to undo the October 1971 share transfer arrangements. In this regard, it is this Court's view that no effect either good or bad followed from the 1989 transfers or from their undoing in 1998. It would follow therefore, that the 1998 developments called for the Company to ensure at the very least for a status quo ante to be restored, that is, calling in the circumstances that prevailed on or before 15-2-1989 with regard to the status of the disputed shares as well as the interests in those shares. Noting that as the beneficial owners of shares it was always open to the petitioner Nos.1 and 2 and their daughter Mariam Ispahani to register the transfers of shares, it is this Court's view that it was not for the Company to actively impede and raise obstacles to the exercise of that choice to register the transfers of shares. Implicit in the deposition given by the respondent No. 3 DW 1 has been the fact that the Company so created these obstacles by its singular mind-set to not to recognise under any circumstances the beneficial interests of the transferees of the shares of MAHI as well as the respondent No.9 Zia Ispahani. For example, the DW 1 in his examination-in-chief deposed that the request made by the petitioner No.1 in 1993 could not be met as the concerned shares had already been transferred to the Hussainia Trust in 1989. He also deposed against the prospect of revisiting that issue after 1998 on the ground of the absence of original share documents and of the share transfer forms not being stamped at all. It is not understood by this Court why the Company with some concerted effort with the petitioner No.1 could not duly address and resolve those issues. Thus Hussainia Trust transfers of both 1989 and 1998 are also shorn of much justification when the DW 1 in his cross-examination attributed the 1989 transfers to the failure on the part of MAHI's heirs to apply to the Company to enter their names in the share register in respect of MAHI's shares. Acknowledging that the 1989 transfers were effected without the express consent of MAHI's heirs, the DW 1 appears to somehow address that lapse by stating that these shares were eventually returned to these very heirs in 1998. The deposition above, in the view of this Court, represents the single-mindedness with which the Company never took into account the possibility of the beneficial interests of the 1971 transfers having survived the contingencies that have appeared in the path of those interests starting from the 1972-1974 period of the abandoned status of the Company and continuing all through the inaction on behalf of the Company under the stewardship of MAI at least up until his demise in 1986 to accede to the requests of the petitioner No.1 to facilitate such registration, as well as the nine-year period that elapsed between 1989 and 1998 when the Hussainia Trust wrongly lay claim to a legal ownership of those very shares. All these factors collectively clothed the petitioner No.1, in particular, at all material dates with the characteristic of disempowerment that this Court is inclined to take into account in deter-mining the reasonableness of the delay in actively seeking registration of the transferred shares. These supervening circumstances, unavoidable to a great extent, must be read as mitigating any indolence, if any, that can be attributed in the facts and circumstances to the petitioners in general in this regard. The other mitigating factors, more positive in their nature and as pointed out by Mr Akhtar Imam, show that several years prior to the filing of this Application in 1994 the petitioner No.1, in particular, actively pursued the matter of registration with the Company. In this regard, the petitioner is shown to have been under the impression, and as late as till September 1991, that MAHI continued to be a shareholder in the Company. An internal memo generated within the Company dated 19-9-1991 and copied to the petitioner No.1 (Exhibit '20') substantiates that impression created and implicit in that memo is a representation that MAHI's and MMI's shares were not transferred to the Hussainia Trust at all. This is the necessary context in which this Court has examined the contents of the communication of the petitioner No.1 to the Company dated 2-8-1992 in which he notified the Company of his father's passing away on 1-9-1991 and consequentially brought in a claim to his father's shares (Annexure 'E'). The response from the Company came in the form of a letter dated 1-9-1992 expressing surprise at the ignorance of the petitioner No.1 as to the fact of the transfers of MMI's shares to the Hussainina Trust on 15-2-1989 (Exhibit '25'). This proved to be the turning point in the trust that the petitioner No.1 had thus far reposed in the Company and made him embark on a process of enquiry and examination of the Company's annual summaries of share capital. That revealed to him the reality of the 1989 transfers and as expressed in his communication of 21-9-1992 to the Company (Annexure 'G'). The Company's unhelpful response having followed on 10-12-1992 the petitioner, thereafter, sent the above-referred letter of 20-4-1993 followed by a legal notice of 25-5-1993 (Exhibit '28').</u>

28. On the basis of the above, this Court remains unconvinced that the petitioner No.1, marginalised as he then was within the administrative structure of the Company, did not take prudent and active steps to ascertain his interests vis-a-vis the shares at the earliest available opportunity. It is noted that in pursuing his own claim the petitioner No.1 at all material times brought forth the claims of not only Mariam Ispahani but also of Ghamar Ispahani who were the other major beneficiaries of the 1971 share transfers. Fundamental to this Court's understanding and appreciation of the sustained and continued beneficial interest in the shares transferred to him in 1971 has been this Court's reading of the true objective and purpose of the equitable relationship that subsists between a transferor constructive trustee and a transferee 'ces tuque trust' pending actual registration of such transfer. That principle in equal measure must also be read as governing the relationship between the respondent No.9 Zia Ispahani and the petitioner No.2 Ameneh Ispahani concerning the transfer to her in 1971 of 1,923 shares. Mariam Ispahani equally benefits from such subsisting and substantive relationship notwithstanding the impediment that equally operated against her up until 1989 when she made an oral gift of her 3000 shares in favour of her brother MR Ispahani the petitioner No. 3. This Court fails to understand why a beneficial interest pending registration in the share register cannot be so transferred by way of an oral gift. As far as the Company is concerned it has already had a declared history of recognising oral gifts of shares and there is no reason why it should without further explanation and justification make a departure from the precedent previously established. Moreover, unlike the purported oral gifts of shares by MAHI and MMI to the Trust, the petitioner No.3 has at least produced before this Court an affidavit sworn by Mariam Ispahani on 16-8-2004 confirming the oral gift to her brother.

29. That being the case, this Court also finds that the beneficial interests and entitlements of the three petitioners must necessarily also extend to the bonus shares declared for the first time in 1990 at the ratio of 1:1.5, bringing the totality of post-bonus ordinary shares to 5,000 for the petitioner No.1, 4,807 for the petitioner No. 2 and 7,500 for the petitioner No.3.

30. In light of the above, this Court now finds that in the facts and circumstances this Application has merited intervention by this Court by virtue of its authority under section 43 of the Act only to the extent of recognising the following claims:

(i) 2,000 ordinary shares (pre-bonus) i.e. 5000 ordinary shares (post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.1 from MAHI in October 1971;

(ii) 1,923 ordinary shares (pre-bonus), i.e., 4,807 ordinary shares (Post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No. 2 from the respondent No. 9 Mirza Zia Ispahani; and

(iii) 3,000 ordinary shares (Pre-bonus), i.e. 7,500 ordinary (post-bonus) owned and acquired by the petitioner No.3 from his sister, Mariam Ispahani.

The other claims stipulated in amended paragraph 29 of the Application did not merit any substantive consideration for disposal by this Court on account of these claims having already been satisfied by the Company in 1999. The claim, in amended paragraph No.29 (iv) as ostensibly stemmed from the 1972 London Agreement, for reasons already stated, stands disallowed.

31. Accordingly, this Court hereby directs the rectification of the share register of the Company by cancelling and deleting all previous entries pertaining to the 5,000 post-bonus ordinary shares, 4,807 post-bonus ordinary shares and 7,500 post-bonus ordinary shares that are now found by this Court to beneficially belong to the petitioner Nos. 1, 2 and 3 respectively and to have the names of these three petitioners to be recorded in the share register upon such cancellation and deletion. This Court further directs the respondent No.1 Company to file pursuant to Section 44 of the Act a notice of the rectification of the share register with the respondent No.7 Registrar, Joint Stock Companies and Firms, within 15 days from the date of the issuance of a certified copy of this judgment and order. It is further directed that the respondent No.1 Company takes care for the names of the petitioner Nos. 1, 2 and 3 to be recorded against the share-holding interests as above recognised by this Court in this judgment in the next filing of its Schedule-X: Annual Summary of Share Capital.

32. In the result, the Application is dis-posed of with the above orders, directions and observations. Let the records received from the office of the respondent 9 No. 7 Registrar be sent back immediately.

33. Also, let the Exhibit '5' series share transfer forms received in their original be handed back to the learned Advocate for the petitioners immediately upon duly attested replacement true copies of the same being received by the Original Side Department. It is noted that the Exhibit 'A-1' notice minutes of the meeting held on 8-1-1989 of the Board of Trustees of the Hussainia Trust is being handed back to the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1 to 6 today.

There is no order as to costs.

End.
