parties:
Radha Shyam Sarker ------ Petitioner
vs
Nani Gopal Sen and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of defendant petitioner calls in question the legality and propriety of judgment and decree dated 18-3-1998 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, third Court, Dhaka, decreeing SCC Suit No. 5 of 1996.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 21-3-1996 Nani Gopal Sur predecessor of Opposite party Nos. 1-7 as plaintiffs instituted SCC Suit No. 5 of 1996 in the third Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka, imp leading the petitioner as defendant for ejectment from the shop room measuring an area 12' x 4' x 6' situated in holding No. 68 of Shakhari Bazar, Dhaka.

3. Plaintiff's case put in a nutshell are that the defendant was inducted in the suit premises as his tenant fixing monthly rent of Taka 400 to be paid within 10th of following month as per Bengali Calendar. Subsequently the defendant became defaulter in payment of rent and as such he instituted SCC Suit No. 8 of 1993 against him, which was decreed on compromise on 28-9-1994, and solenama was made part of decree. Accordingly rent was enhanced to Taka 500 effective from Ashwin 1401 BS and it was decided that the rent will be paid to him within seventh of the following month as per Bengali Calendar Defend tint paid rent irregularly up to Ashar, 1402 BS, thereafter he became a defaulter. Moreover, he has bonfire requirement of suit premises. Accordingly on 1-11-1995 he served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon defendant asking him to vacate the suit premises with the expiry of the month of Agrahayan, 1402 BS. On receipt of notice defendant failed to do so Hence the suit.

4. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all material allegations made in plaint contending inter alia that suit premises situated in the ground floor of Municipal holding No. 68, Shakhari Bazar, Dhaka, which is a six-storied building and besides the suit premises there are seven shops in the ground floor, of which one shop is under khas possession of plaintiff and rest are rented to different tenants. In 1973, he was inducted into the suit premises as a tenant at the rent of Taka 100 per month, on payment of Taka 7,500 to plaintiff as advance. Rent was subsequently enhanced to Taka 300 per month. Later on, for the cause of repair, he handed over possession to plaintiff and further paid Taka 32,500 as advance. Pursuant to agreement dated 28-7-1987. Afterwards, possession was restored to him but advance money for Taka 7,500 + 32,500 = 40,000, was neither adjusted nor refunded to him, however, he was paying rent regularly up to Ashar 1402 BS. Since Sravan 1402 BS the plaintiff refused to accept the rent. Since then he is depositing rent to House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 117 of 1985. He is not a defaulter in payment of rent rather his Taka 40,000 paid as advance to plaintiff is still lying with him. Moreso, plaintiff has no bonafide requirement of suit premises. Thus the suit having no cause of action is liable to be dismissed.

5. On the pleadings different issues were settled including issue of maintainability and issue whether defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent and plaintiff has bonafide requirement of suit premises.

6. The trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree decreed the suit. Hence the Rule.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for petitioner supports the Rule and submits that the petitioner is not a defaulter in payment of rents inasmuch as he paid rent up to Ashar, 1402 BS to plaintiff and since Sravan 1402 BS he is paying rent to house Rent Controller. He adds that terms and conditions of solenama of earlier suit has no legal effect, in the instant suit keeping huge amount of advance money with the landlord plaintiff. The Court below without considering the facts and legal aspects decreed the suit, which cannot be sustained.

8. In order to appreciate their submissions I have gone through the records and given my anxious consideration to their sub-missions.

9. The point for determination whether the impugned judgment and decree calls for interference by this Court.

10. On going to materials on record, it transpires that in 1973, defendant was inducted into the suit premises as tenant at the rent of Taka 100 per month by the plaintiff on receiving Taka 7,500 as advance. Subsequently rent was enhanced from time to time. Later on plaintiff took Taka 32,500 as advance for repairing of the suit premises and fresh tenancy agreement was made between them, on 24-7-1987. It is pertinent to point out that plaintiff filed to adjust or refund the advance money for total Taka 40,000 pursuant to the agreement dated 28-7-1987. Even then, defendant paid the rent regularly up to Ahsar, 1402 BS (Exhibit q series), when the plaintiff refused to accept the rent for Sravan 1402 BS the defendant sent it through money order on 6th Vadra 1402 BS (Exhibit 1). Afterwards the defendant is depositing the rent in House Rent Case No. 117 of 1985. Significantly, Taka 40,000 paid by defendant to plaintiff as advance is still 'lying with the plaintiff. On appraisal of evidence on record it appears that evidence of defendant regarding payment of rents, advance money etc are uniform, consistent and corroborative to the material facts. So the same are invulnerable to the credibility.

11. With this regard, sections 18(1), 18(5) and 19(1) of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 (briefly as Act, 1991) are required to be considered, which read as hereunder:

"18(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (IV of 1882), or the Contract Act, 1872 (IX of 1972), no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance and perform the conditions of the tenancy.

18(5) No tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of this section in respect of any premises unless he pays the rent due by him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance within the time fixed in the contract with his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, or in the cases provided for in section 19, unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of such premises as provided in that section together with, in the case mentioned in sub-section (1)(b) of that section, the cost of transmission referred to in that sub-section within the time specified in that section.

Explanation—A landlord shall not for the purposes of this sub-section be deemed to have refused to accept any rent unless the rents remitted within the period referred to above in this subsection by postal money order to the address of the landlord and the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered either on account of the landlord having refused to accept payment thereof or for any other cause. 19(1) When a landlord refused to accept any rent referred to in section 18 remitted by postal money order by a tenant in respect of any premises, tenant may—

(a) Deposit such rent within a fortnight of the date on which the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as under livered; and

(b) Unless the landlord signifies by notice in writing to the tenant his willingness to accept any subsequent rent which becomes due in respect of such premises, also deposit such subsequent rent within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due, from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under section 18(5) together with the cost of transmission by postal money order of the money deposited to the landlord.

<u>12. It is to be observed that Act 1991 has made substantial encroachment into the tenancy law of the County its purpose is to protect the tenant from ejectment from the tenanted premises and has given the tenant certain benefits, notwithstanding the Provisions of the Transfer of the Property Act or the Contract Act. The general law governing relationship of landlord and tenant relating to premises are to be kept in view, while interpreting the sections of the Act 1991. Under the Transfer of Property Act which is the general law governing the relationship of landlord and tenant for this kind of tenancy, the landlord has the right to terminate the tenancy by giving a notice quit on the tenant in the manner prescribed under section 106 of the Act. This right has been substantially curtailed by the Act 1991. The Act 1991, however, has not totally done away with the operation of the provisions of Transfer of Property Act but has made serious encroachment on the rights of the parties in a tenancy agreement, the right of landlord being curtailed.</u>

13. We now turned to the three Provisions set out earlier of the Act 1991 to see the combined effect of them in case of ejectment of such a tenant. These three Provisions mainly relate to default in payment of rent by the tenant. As said earlier the Act 1991 seeks to give protection to the tenant from ejectment to some extent and one of such is that, if the tenant pays rent of the full extent permissible under the Act 1991, amongst others, he is protected from ejectment. We are, therefore, to see how for the Act 1991 as given the protection to the tenant and how far the landlord's right to eject on this score has been curtailed.

14. Section 18(1) says that notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act 1882 or the Contract Act, 1872 no order or decree for recovery of possession of any premises shall be made so long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Act, 1991 and performs the conditions of the tenancy. It is limited by five provisions but they do not concern us for the present and so they need not be gone into. The Provisions of section 18(5) have been set out above.

15. To turn to section 19 which deals with the deposit of rent, I find that the relevant Provisions is that when a landlord refuses to accept rent referred to in section 18 remitted by postal money order by the tenant, he may deposit such rent within a fortnight of the date on which the rent due so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered, unless the landlord signifies by the notice in writing to the tenant of his willingness to accept any subsequent rent which has become due in respect of such premises. There are other conditions as to the deposit of rent but they do not call our attention in the context of the present case and we refrain from dilating on them.

<u>16. In the case of default in the payment of rent the combined effect of the three Provisions set out about clearly shows that a tenant is protected, notwithstanding the Provisions of Transfer of Property Act or the Contract Act from ejectment as long as he pays rent to the whole extent allowed by the Act 1991 and he performs the conditions of the tenancy. The expression as long as tenant pays rent in our opinion no doubt indicates that the point of default on the part of the tenant will be not only the date of filing of the suit but will continue till decree is past. It does not, however, mean that if the tenant subsequent to the filing of the suit has deposited the rent with Rent Controller, the default incurred earlier is cured. On the contrary the tenant's liability for default even after the filing of the suit continues under the law till the passing of the decree.</u>

<u>17. Moreover, admittedly Taka 40,000 paid by defendant as advance is still lying with the plaintiff. Until entire amount of advance money taken by plaintiff at the time of creating subsequent tenancy, was adjusted, the defendant could not be said to have defaulted in paying rent within the meaning of aforesaid sections.</u>

<u>As long as the plaintiff had the unadjusted amount in his hands, he could have adjusted it towards the payment of rent for the months of Sravan, 1402 BS. In view of the Provisions of section 18(5) of the Act, 1991 which do not seem to hate been contravened by the defendant, no default appears to have been made by him in paying the rent for the aforesaid period.</u>

18. In the case of Shamsuddin Ahamed vs Md Hassan 31 DLR (AD), 155 held:

"According to the section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1963, the aforesaid provisions, the tenant must pay the rent within the time fixed in the con-tract with his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable. If the landlord refused to accept any rent sent within the aforesaid period as mentioned in the Explanation to section 18(5), the tenant is to deposit the rent as mentioned in section 19 of the Ordinance.

The learned Counsel submitted that until the entire amount of Taka 19,200 taken by the respondents at the time of creating the tenancy was adjusted, the appellant could not be said to have defaulted in paying rent within the meaning of the aforesaid section. It cannot be denied that there is considerable force in this argument. As long as the respondents had the unadjusted amount in their hands, they could have adjusted in towards the payment of rent for the months of October, November, and December.

In view of the provisions of section 18(5) of the Ordinance which do not seem to have been contravened by the appellant no default appears to have been made by him in paying the rent for the month of October, November, and Decembers, 1973" .

<u>19. With regard to the submissions regarding "Solenama" made between the parties in former SCC suit, it may be answered to the effect that terms of solenama of former suits shall be automatically annulled after creating fresh tenancy agreement between the parties, which has been done in this case. Therefore, the solenama of former suit has no binding effect in this suit. Therefore, I hold that the defendant is not a defaulter within the meaning of aforesaid Provisions and the plaintiff failed to prove by evidence that the defendant is a defaulter and he has bonafide requirement of suit premises.</u>

20. Moreover, the impugned judgment and decree in its entirety are not well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So, the grounds urged and contentions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner are the correct exposition of law and facts. So the legal pleas taken by him prevails appears to have a good deal of force. On the contrary I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by learned Counsel of the opposite parties.

21. In the light of discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authority referred to above, I am of the view that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from legal infirmities which calls for interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

22. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 18-3-1998 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, third Court, Dhaka, in SCC Suit No. 5 of 1996 is here-by set aside Accordingly the SCC. Suit No. 5 of 1996 is dismissed. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Office is directed to send down the records of the case at once.

End.

parties:
Major General Amjad Khan Chowdhury (Retd)  ----- Petitioner
Vs
Parle Agro Products Ltd. & another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman J: This application, under section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009, praying for rectification of the Register of Trade marks by removing the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in class No. 32 from the register, having been contested by the respondent, the same is disposed of by this judgment.

Facts of the case:

2. It has been asserted in the application that the petitioner is engaged in business of manufacturing and marketing of fruit juice of international quality and launched the product for marketing in the year 2007 in PET bottles of 250 ml. 500 ml, and 1000 ml. and with a view to distinguishing the product of the petitioner from the rest of the others, the petitioner adopted a trademark consisting of the word "PRAN FROOTO" in distinctive colour scheme, design and get up. The petitioner applied for registration of the trademark in the Department of Patents, Designs and Trade marks on 14th day of October, 2008 under application No. 118828 in Class No. 32. But the Trade mark Registry, instead of registering the Trade mark of the petitioner served a notice for show cause on 21-12-2009, as to why the petitioner application shall not be rejected on the ground that the Trade mark No. 31112 in Class No.32 was registered for the Trade mark "FROOTI" by the respondent No. 1 Parte Agro Products Limited, India. Since the said Trade mark is similar to the petitioner's trademark, the same is an obstacle to the registration of the petitioner's Trade mark Application No. 118828.

3. It has been asserted that the respondent no. 1 while filing the application for registration of the Trade mark being No. 31112 in Class No. 32 in respect of mango drink bearing the Trade mark "FROOTI" in Class 32 had no intention to use the mark in relation to the goods included in the application, yet the said mark was registered.

4. It has been further asserted that the superior quality of the fruit juice manufactured and marketed by the petitioner and the continuous use of the Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" from the date of launching and due to vigorous sales promotion measure under-taken by the petitioner from time to time, the said Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" on label acquired distinctive status in the class of manufacturing and marketing the fruit juice so that any reference as to the Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" is always makes a reference to the product manufactured and marketed by the petitioner under the aforesaid brand. The Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" is the property of the petitioner. A total volume of sale of "PRAN FROOTO" mango juice is at Tk. 4376.70 million in four years starting from 2007 and as a matter of fact the "PRAN FROOTO" brand mango juice occupies 52% of the market share of all Fruit juice marketed by different companies in Bangladesh. Upon such circumstances the petitioner prays for the removal of the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in class No. 32 from the Registrar of Trade mark Register.

5. Pursuant to the notice served, the respondent No. 1 Parle Agro Product Limited appeared in the proceeding on engaging the learned Advocate Mr. ABM Shamsud Doulah who preferred affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the respondent No. 1 denying all the material allegations as made in the petition and stating that the petitioner has no right to file the application and to obtain the relief sought therein prior to enactment of the Trade mark Act 2009 read with the Provisions of the agreement on Trade Related aspect of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) under the World Trade Organization and the Paris Convention for the protection of intellectual property, the People's Republic of Bangladesh is signatory to both. Both the aforesaid international conventions confirm that the countries to which the convention applied shall constitute a Union for the protection of intellectual property and, as such, extend protection against unfair competition.

6. It has been further asserted that the Trade mark "FROOTI" is registered as well known Trade mark in many countries under Class 32 including Bangladesh. The "FROOTI" food juice is manufactured in India and widely marketed in various countries among the millions of customers in India, USA, UK, Canada, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Singapore, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Nepal and many other countries and the Trade mark "FROOTI" is internationally used by the respondent No. 1 in more than 30 countries and accordingly the Trade mark of the respondent No. 1 "FROOTI" was duly registered and renewed in Bangladesh Trade mark registry as registered trademark No. 31112 in Class No. 32. But the petitioner applied for registration of an infringed Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" under Trade mark Application No. 118828 in Class No. 32 violating the Trade mark No. 31112 in the same Class No.32 of the respondent No. 1 by way of unfair competition. The Petitioner filed this application referring the provisions of section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009 alleging non-use of the registered trademark "FROOTI". But the trademark of the respondent No. 1 being internationally used in more than 30 countries including Bangladesh, by widely (published) advertisements for its branded product "FROOTI" through Newspapers and various TV channels, several Bangladeshi traders made small imports from the respondent No.1 its branded fruit juice item bearing Trade mark "FROOTI", in Bangladesh some of such sellers in Bangladesh made publicity in the local dailies one of such importer is M/s Rana Fruits & Juice Company of A/2 Powell Super Market, Naya Paltan, Dhaka, which advertised in Bengali daily Inquilab, dated 26-8-1996 and by M/s Zinnat International of 242 Nowabpur Road Dhaka, in Bengali daily Ittefaq dated 25-9-1997. Although those are small imports in Bangladesh yet the proprietor of the registered Trade mark "FROOTI" has plan to widely distribute the drink in Bangladesh by appointing agent for which it has been concluding negotiation with a Bangladeshi business house. The application of the petitioner for registration of similar trademark is an infringing one and, as such, correctly not accepted by the Trade mark Registry in Dhaka. The petitioner by furnishing misleading information wanted to manage a Trade mark registration in the name of "PRAN FROOTO" making infringement of the respondent No. 1 internationally well known registered and globally widely popular "FROOTI" brand.

7. It has been further asserted in the affidavit-in-opposition that the Paris Convention for Protection of intellectual Property provides that there will be no requirement as to domicile or establishment in the country where protection is claimed which may be imported by the nationals of countries of the union and under no circumstances the Trade mark registration of any party can be cancelled unless the person concerned is not justified in action. There being no Provisions in the Trade mark Act 2009 for manufacturing of the product within the countries wherein the Trade mark has been registered, the alleged claim of the petitioner for its non-use does not arise at all. The petitioner is using the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class No. 32 internationally within the union and in Bangladesh by various means and therefore, the petitioner's allegations as to non-use have no basis and accordingly the instant application for rectification of the register by removing the Trade mark of the respondent No. 1 '"FROOTI"' is liable to be rejected.

8. The learned Advocate M Moazzam Hosain appeared on behalf of the petitioner while the learned advocate ABM Shamsud Doulah represented the respondent No.1.

Arguments of the parties:

9. The argument of the learned Advocate Mr. M. Moazzam Hosain, appearing on behalf of the petitioner centers round the point that the petitioner being the manufacturer of a mango juice drink under the Trade Name "PRAN FROOTO" widely marketed the product within the Bangladeshi market through the various promotion measures undertaken by the petitioner from time to time and, as such, the Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" acquired distinct status and became a distinctive mark in its class of food fruit juice manufactured and marketed by the petitioner under the aforesaid brand and, as such, a total volume of sale of "PRAN FROOTO" Mango Juice rose at Tk. 4376170 million in four years starting from 2007 accordingly it acquired 82% of the market share paying a good amount in taxes to the Government and therefore, the petitioner is entitled to register its Trade mark under Class-32. But due to the existence of a Trade mark under the name "FROOTI" registered under No. 31112 in Class - 32 the respondent No. 2 the Registrar of Trade mark most illegally refused to registrar the petitioner's trademark "PRAN FROOTO" on the false ground that the registered trademark "FROOTI" has similarity with the petitioner's mark.

10. The further argument of the learned Advocate M Moazzam Hosain rest on the point that although the registered Trade mark .No. 31112 in Class -32 was existing in the register of Trade mark Registry but it has not been used for a continuous period of five years specially one month prior to filing the instant petition and there has been no bona fide use of the mark in relation to the goods included in the mark. Further it has been admitted by the respondent no. 1 in the affidavit-in-opposition that they have never used the mark "FROOTI" within Bangladesh as they are going to establish business relationship with others in Bangladesh for the purpose of marketing the product "FROOTI" within Bangladesh and, as such, the petitioner is entitled to obtain an order under the Provisions of section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009 for removal of the said mark "FROOTI" from the register of trademark since the non-user of the mark "FROOTI" for five years and within one month before the presentation of the application under section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009 is a good reason for removal of the said registered Trade mark from the register. His further contention is that since no infringement suit has been initiated by the respondent No. 1 against the petitioner at any point of time the fact of no-user of the mark "FROOTI" has been well established.

11. In support of these contention about non-user of Trade mark the learned Advocate Mr. M. Moazzam Hosain relied on the case of Chiswick Products vs The Registrar of Trade mark, Karachi reported in PLD 1975 Karachi 421 and also the case of Abdul Aziz vs Seven-up Company, Karachi reported in PLD 98 Karachi 10.

12. Whether the petitioner is a aggrieved party within the meaning of section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009 the learned Advocate M Moazzam Hosain further argues that by the existence of non-used trademark "FROOTI" the petitioner's right to registrar his mark "PRAN FROOTO" since been prejudiced as such, the same entitled the petitioner to be aggrieved party and, as such, the petitioner is entitled to approach this court under the provisions of section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009. In this respect he relied on the case of Powell vs Birmingham Vinegar Brewery Co. (1893) 10 RPC 63 Ch. D.

13. On the other hand the learned Advocate Mr. ABM Shamsud Doulah appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 submits that the non- user of the Trade mark as provided in section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009 has a wide implication as to the meaning of the section which this court shall consider on the basis of factual aspects.

14. He further submits that the legislation Trade mark Act 2009 is required to be read with the provisions of agreement on Trade Related aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) under World Trade Organization and the Paris Convention for Protection of Industrial Property both to which the People's Republic of Bangladesh is a signatory and this convention has confirmed that the countries to which the convention apply shall constitute a union for the protection of industrial property and, as such, it extended protection against the practice of unfair competition.

15. The learned Advocate ABM Shamsud Doulah, relying upon such provisions argues that Bangladesh, India and many other countries being the signatory of the Paris Convention have formed a union and, as such, any registration of trademark within the union country will be as a protection to the registered Trade mark for any infringement and the use of the Trade mark with any prior registration within the Union countries will constitute a protection against the allegation of non- user.

16. The. learned Advocate ABM Shamsud Doulah argues that the petitioner has approached to this court on the allegation that the respondent No.1 has failed to use the registered Trade mark No. 31112 within Bangladesh which not being the factual aspect of the case has been too far from the fact as the respondent No.1 is not only using the Trade mark "FROOTI" within the Bangladesh through various means but also using the same in the union country India and within twenty other countries of the world simply proves that the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class-32 is in use and therefore, an allegation of non-user of the aforesaid Trade mark does not arise at all.

17. The learned Advocate ABM Shamsud Doulah further argued that the respondent No. 1 registered the Trade mark "FROOTI" on 29th July, 1990 and thereafter, the said Mark was renewed on 16.4.2001 for fifteen years from 29-7-1997 and since the respondent No. 1 is now preparing to commence business relations with the Bangladeshi party and the product will be marketed in Bangladesh although the product "FROOTI" is being marketed in Bangladesh by the several parties who import the said product in Bangladesh and those are widely advertised in Bangladesh through the newspaper advertisements specially in Daily Inquilab and Daily Ittefaq. The proprietor of Trade mark No. 31112 in Class -32 also advertised the product through the various Indian TV Channels which are seen in Bangladesh everyday and therefore, no question of non-use of Trade mark arises at all.

18. The learned Advocate Mr. A.B.M Shamsud Doulah, argued that the provisions of section 42 of the Trade mark Act does not provide that the 'use' must be within the territory of Bangladesh, rather the Paris Convention has provided that any of the Trade mark within the union countries will be sufficient for the purpose of the keeping the Trade mark within the register and since the petitioner in using the Trade mark in Bangladesh along with 20 other countries of the world by wide circulation and marketing the product "FROOTI" the provisions of section 42 cannot be invoked against the respondent No. 1 registered Trade mark "FROOTI". Therefore, the learned Advocate prays for rejection of the application.

19. In support of the contention made by the learned Advocate Mr. ABM Shamsud Doulah the Article 6 and 6b of the Paris Convention are relied upon by him as to the submission of him regarding the point that well known Trade mark to be registered under the provisions of the said convention.

20. The learned Advocate Mr. A.B.M Shamsud Doulah further relied upon the provisions of the Trade mark legislation as prevailed in Pakistan and also in India. He further relied upon the provisions of section 119 and 120 of the Trade mark Act 2009 which says about the Paris Convention and also the provisions of section 71 of the Trade mark Act 2009 wherein the meaning of the user of Trade mark has been provided.

Deliberation:

21. We have heard the learned Advocates of the parties, perused the materials on record and also considered the argument advanced at the bar.

22. Admittedly the respondent No.1 is the owner of the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class -32 for the Trade Name "FROOTI". The petitioner upon manufacturing and marketing the mango Juice adopted the Trade Name "PRAN FROOTO" applied for registration of his Trade mark in Trade mark Application No. 118828 in Class -32. But the respondent No. 2, the Registrar of Trade mark, served a notice under Section 14 (1) of the Trade mark Act 1940 upon the petitioner as to show cause why the said trademark application No. 118828 in Class -32 shall not be refused on the ground that there existed a registered Trade mark for the same Class -32 under the Trade Name "FROOTI" being registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class -32. The petitioner upon getting such show cause notice approached this court under the Provisions of section 42 of Trade mark Act 2009 praying for removal of the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class -32 for the Trade Name "FROOTI" for its removal from the register on the allegation that the aforesaid registered trademark has not been in use within five years and specially one month before the filing of the present application. The respondent No.1 upon appearing before this court relied upon the sole point that the registered Trade mark being No. 31112 in Class-32 for the Trade Name "FROOTI" is in use in Bangladesh and also in thirty other union countries of the world by marketing the product "FROOTI" and using the trademark in advertisement and in all other materials and means. Therefore, the following two questions arose to be adjudicated by this court;

1. Whether the registered trademark "FROOTI" is liable to be removed from the register of trademark for non-user as alleged?

2. Whether mark "PRAN FROOTO" is similar to the mark "FROOTI" so that the refusal of the registrar was justified.

25. The allegation of non-user of the mark FROOTO has been based by the petitioner upon facts:—

I. That no infringement suit has been filed against the petitioner although the petitioner is using the mark "PRAN FROOTO"

II. That the mango juice "FROOTI" is not in the market of Bangladesh.

26. Although bulky arguments have been advanced on the point by both the learned Advocate, but the moot contention of the learned Advocate M. Moazzam Hosain is that the user of the Trade mark will be treated if the product for which the Trade mark was registered is marketed within the territory of Bangladesh by way of either manufacturing or trading in any means through import and the Provisions of section 71 of the Trade mark Act 2009 clearly rest on such contention and accordingly the learned Advocate Mr. M. Moazzam Hosain contended that since the respondent No.1, being an Indian company does not export the product "FROOTI" in Bangladesh, as admitted in the affidavit-in-opposition, the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class-32 shall be treated as has not been used in Bangladesh within five years from the date of filing the application.

27. Contrary to this contention on behalf of the learned Advocate ABM Shamsud Doulah for and on behalf of the respondent No.1 relied upon the advertisements as published by M/s Rana Fruits & Juice Company in daily Inquilab on 26.8.1996 and by one M/s Zinnat International in daily Ittefaq on 25-9-1997 as to the marketing of the product "FROOTI" manufactured by the respondent No.1 and also on the provision that there is no requirement within the provisions of the registered Trade mark Act 2009 that the Trade mark must be used within the territory of Bangladesh by marketing the product within the territory and secondly, that the respondent No. 1 since used the Trade mark by all other means in Bangladesh through their unofficial importers and also within the union countries, the allegation of non-use has no basis for consideration.

28. The contrary contention appears to have substance. The two Bangladeshi concern M/s Rana Fruits & Juice Company and M/s Zinnat International advertised in the national daily Newspapers as to the marketing of the mango food drink "FROOTI" within the Bangladesh in the year 1996 and 1997 which clearly comes under the provisions of section 71 of the Trade mark Act 2009 as to the meaning of use of Registered Trade mark.

29. But, so far the argument about the non-requirement of marketing of the product within the territory of Bangladesh, so as to mean the user of the register Trade mark if the same is used within the union countries as mentioned in the Paris Convention, this court is unable to concede to the argument since the Municipal Law shall prevail over the International Convention if any of the provisions of the International Convention has not been adopted in the municipal legislation. It appears from the Section 119 and 120 and 121 of the Trade mark Act 2009 that the Paris Convention and also the other International Convention has been taken into consideration by the legislature while enacting the Trade mark Act 2009 in the following manner:—

ট্রেডমার্ক আইন ২০০৯:

ধারা ১১৯: কনভেনশনভুক্ত দেশের ক্ষেত্রে বিশেষ বিধান-প্যারিস কনভেনশন বা বিশ্ব বানিজ্য সংস্থার সদস্যভুক্ত কোন রাষ্ট্র ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধন এবং উহা সংরক্ষনে উহাদের নাগরিকদের জন্য যে সুবিধা প্রদান করে, সে রকম সুবিধা বাংলাদেশের কোন নাগরিককে প্রদান করিলে, উক্তরুপ রাষ্ট্রের সহিত সম্পাদিত চুক্তি, কনভেনশন বা সমঝোতা বাস্তবায়নের লক্ষ্য উক্তরুপ রাষ্ট্র কনভেনশন রাষ্ট্র হিসাবে গন্য হইবে ৷ ধারা ১২০8 কনভেনশন আবেদনের ক্ষেত্রে বিশেষ বিধান ।

(১) যদি প্যারিস কনভেনশন অথবা বিশ্ব বাণিজ্য সংন্থাভুক্ত কোন রাষ্ট্র ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের জন্য আবেদনকারী কোন ব্যক্তি বা তাহার আইনানূগ প্রতিনিধি, উক্ত আবেদনের ৬(ছয়) মাসের মধ্যে উহার পূর্নবিবরন এবং অগ্রাধিকাৱ আবেদনের সত্যায়িত কপিসহ বাংলাদেশে উক্ত ট্রেডমার্ক

নিবন্ধনের জন্য আবেদন করেন এবং উক্ত ট্রেডমার্ক এই অধ্যাদেশের অধীন নিবন্ধন করা হয়, তাহা হইলে যে তারিখে কনভেনশনভুক্ত রাষ্টে তিনি ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের আবেদন করিয়াছিলেন, সে তারিখ হইতে উক্ত নিবন্ধন কার্যকর হইয়াছে বলিয়া গন্য হইবে ।

(২) যদি বা ততোধিক কনভেনশনভুক্ত রাষ্টে ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের আবেদন করা হয়, তাহা হইলে উপ-ধারা (১) এ উল্লিখিত ৬(ছয়) মাস, প্রথম আবেদনের তারিখ হইতে গননা করিতে হইবে ৷

(৩) এই আইনে যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, কোন ট্রেডমার্কের স্বত্বাধিকারী এই আইনের অধীন নিবন্ধনের জন্য আবেদন দাখিলের পূর্বে অর্জিত অধিকার লঙ্ঘনের জন্য ক্ষতিপূরণ

দাবি করিতে পারিবেন না ৷

ধারা ১২১: পারস্পরিক সম্পর্ক বিষয়ক বিধান ।-ধারা ১১৯ এর অধীন কোন রাষ্ট্রকে কনভেনশন রাষ্ট্র হিসাবে" গন্য করা হইলে উক্ত রাষ্ট্র ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধন ও সংরক্ষনের জন্য উহার নাগরিকদের যে সুবিধা প্রদান করে, উহা যদি বাংলাদেশের নাগরিকদের জন্য প্রদান না করে, তাহা হইলে উক্ত দেশের কোন নাগরিক বাংলাদেশের কোন ব্যক্তির সহিত এককভাবে বা যৌথভাবে-

(ক) নিবন্ধন বহিতে কোন ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের জন্য আবেদন করিতে বা ট্রেডমার্কের নিবন্ধিত স্বতাধিকারী হইবার অধিকারী হইবেন না;

(খ) কোন নিবন্ধিত ট্রেডমার্কের স্বত্বাধিকারীর আইনানুগ প্রতিনিধি হইবার অধিকারী হইবে না; অথবা

(গ) ধারা 8৫ এর অধীন নিবন্ধনের জন্য আবেদন করিতে বা কোন ট্রেডমার্কের নিবন্ধিত ব্যবহারকারী হইবার অধিকারী হইবেন না।

30. The provisions as arranged by the above sections whether has been extended to India has not been established before this court. Those Provisions will only be applicable if reciprocal arrangement exist in between these two countries. The argument as to the use of the Trade mark within the union countries shall have implication if reciprocal agreement with Bangladesh exists. Therefore, apart from this question, this court finds that the respondent No.1 having used the registered Trade mark "FROOTI" within the territory of Bangladesh within five years from the date of application does not come under the provisions of section 42 of the Trade mark Act 2009.

31. But the dispute lies elsewhere in between the parties, which is practically a dispute in between the petitioner and the respondent No. 2 the registrar of Trade mark. It appears that a show cause notice under Section 14(1) of the now repealed Trade mark Act 1940 was served upon the petitioner on the ground that since there existed a registered Trade mark under the Trade Name "FROOTI", then why the petitioner application no. 118828 shall not be refused. This court finds that the petitioner applied for registration of the Trade mark "PRAN FROOTO" and the registered Trade mark No. 31112 under Class No-32 contains the word "FROOTI". Those are two distinct Trade Names, since "PRAN FROOTO" is as distinct from the Trade Name FROOTO as mango is from Jack Fruit.

32. The refusal to register similar trademark has been provided in section 10 of the Trade mark Act 2009 in the following Bengali language;

ট্রেডমার্ক আইন ২০০৯:

ধারা ১০:

সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ বা প্রতারনা মূলকভাবে সাদৃশ্যপুর্ণ ট্রেডমার্কে নিবন্ধনে বাধা নিষেধ ৷-

(১) উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, ভিন্ন কোন স্বত্বাধিকারীর নামে কোন পণ্য বা সেবা অথবা, পণ্য বা সেবার বর্ননা নিবন্ধিত থাকিলে, উক্তরুপ পণ্য বা সেবা অথবা পণ্য সেবার বর্ননার অনুরুপ বা প্রতারনামুলক ভাবে সাদৃশ্যপুন্য কোন মার্ক নিবন্ধন করা যাইবেনা ৷

(২) সৎ উদ্দেশ্যে যুগপৎ ব্যবহার বা অন্য কোন বিশেষ কারনে একই পণ্য বা সেবার একই বর্ণনার পণ্য বা সেবার প্রায় সাদৃশ্যপূণ্য হইলেও উক্ত বিষয়ে কোন ট্রেডমার্ক একাধিক স্বতাধিকারীর নামে নিবন্ধন করা প্রয়োজন বিবেচনায় নিবন্ধক, উপযুক্ত শর্ত ও সীমাবদ্ধতা সাপেক্ষে, একাধিক স্বত্বাধিকারীর নামে কোন ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের অনুমতি দিতে পারিবেন।

(৩) একই পণ্য বা সেবা অথবা একই বর্ননার পণ্য বা সেবা সংক্রান্ত অভিন্ন বা প্রায় সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ কোন ট্রেডমার্কের স্বত্বাধিকারী হিসাবে নিবন্ধিত হইবার জন্য বিভিন্ন ব্যক্তি পৃথক পৃথক আবেদন করিলে, নিবন্ধক পূর্ববর্তী তারিখের আবেদন নিস্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত পরবর্তী তারিখের আবেদন গ্রহণের বিষয়টি মূলতবী রাখিয়া পূর্ববর্তী আবেদন সম্পর্কে প্রদত্ত সাক্ষ্য ও বিরোধিতার আলোকে পরবর্তী তারিখের আবেদনটি নিস্পত্তি করিতে পারিবেন ৷

(8) কোন পণ্য বা সেবার জন্য এমন কোন ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধন করা যাইবে না, যাহা অন্য কোন ব্যবসা প্রতিষ্ঠানের অনুরূপ পণ্য বা সেবার ক্ষেত্রে বাংলাদেশে সুপরিচিত কোন ট্রেডমার্কের সহিত সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ বা বিভ্রান্তিমূলকভাবে সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ বা অনুরুপ কোন মার্ক বা ট্রেড বর্ণনার অনুবাদ সহযোগে পঠিত ৷

(৫) কোন পণ্য বা সেবা বাংলাদেশে নিবন্ধিত সুপরিচিত কোন ট্রেডমার্কের সহিত সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ হইলে, উক্ত পণ্য বা সেবার ক্ষেত্রে উক্তরুপ ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধন করা যাইবে না, যদি-

(ক) উক্তরুপ কোন ট্রেডমার্ক এমনভাবে ব্যবহার করা হয়, যাহা দ্বারা নিবন্ধিত স্বত্বাধিকারীর সহিত উক্ত কোন পণ্য বা সেবার সম্পর্ক আছে মর্মে ভুল ধারণার সৃষ্টি করিতে পারে; বা

(খ) উক্তরুপ ব্যবহারের ফলে নিবন্ধিত ট্রেডমার্কেরস্বার্থ ক্ষুন্ন হইবার আশংকা থাকে ৷

(৬) উপধারা (৪) ও (৫) এ বর্ণিত কোন মার্ক সুপরিচিত কিনা উহা নির্ধারণের ক্ষেত্রে, বাংলাদেশে উক্ত মার্কের বিজ্ঞাপন প্রচারের মাধ্যমে প্রাপ্ত ফলাফলসহ উক্ত মার্ক সম্পর্কে সংশ্লিষ্ঠ ভোক্তা সাধারনের সাধারণ ধারণা বা জ্ঞান বিবেচনায় লইতে হইবে ৷

(৭) এই ধারার কোন বিধান ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনে কোন বাধা সৃষ্টি করিবে না, যদি নিবন্ধনের ক্ষেত্রে পূর্ববর্তী কোন ট্রেডমার্কেৱ স্বত্বাধিকারী বা পূর্ব অধিকারসম্পন্ন অন্য কোন ব্যক্তির সম্মতি থাকে ।

ব্যাখ্যা ৷ এই ধারার উদ্দেশ্য পুরনকল্পে “পূর্ববর্তী ট্রেডমার্ক" অর্থ এম নিবন্ধি ট্রেডমার্ক যাহা প্ৰশ্নযুক্ত ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের আবেদন দাখিলের পূর্বে নিবন্ধিত হইয়াছে ও ট্রেডমার্ক হিসাবে দাবি করিবার ক্ষেত্রে অগ্রাধিকারী, এবং যাহা নিবন্ধনের জন্য ইতোপূর্বে আবেদন দাখিল করা হইয়াছে ও উক্ত আবেদনের ভিত্তিতে নিবন্ধিত হইলে, পূর্ববর্তী ট্রেডমার্ক হিসাবে গণ্য হইত এইরুপ ট্রেডমার্ক ও ইহার অন্তর্ভুক্ত হইবে।

(৮) নিবন্ধক যদি এই মর্মে সন্তুষ্ট হন যে, কোন ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের মেয়াদ অতিক্রান্ত হ্ইবার পূর্ববর্তী ২(দুই)বৎসর পর্যন্ত সৎ উদ্দেশ্যে ব্যবহৃত হইয়াছে, তাহা হইলে উক্ত ট্রেডমার্কের নিবন্ধনের মেয়াদ অতিক্রান্ত হওয়া সত্বেও পরবর্তীতে উক্ত মার্কের নিবন্ধন যোগ্যতা নির্ধারণের ক্ষেত্রে মেয়াদ অতিক্রান্তের সময় হইতে পরবর্তী ১ (এক) বৎসরের জন্য নিবন্ধন বহাল রহিয়াছে বলিয়া বিবেচিত হইবে ৷

33. In the case of Anil Kumar Ghosh vs Shamir Kumar Ghosh reported in 54 DLR 273 this bench, differently constituted, on the point of similarity of two marks held as under:

"While considering the trademark applications all the surrounding circumstances, must be taken into consideration so that each of the trademarks used in a normal way may not create confusion in the mind of the people. The trademark of both the opposite parties "New Baghabari Khati Gawa Ghee" and "No. 1 Baghabari Khati Gawa Ghee" are similar to the registered trademark of the petitioner is "Bangladesh Special Khati Gawa Ghee" with the same label of cow, colour scheme and other details, thus they are bound to cause confusion in the minds of the public even after amendment is allowed to "New Baghabari Khati Gawa Ghee" by the registrar, Trade marks. The main emphasis should be put on the interest of the public so that there is no confusion regarding the production of the Gawa Ghee."

34. Their lordship in the Appellate Division in the Case of BCIC vs Sattar Match Works reported in 44 DLR (AD) 208 laid the principle as to refusal to register similar trademark by registrar in the following language: "Registration of identical or similar trademark-Such registration in favour of two persons -About the propriety of such registration the registrar has to satisfy himself and he may put conditions and limitations as he may think fit to impose. In permitting identical trademarks he has to provide for some ways and devices for protecting the interest of competing proprietors and the interest of the public in general to save them from possible deception and confusion. In the absence of fraud, there could be no direction under Section 46 of the Act with regard to registration of trademark."

<u>35. Therefore, the show cause notice as served upon the petitioner appears to have been served without any lawful basis. There is no conflict in between these two Trade Names nor the public at large will be confused by the two Trade Names if both the products with their respective Trade Name appears in the shelf of the market shops. "PRAN FROOTO" having a good reputation in the country has its own distinctive mark and the reputation and the registered Trade mark "FROOTI", being completely dissimilar with the petitioners Trade Name "PRAN FROOTO" will not confuse or mislead the customers at large in Bangladesh in purchasing the said product, if available within the Bangladeshi market. Therefore, this court finds that the instant application is required to be allowed in different manner.</u>

<u>36. Accordingly, the application is disposed off.</u>

37. The show cause notice as served upon the petitioner on the petitioner on 21-12-2011 under the Provisions of section 14(1) of the Trade mark Act 1940 is hereby declared to have been issued without lawful basis and therefore, the respondent No. 2 is directed to register the Trade Name "PRAN FROOTO" under the Trade mark Application No. 118828 as a complete dissimilar distinctive mark from the registered Trade mark No. 31112 in Class -32 for the Trade Name "FROOTI", in accordance with law.

However, there shall be no order as to costs.

End.

Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner. (In both the cases).
No one ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Al-Hajj Mirjahan ----- Petitioner. [In CP No. 106 of 1993]

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 6.1.93 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 675 and 674 of 1990).
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ : Two co-sharer landlords have filed these two leave petitions separately and the tenant is the common Respondent in both the petitions. The High Court Division, by two separate judgments, bearing the same date, 6 January 1993, allowed two corresponding Civil Revision Nos. 674 and 675 of 1990 and directed thereby the Rent Controller to accept a monthly deposit of rent made by the tenant under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance.

2. Respondent-tenant, M/s Golden Biscuit Company was monthly tenant in respect of the premises in question, carrying on business there and paying rent regularly to its owner Alhaj Md. Ashraf Ali for last 22 years. This landlord, by two registered deeds dated 2 November, 1987, sold away the premises to the Petitioners, Alhaj Mirjahan and Alhaj Md. Rafiqure Miah in equal share, and by a letter dated 16 November 1987, advised the tenant to pay rent henceforward to the two new landlords. The two purchasers-landlords, also informed the tenant in a similar manner about the change of ownership of the premises. The rent for the premises was Taka 1200.00 per month. The tenant remitted the rent for the month of November 1987 by postal money order to the new landlords. Allegation of the tenant is, that the new landlords purposely avoided receipt of the money order by constantly remaining absent from their houses. Thereupon, the tenant filed an application before the Rent Controller within the prescribed time to deposit the rent. But upon an objection from the two landlords, the deposit was refused. The tenant filed an appeal, but it was also dismissed by the Subordinate judge. Thereupon, the tenant came to the High Court Division with two revisional applications, as mentioned above, and obtained a favourable order in each case.

<u>3. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, has appeared for the petitioner in both the matters. He contends that the tenant was not entitled to make the deposit at the first instance as he did not pay or tender the rent personally to the landlords. The learned Advocate has referred to section 19(1) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and has submitted that if a tenant offers the rent, and the landlord refuses to accept it, then the tenant will remit the rent by postal money order and that if the postal money order is returned undelivered, then only the tenant will make the deposit with the Rent Controller. In this case, the learned Advocate contends, remittance of the rent by Money Order without first approaching the Landlord with "personal tender" is not contemplated in law. The learned Advocate, however, does not dispute that rent for the month of November 1987, that is, the month in which the premises was sold, was remitted by postal money order well within the prescribed time. The dispute is as to the manner of tendering the rent. The learned Advocate has failed to show us any law which requires that rent is to be paid or tendered personally by the tenant to the landlord. If, for instance, the landlord resides in a different place, the tenant may send the rent by Money Order or by Bank Cheque or Bank Draft according to any arrangement between the landlord and the tenant. In the instant case, the tenant remitted the rent well within the prescribed time and when the money order was returned undelivered, the tenant was entitled to make the deposit.</u>

<u>4. Before the Rent Controller, the landlords, however, took a different ground of objection, which was that, by remitting half of the rent to one landlord and another half to other landlord the tenant bifurcated the tenancy itself. The ground was totally baseless, for, when the premises was sold to two different persons under two separate registered deeds, the payment of the rent to both the landlords who became co-sharers in the premises did not violate any provision of law. It is for the new landlords to give instruction to the tenant to whom the rent was to be paid. Section 19(2) of the Ordinance permits the tenant to deposit rent in case of any bonafide doubt or dispute as to the person entitled to receive the rent. We do not find any wrong in the impugned order of the High Court Division allowing the tenant's application for making deposit of rent.</u>

5. Both the petitions are dismissed.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J: This appeal at the instance of the defendant tenant is directed against the judgment passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka on 31st of July, 1980 in a suit for ejectment of a monthly tenant and for realization of arrears of rent.

2. The plaintiff's case, in brief, is that he is the owner of a shop room in holding No. 18 Imamganj, Dhaka and the said shop room was let out to the defendant as an ordinary monthly tenant by executing a deed of agreement of lease on 18.8.76 on a monthly rental of Taka 1000/- payable according to the English Calendar month. According to the plaintiff, the defendant defaulted in payment of rent from the month of May, 1977 and the defendant did not pay any rent from the month of May, 1977 as such he is a habitual defaulter and he is liable to be evicted under the law. The plaintiff by serving a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminanted the tenancy. The defendant after receiving the notice did not vacate the premises and hence the suit for eviction and realisation of the arrear rents. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiff No. 2 filed an application under Order 22 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be added as a co-plaintiff on the assertion that he has purchased the suit property from plaintiff No.1. The trial court considered the prayer and added the plaintiff No. 2 as a co-plaintiff in the suit.

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement contending inter-alia that there is no relationship of landlord and tenant between them since the property is a vested and non-resident property and that the suit in the present form is not maintainable without making the Government a party. According to the defendant the plaintiff represented himself to be the owner of the suit holding and inducted him as a monthly tenant and the defendant also paid rent for some time; but thereafter, the defendant did not pay as the property was a vested property. The defendant also filed two additional written statements wherein he asserted that he did not make the payment of went to the plaintiff as he was directed not to pay rent to the plaintiff. Subsequently, the plaintiff fraudulently managed to obtain an order of release from the A.D.C. (Revenue), Dhaka and the said order was appealed by the defendant and further proceedings were stayed. Subsequently by the order of the joint Secretary, the proceeding was stayed and the matter being still pending, the defendant did not make the payment as the plaintiff is not entitled either to the rent or to evict the tenant on the ground of defaulter from the premises.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. Hence the appeal by the tenant.

5. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant has taken us through the entire materials on record and has also made an elaborate submission on point of fact and law involved in this case.

6. Before answering to the points raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant in the present case, we are to keep in mind the scope of the present suit. This is a suit for objectment of a monthly tenant and for realisation of arrears of rent and the basis of the claim is the contract of tenancy and in deciding this question we shall have to consider the arguments of the learned Advocate for the appellant. Keeping this in mind, we will gradually proceed to decide the main points raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant in this case.

7. The learned Advocate argued that the property being a vested property, the defendant did not pay the rent to the plaintiff as he had doubt that the landlord is not entitled to the rent and in such circumstances the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree as obtained in the suit. At the very outset we like to point out that we have no manner of doubt in our mind that the suit as filed, the question of title of the present suit and to which we will refer hereinbelow in great details.

8. It is not disputed before us by the parties that this is a suit purely for eviction of the monthly tenant and for realisation of arrears of rents. The defendant admits that he was inducted in the premises by the plaintiff as a monthly tenant. The defendant also admitted the plaintiff as landlord by paying rent from 1976 to May, 1977 and obviously therefore there is a relationship of the landlord and tenant between the parties. According to the defendant the relationship however ceased as the property subsequently was vested and non-resident property.

9. Mr. Gafur, the learned Advocate for the appellant firstly submits that the property is vested in the Government as vested and non-resident property and as such the defendant did not pay the rent to the plaintiff and the trial court acted wrongly in holding that the defendant is a defaulter and wrongly decreed the suit for eviction. In reply to this, it is to be stated that whether the property is a vested and non-resident property is a matter not strictly within the scope of this suit and if the Government or other party is interested to show that the property is a vested property then a separate proceeding should lie in proper forum between the custodian and the plaintiff. As a matter of fact there is no such proceeding between the plaintiff and the custodian and the custodian is also not a party in this present case.

We also find that the custodian ever thought it fit and proper to appear in the fore corner of the proceeding. Be that as it may, from Ext.8 letter to the plaintiff dated 7th April, 1977 passed in Memo No. 781(32) V.P. Case it appears that the suit holding was released in favour of the plaintiff by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka. A reference to the Exhibit 6(c) will show that no such order was passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka not to pay rents by the tenant and as such exhibit 6(b) which was passed under the signature of the Superintendent, Vested Property on 6.6.77 was amended. We have also perused the exhibit 6 series and exhibit A series from where we find that the V.P. case was really continuing before the relevant authority at the instance of the defendant-tenant. On our query to Mr. Gafur to show from these exhibits that the custodian ever appeared in the proceeding of the V.P. case or for that matter any relevant authority of the Government appeared in the proceeding to say that the property is a vested and non-resident property, Mr. Gafur could not lay his hand on any materials nor could show anything from the record. From these materials as has been referred to above, we find that the fight was going on between the land-lord and the tenant and the present V.P. case was started by the tenent. Mr. Gafur primarily argued that his client did not pay the rent as he thought it to be vested and non-resident property and on this plea the tenant occupied the premises since 1977 without paying any rent either to the plaintiff or to the custodian, who according to the defendant is entitled to the rent. On a careful consideration of the first point of the learned Advocate for the appellant we are of the view that within the scope of the suit the question of vested and non-resident property does not in fact assume so much importance as has been emphasised by the learned Advocate for the appellant before us in this appeal. The trial court has correctly said that the question of vested property is a matter to be decided in a separate proceeding and consequently, the first point of the learned Advocate for the appellant is beyond the scope of the suit.

10. The learned Advocate for the appellant secondly, contends that there being no relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties, the defendant is entitled to deny the title of the plaintiff. Admittedly, the defendant was inducted as a tenant of the basis of exhibit 1 and paid rent for some time and thereafter defaulted. Keeping this broad fact in mind, we shall see whether the defendant can deny the title of the plaintiff. Mr. Gafur has cited some decisions on this point. The decision appears to us to be irrelevant for our purpose, yet we will take note of those decisions since the learned Advocate has prayed for incorporating those in the judgment. According to the learned Advocate the theory of estoppel as enunciated in Section 116 of the Evidence Act will not be applicable in the present case. A reference to Section 116 of the Evidence Act shows that a tenant during the continuence of the tenancy who has been inducted into possession by the landlord cannot deny his land lords title, we are of the view that in the facts of the present case by the doctrine of estoppel, the defendant-tenant is precluded from challenging the title of the plaintiff as admittedly the defendant went into possession on the basis of an agreement of tenancy from the landlord.

<u>11. Mr. Gafur submitted that the plaintiff practiced fraud on the defendant and the defendant entered into the agreement and admitted the plaintiff as landlord and paid rent for about one year or so. According to him since the defendant thought it to be a vested property he defaulted in making payment thereafter. We must state here that fraud and misrepresentation on the part of the plaintiff must be specifically pleaded in the written statement and must be borne out from the evidence on record, we fail to find out such a case in the written statement and on the evidence on record. The trial court's finding regarding fraud is quoted herein below—</u>

<u>"But no such case has been stated in the W/S. No story of mis-representation or fraud has been stated. There is no evidence to show that at the time of agreement the property was vested and non-president property. Thus I find that there was no fraud and as such Section 116 of the Evidence Act is applicable".</u>

<u>Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan, the learned Advocate defendant No. 2 and admittedly the defendant No. 1 being out of possession, the defendant No. 2 being a and not inducted by the plaintiff can challenge the title of the plaintiff and the Curt found the real dispute is between the landlord and defendant No.2. Thus on the fact of that case as mentioned above it was held that 116 of the Evidence Act is qualified to the extent that the tenant is not estopped, either before or after the expiration of the lease from challenging the landlords title. We have no manner of doubt in our mind that Mr. Gafur without reading the cases cited them before us.</u>

<u>12. The learned Advocate for the appellant next contended that the defendant was in doubt as to whom he is to pay the rent and as such he was not a defaulter. Section 19(2) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance speaks that in the case of bonafide doubt or dispute as to the person who is entitled to the rent, the tenant is to make deposit to the House Rent Controller. But in the present case no deposit was made and the tenant is undoubtedly a defaulter under the law. Mr. Gafur argued that the tenant thought that he is not to pay rent to the plaintiff as the property is a vested property The tenant went into possession under an agreement of tenancy and he is guided by the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and if there is a bonafide doubt the is to deposit cate appearing for the respondent has rightly pointed out that the case of fraud or misrepresentation having not been at all made out and the admitted position being that the defendant is a tenant he is precluded to challenge the title of the landlord. The learned Advocate for the respondent placed before us the deed of agreement Exhibit 'A' and the tenancy is determined by this agreement where the plaintiff asserted that he is absolute ownerin the suit holding and the defendant accepted the same and proposed to occupy the same premises on payment of the rent. In such circumstances, we agree with the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the defendant is precluded to question the title of the plaintiff. Let us now take up the decision cited by the learned Advocate on this point. Mr. Gafur cited a case reported in A.I.R. 1928 Bombay 265. In that reported decision it has been held that if once the relationship of landlord and tenant is established between the parties, the tenant is precluded from disputing the title of the landlord. The reported decision was a case where the tenant was in possession before the new tenancy began and he executed a lease of tenancy which constituted a new tenancy and allotment . So in that case the question was whether a new tenancy had arises or not, whether the tenant had been let into possession by the landlord. Thus, this decision has got no manner of application in the facts of the present case. In that reported decision the tenant asserted that the contract of tenancy is void or vioidable on account of misrepresentation or fraud. In that decision the decree of the trial court was uphold for recovery of rent even by holding that if the tenant contends that the land does not belong to the plaintiff and title lies somewhere, it is open to him to surrender the possession and to establish his title in a different suit. We fail to understand who the decision is applicable in the facts of the present case. The next case cited is A.I.R. 1926 Calcutta that was a case where through ignorance landlord or by fraud in the matter of execution of the kabuliyat the tenants adorned the landlord and the tenants are not altogether estopped but can show that the land-lord had no title either when the kabuliyat was executed or attotnment was made by payment of rent. In the reported decision the tenants were also in possession of the holding from before whereas in the present case with which we were dealing the tenant was inducted by the landlord and the present case is not a case of attornment and the tenant was inducted into possession by the plaintiff. Thus, we fail to understand how Mr. Gafur can cite such a case which is not relevant for the present decision. In A.I.R. 1956 Calcutta 148 it has been clearly held that the estoppel under section 116 of the Evidence Act is confined to the time when the tenancy commenced and the reported case was a money suit for compensation only for use and occupation. Further in that decision it was held that the suit was one purely for money and not a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property as such this decision is also of no help to the learned Advocate for the appellant. Mr. Gafur also cited the case reported in XXXIII D.L.R. (AD) 37, which was a case of attornment; means the act of the tenant putting one person in place of another as his landlord. It was further held in that decision that in the case of attornment the tenant may not be estopped and the Rule is not infleible. Thus reading of this decision we are of the view that this being a case of attornment of subsequent landlord under a mistaken fact has no manner of application to the fact the appellant cited a case reported in XXIV D.L.R. 202. In that reported decision the plaintiff Dr. Rati Ranjan Chowdhury filed a suit for ejectment against defendant No. 1 Parul Bala Marwari and defendant No. 2 Md. Ibrahim. Defendant No. 2 as her sub-tenant in the holding stated that after the death of her husband she inducted defendant No. 2 . In the written statement defendant No. 2 denied the title of the plaintiff. Thus, the court found that there is no nexus between the plaintiff and the rent before the House Rent Controller. But the tenant cannot take the plea that he is not to deposit the rent anywhere and continue to remain in possession for such a long time without payment of rent to anybody. The learned Subordinate Judge has correctly held that the defendant should at least deposit the rent before the House Rent Controller under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. The tenant having not done so is to be held to be a defaulter in the eye of law. When we put the question to Mr. Gafur the learned Advocate for the appellant as to why the rent was not deposited he submitted that the defendant was under the impression that the custodian is the proper authority for obtaining the money. This is a flimsy argument and the argument was untenable because of the simple fact that no money was also paid to House Rent Controller for protection of his tenancy. The learned Subordinate Judge has rightly rejected this point. Mr. Gafur further submitted that under section 36 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance the defendant is not to pay the rent to the plaintiff. We fail to understand how such an argument can be advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellant when there is nothing on record to show that the suit holding in question is owned by the Government and there is no iota of evidence that the custodian ever claimed the property as such. Thus this point is also of no substance.</u>

13. Mr. Gafur the learned Advocate for the appellant submitted that the trial court wrongly decreed the suit in favour of both the plaintiffs. This argument is also untenable because the plaintiff No.1 filed the suit for ejectment of the tenant and for arrears of rent. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiff No. 2 purchased the property hence he acquired interest and applied to the court for adding him as a party and both the plaintiffs continued with the suit and the decree was passed. Thus in the facts of the case it is found that the plaintiff No. 2 obtained title by purchase during the pendency of the suit.

14. The learned Advocate for the appellant also argued that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of his own case and cited the case reported in AIR: 1946 Privy Council 59. This is admitted by all concerned that the plaintiff is to prove his case and due to the defect of the defendant's case he is not to get a decree. In that reported decision it has only been said that in a suit for ejectment, the plaintiff will succeed on the strength of his own case.

15. Thus on a careful consideration of the entire materials on record, we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly found that the defendant is a habitual defaulter, as from the materials on record we find that since May, 1977 till today he did not pay any rent nor deposited the same to the Officer of the House Rent Controller.

16. Mr. Gafur also submitted that the trial court ought to have considered the case of fraud. We have already held earlier that the defendant totally failed to make out any case of fraud or misrepresentation. The trial Court has correctly referred to that in his judgment. Fraud or misrepresentation is a matter which is to be specifically pleaded and proved. In the facts of the present case there is only a statement in the written statement that the deed of agreement if produced will be found to be forged and fraudulent created by coercion and misrepresentation of fact. We have already referred above that we do not find any evidence of fraud in the case. In such circumstances, the decree as passed is on proper consideration on the materials on record and there is no error of fact and law in the impugned and decree. Consequently, there is nothing to interfere with the same.

17. Thus we do not find any substance in the points raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant.

In the result, this appeal is dismissed with cost.

End.
