full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J:- This appeal arises from Civil Revision No.506 of 1973 decided by the High Court Division, Dhaka Bench on October 13. 1982. 

2. An application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed by respondent Nos. 1-3 for pre-emption of .76 acres of land in three plots which were transferred by a registered kabala on 12th May, 1970, claiming that they were tenants holding land contiguous to the plots transferred under the aforesaid deed. Appellants challenged the locus standi of the pre-emptor-respondents. They claimed to be owners of contiguous lands. On 27th July, 1970 appellants filed an application to share rateably with the respondents if the latter were found entitled to pre-empt. The trial court allowed the application for pre-emption and rejected the appellants' application for rateable pre-emption as being barred by limitation. The decision was affirmed by the first appellate court. Appellants moved the High Court Division and during the hearing of the Civil Revision Case No.506 of 1973, submissions were made on the construction of sub-sections (4) and (5) of 96 of the Act which are as follows: 

"(4). When an application has been made under sub-section (1), any of the remaining co-sharer tenants including the transferee, if one of them, and the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred may, within the period referred to in sub-section (1) or within two months of the date of the service of the notice of the application under clause (b) of sub-section (3), whichever be earlier, apply to join in the said application; any co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred, who has not applied either under sub-section (1) or under this sub-section, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section. 

(5)(a) If (i) a co-sharer whose interest has accrued by inheritance and (ii) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by purchase and (iii) a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred apply under this section and comply with the provisions herein contained, the applicant or applicants shall have the prior right, to purchase under this section in the order in which they have been mentioned above. 

(b) If more than one tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred apply under this section, the Court shall determine the Order of priority as among such tenants having regard to—

(i) the total quantity of land in possession of each of the tenants applying; 

(ii) whether the contiguous land of the tenant is homestead land or any other class of land; 

(iii) extent of contiguity; 

(iv) to what extent it is necessary for the applicant to have possession of the contiguous land; and 

(v) the right to easement, if any, of the applicants," 

3. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Counsel for the appellants, who appeared before the learned Judge of the High Court Division made similar submissions before us. His submissions are that the words "any of the remaining co-sharer tenants including the transferee, if one of them" being separate from the words "and the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred", the words "including the transferee, if one of them" not governing the latter words, namely, "tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred", the provisions regarding the application for pre-emption in sub-section (4) are not applicable to transferees who are tenants of contiguous lands. For a clear representation of the effect of his submissions, he submitted that if sub-section (4) was redrafted as follows, without excluding anything from the sub-section as it stands, it would convey the interpretation he was asking for us to accept. Sub-section (4) as redrafted by him for giving the interpretation as being suggested by him is as follows: 

"When an application has been made under sub-section (1), any of  the remaining co-sharer tenants and the tenants holding contiguous to the land transferred including  the transferee, if one of them, may within the period referred to in sub-section (1) or within two months of the date of the service of the notice of the application under clause (b) of sub-section (3), which-ever is earlier, apply to join in the said application; any co-sharer tenant or tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, who has not applied either under sub-section (1) or under this sub-section, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section."

4. For the purpose of understanding what he was trying to convey, he underlined the sentences concerned in sub-section (4) as rearranged by him. 

5. Drafting an enactment is an art requiring great skill and clear conception of the subject-matter of the enactment. After a draft of an enactment is presented before the legislature, great attention is paid to the text during the consideration of the bill. The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act dealing with the most intricate tenancy laws of the country is a carefully drawn legislation. In sub-section (4) of section 96, the same degree of care and attention appears to have been given. In section 96(4) of the Act, there is neither any ambiguity nor any omission in it which requires the adoption of a separate form as suggested by the learned Counsel to cover up any omission or to make its meaning clearer and more expressive. Sub-section (4) as it stands, provides for a period of limitation, that is, two months for joining in an application for pre-emption by a co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred. According to the learned Counsel, since the words "including the transferee if one of them" do not occur for the second time after the words "tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred" such transferees meaning those falling in the category of contiguous land owners are not bound by the period of limitation mentioned in sub-section (4). He submits that the suggested improvements in sub-section (4) which appear from the draft suggested by him may, if conceded, show up clearly what he wants to say. But, in my opinion, the sub-section in its present form, convey the same meaning as his draft is intended to express. In considering the provisions of an enactment the intention of the legislature is to be gathered from the words used in the enactment. If sub-section (4), by employing expressly such expressions as "including the transferee, if one of them" wants to restrict such transferee within the two months period for joining in an application for pre-emption, can it be said that the legislature intended differently in case of a transferee who falls in the category of contiguous land owners. Such transferee cannot expect to claim more privilege than a transferee who is a co-sharer, either by inheritance or purchase, with regard to limitation for an application for pre-emption as mentioned in the sub-section and on that ground seek total exemption from the period of limitation which cannot be said to have been intended by the legislature. Such a transferee must, therefore, come within the period of limitation applicable to a transferee co-sharer tenant. The lack, if any, of a better and more expressly, drafted text of sub-section (4) does not entitle a transferee contiguous owner to seek exemption from the restriction imposed in the matter of joining in an application for pre-emption as mentioned in the sub-section. Moreover, when the contiguous land owner is bound by the period of limitation prescribed by sub-section (4), a transferee from this category cannot be left free to seek pre-emption whenever he likes. 

6. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed also tried to convince us that when a contiguous owner is the transferee he is not bound by the period of limitation provided in sub-section (4), as this becomes evident from reasons app-earing from a reading of sub-section (5) of section 96. This sub-section provides for priority of different categories of persons entitled to apply for pre-emption: (a) when a co-sharer by inheritance applies for pre-emption no one other than another such co-sharer can apply to join, (b) when a co-sharer by purchase applies for pre-emption only another co-sharer from the category can apply to join, and (c) when a contiguous tenant applies any co-sharer may apply to join. 

7. According to him, the provisions for priority among the different categories of per-sons as mentioned in sub-section (5) does not bring in a transferee contiguous owner within the ambit of sub-section (4) of section 96. His argument in support of this contention appears something like this : Sub-section (4) is to be construed in the light of the provisions for priority in sub-section (5), and the words "any of the remaining co-sharer tenants including the transferee, if one of them" will mean that if the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance, the transferee may apply to join if only he is a co-sharer by inheritance but not otherwise; similarly, if the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by purchase, the transferee may apply to join if only he is a co-sharer by purchase. A co-sharer of either category may, of course, apply to join in a case of pre-emption by a contiguous tenant when the transferee is either a stranger or another contiguous tenant; if no co-sharer applies to join in such a case priority amongst contiguous tenants will be decided according to provisions of clause (b) of sub-section (5). 

8. Ile, therefore, contended that when the transferee is a contiguous owner and another contiguous tenant has applied for pre-emption, the transferee did not apply to join as a contiguous tenant, he being the owner by the transfer in question. He, therefore, considered that the application to join by a transferee contiguous tenant was a mere superfluity and the provisions regarding limitation as laid down in sub-section (4) does not apply to the appellants who are transferee contiguous owners, though such limitation would apply to other contiguous tenants who are not transferees. The arguments and reasonings of the learned Counsel seem to be ingenious but farfetched. When the intention of the legislature appears to be clear from the reading of sub-section (4) itself, there is no need to travel farther and on some supposed analogy with the principle of priority laid down in sub-section (5) distort the legislative intention as app-ears in sub-section (4). 

9. For the reasons stated above, the contentions of the appellants' Counsel are unacceptable. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.

Iftekhar Ali (Md)  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Sri Sailendra Nath Roy and another ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 2-7-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Rajshahi in SCC Suit No.1 of 2002 should not be set aside.

2. The opposite parties as plaintiff instituted SCC Suit No.2 of 1996 before the Court of learned SCC Court which was transferred to the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court and numbered as SCC Suit No.9 of 2001 and lastly it was transferred to the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Rajshahi by an order of the learned District Judge, Rajshahi and renumbered as SCC Suit No.1 of 2002.

3. The opposite parties filed the suit for eviction of the defendant from the suit premises and for recovery of possession on the ground that the defendant tenant is a defaulter and that the suit premises, an old building of 150 years which may collapse at any time and they want to demolish the said building immediately for which the plaintiff served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the defendant on 19-10-1995 through Mr Md Akteruzzaman and terminated the relationship of landlord and tenant on 1-12-1995 but the defendant did not vacate the suit premises, hence the suit for eviction.

4. The defendant-tenant appeared and contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint stating that the suit is not maintainable in its present form, barred by limitation, estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and further stated that the original owner of the suit premises was late Mohanlal Roy and created a will regarding the suit premises along with other properties to Sri Laksmi Narayan Deb Bigroha Thakur. Mosammat Dilara Begum, the mother of the defendant, took lease of the suit premises in the year 1965 at a rental of Taka 50 per month and running a sanitary business. Subsequently, the defendant-tenant entered into a tenancy agreement with the plaintiff's on 21-5-1977 and the monthly rent of the suit premises were fixed at Taka 60 per month. It was stipulated in the said agreement that the rent of each month is to be paid within the 1st week of the next month. Subsequently, the rent of the suit premises was enhanced to Taka 105 per month. The tenant was running the suit shop in the name and style "Messrs Mufti Enterprise" and the defendant had earned goodwill and reputation in the market. The defendant received a legal notice from Santosh Kumar (now deceased), Satya Priya and Kedar Nath claiming themselves as shebait of the diety and, as such, the defendant was in doubt of the actual shebait of the bigraha. Consequently, defendant started depositing the rent before the House Rent Controller from the month of February 1993 in House Rent Case No.36 of 1993. The defendant is not a defaulter but the said House Rent Control Case No.36 of 1993 was dismissed in 1998. Therefore, the defendant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.27 of 1998 before the learned District Judge, Rajshahi. The said miscellaneous appeal was dismissed on contest on 23-6-1999 and the appellate Court directed the defendant-tenant to pay the entire rent of the suit premises to the plaintiffs. The defendant offered entire rent of the suit premises to the plaintiff's but they refused to accept the rent. Consequently, the defendant-tenant again deposited the entire rent to the Rent Controller. Though the defendant had earlier deposited the monthly rent of the suit premises regularly in House Rent Control case No.36 of 1993 as such, the defendant-tenant is not a defaulter. It was denied that the demised premises is a very old building and that the plaintiffs were directed to demolish the suit premises, are not correct and that taking the plea they will sell out the entire suit premises and leave the country for India.

5. The said SCC Suit No.1 of 2002 came up for hearing before the Court of learned SCC Judge, Rajshahi and the plaintiff examined 2 witnesses and the defendant-tenant examined himself as DW 1.

6. After hearing the learned Advocates of the parties and considering the materials on record the trial Court decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 2-7-2002.

7. Against the said judgment and decree dated 2-7-2002 the defendant-tenant preferred this revisional application under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act and obtained the Rule and an order of stay.

8. Mr MA Samad with Mr MGH Ruhullah, learned Advocates appeared for the petitioner and Mr.A Baset Majumder, learned Advocate with Miss Farida Yeasmin appeared for the plaintiff-opposite parties.

9. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the tenant-defendant is not a defaulter and, as such, the finding arrived at by the trial Court is an erroneous finding based on no evidence. He further submits that under section 18(s) if any person claims bonafide requirement he is to prove the same by adducing proper evidence. He further submits that the claimant of the suit premises are not the real shebait of the suit premises and after the death of original shebait the attorney holders cannot act on behalf of the original shebait. He lastly submitted that since the tenant is an owner of a commercial enterprise, the plaintiffs may be directed to allot him a shop if the same are constructed.

10. Miss Farida Yeasmin, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, stated that the defendant-tenant was depositing rent before the Rent Controller in the name of the plaintiff's and, as such, he has accepted the plaintiff as the landlord of the suit premises and, as such, the plea taken by the tenant-petitioner has no leg to stand. She further submits that as it appears from the record even though the tenant is not a defaulter, there are good grounds of bonafide requirement of the suit premises to demolish the building of the premises. She further submits that the prayer as has been made before this Court for a shop for the tenant for his commercial enterprise has never been prayed for before the trial Court and she further submits that there was no prayer by the tenant under rule 4 of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. She further submits that from the record it appears that the suit premises is an old building of 150 years and the condition of the building is very dilapidated and alarming and at any moment it may collapse and then may cause injury to the public at large. The local newspapers are publishing series of news and in mental agony regarding the condition of the building of the suit premises. Rajshahi Development Authority, City Corporation also directed the plaintiff's to demolish the suit premises immediately or to deposit the cost of demolition to the City Corporation. Accordingly, the plaintiff's deposited the cost of demolition to the Rajshahi City Corporation but due to the suit Rajshahi City Corporation cannot demolish the said building. She further submits that for the sake of security tenant-defendant should leave the suit premises.

11. I have checked up all the documents on record, it appears that the tenant defendant was a tenant according to the agreement dated 21-5-1977 and he paid rent regularly and after refusal he has deposited the rent to the Rent Controller regularly. According to the direction of the Court made in Rent Control Case No. 36 of 1993 and according to the direction of Miscellaneous Appeal No.27 of 1998, he has deposited the rent to the Rent Controller within the specified time. It appears that the tenant is not a defaulter according to the law and, as such, the finding made by the trial Court that the tenant-defendant is a defaulter is an erroneous finding and not sustainable in law. It appears that the tenant-defendant is depositing the rent in the name of the plaintiff's and, as such, the plea taken by the defendant-tenant that they are not the landlord of the suit premises has no leg to stand.

<u>12. It appears that the suit premises situated under a very old building of 150 years which is at a dilapidated condition and it may collapse at any time which may cause injury to the public at large. The local newspapers and the public are in mental agony regarding the condition of the building. Rajshahi Development Authority, Rajshahi City Corporation on several occasions requested the plaintiff to demolish the said building and lastly, Rajshahi City Corporation directed the plaintiff's to deposit the cost of demolishing of the building. Accordingly, the plaintiff's deposited the cost and accordingly, Rajshahi City Corporation vide memo No.2634(12) dated 12-12-1999 fixed the date for demolish of the building on 14-12-1999 at 9-30 AM. But due to the proceeding before the Court of law, no action for demolition could be taken. It further appears from the record that the plaintiff has obtained an approved plan for construction of market and commercial building on 3-12-1992 but due to the suit they could not demolish the suit premises. The tenant-petitioner ultimately prayed for a direction upon the plaintiff's to give him accommodation of a shop. Regarding the matter the learned Advocate for the petitioner as well as the opposite-parties agreed that they will settle the matter out of Court between themselves. In that view of the matter, I do not feel to pass any order in this respect.</u>

<u>13. It appears that the contention of the plaintiff-opposite parties that the suit premises are bonafide required by the plaintiffs are well proved by adducing convincing evidences on record. I do not find any substance in the Rule.</u>

In that view of the matter, the Rule is discharged without any order as to the costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, CJ: This appeal by leave at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant is against the judgment and decree passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 742 of 1989 on 21.4.93, setting aside the judgment and decree of the Additional District Judge, Gazipur passed in Title Appeal No. 13 of 1986 on 31.7.89 which in turn affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Kapasia in Title Suit No. 6 of 1985 on 19.2.86, decreeing the suit for redemption of mortgage.

2. The plaint case is that the plaintiff by a registered deed of mortgage dated 26.3.62 transferred the suit land to one Abdul Gafur-Mridha, predecessor-in-interest of the defendants for a consideration of Tk. 1500/- with a stipulation that the mortgagor or his successors would reconvey the property within ten years from the date of mortgage. The plaintiff received Tk. 1100/- in cash and remaining Tk. 400/- was lying with Abdul Gafur Mridha for clearing dues of the Agricultural Development Bank. After the death of Abdul Gafur Mridha the plaintiff requested the defendants to deliver possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff together with mortgage deed as the money paid to the plaintiff and interest accrued thereon has already been redeemed. The defendants did not deliver possession of the schedule property. The plaintiff filed L.M.O. case No. 76 of 1973 before the Sub-Divisional Officer (North), Dhaka for restoration of the possession of the mortgaged property. The said miscellaneous case was transferred to the Circle Officer (Development), Kapasia for disposal. The said case having not been disposed of, the plaintiff filed the suit for redemption of mortgage.

3. The case of the defendants is that the plaintiff transferred the land for a consideration of Tk. 1500/- by a registered sale deed on 26-3-62 to Abdul Gafur Mridha who was enjoying the property. According to the defendants the plaintiff in collusion with the scribe inserted the term of reconveyance at the time of presentation of the deed for registration beyond knowledge of the said Abdur Gafur Mridha. According to the defendants, the deed in question was out and out a deed of sale and hence the suit for redemption of mortgage is not maintainable.

4. The trial court on consideration of the oral and documentary evidences on record held that the registered deed in question is a complete usufructuary mortgage with a stipulation to return the land in question within 10 years as incorporated in the deed. The trial court also held that the suit for redemption of mortgage was maintainable and the suit was not barred by limitation. The lower appellate court as the last court of fact disbelieved the defendant's case that the plaintiff collusively inserted the stipulation of reconvey the suit land to the plaintiff at the time of registration of the deed. The lower appellate court also concurred with the finding of the trail court that the deed in question is not an out and out sale deed but a deed of mortgage.

5. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in revision set aside the concurrent findings of fact and held, inter alia, that the registered deed in question is a sale deed and not a mortgage deed; that the stipulation to reconvey the land was fraudulently inserted in the deed; and that the suit for redemtion of mortgage was not maintainable as in view of P.O. No. 88 of 1972 the transaction between the parties became a past and closed transaction.

6. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate, for the plaintiff-appellant:-

(1) Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the suit for redemption of mortgage is maintainable or not and further whether reference of P.O. No. 88 of 1972 and the past and closed nature of the transaction are relevant for the purpose of the suit.

(2) Whether the plaintiffs suit for redemption of mortgage having been filed within 60 years from the date of accrual of cause of action the learned Single Judge correctly held that the suit is barred by limitation.

(3) Whether the learned Single Judge acted wrongly in reversing the concurrent findings of fact of the courts below to the effect that the deed in question is a mortgage deed and wrongly held that the deed is an out and out sale deed.

(4) Whether the learned Single Judge misconceived the relevant law governing the suit for redemption of mortgage and erroneously reversed the judgment of affirmance of the lower appellate court.

7. Both the trial court and the lower appellate Court on consideration of the recitals of the document construed that the deed dated 26-3-62 is a deed of mortgage and not a deed of sale out and out as asserted by the defendant. As a matter of fact, the lower appellate court being the last court of fact concurred with the finding of the trial court and found from clear recitals of the document that the columned is a deed of mortgage. The revisional court most illegally and wrongly set aside this concurrent finding of fact that the registered deed is a mortgage and wrongly held that the same is a sale deed and held that the stipulation to reconvey the land was fraudulently inserted in the deed. As a matter of fact, there is no evidence whatsoever to hold such a view and there was no argument in the courts below as well that the stipulation to reconvey the land was fraudulently inserted to convert a deed of sale into a deed of mortgage. As a matter of fact, it was a total misconstruction of the document as the recitals are as follows:-

“প্রকাশ থাকে যে বর্তমান সন হইতে আগামী দশ বতসরের মেয়াদের অঙ্গীকারে আপনার নিকট নিম্ন তপছিল বর্ণিত জমি বিক্রয় করিয়া এতদ্বার্থে স্বেচ্ছায় স্বজ্ঞানে অত্র সাফ কবলা দলিল লিখাইয়া সম্পাদন করিয়া দিলাম।”

In another portion of the document the recital is as follows:-

“ফেরত দেওয়ার অঙ্গীকারে বিক্রয় করিলাম দশ বৎসর ম্যাদ মধ্যে ফেরৎ দলিল করিয়া দিবেন।”

8. Thus there are clear recitals in the document. The document is a document of mortgage which has been rightly found by the court of fact. Apart from these recitals in document itself, P.W.1 Asmat Ali testified both in his examination-in-chief and cross-examine on that the impugned document is a deed of mortgage and he kept the land in mortgage with Abdul Gafur Mridha with a condition to reconvey the same within 10 years. The lower appellate court also found that the oral evidence of P.W.2 corroborates P.W.1 which is in conformity with the recitals of the document itself. It is also on record that D.W.1 accompanied his father Abdul Gafur Mridha went to the Sub-Registrar's Office and he admitted that the document was read over to them and he knew that this was a mortgage deed. Thus, the lower appellate court as a court of fact believed the plaintiffs witnesses and held the document to be a mortgage deed. It is very surprising that on the face of such evidence on record both oral and documentary the learned single Judge of the High Court Division held that the document is an out and out sale deed. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division wrongly took note of sections 54 and 55 of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 54 of the T. P. Act defines sale and section 55 speaks of rights and liabilities of buyer and seller. It is very difficult to understand why reference of Section 54 and 55 of the T.P. Act was pointed out by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division. Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act contemplates mortgage by conditional sale wherein it has been clearly laid down that where the mortgagor ostensibly sells the mortgaged property on condition that on such payment being made the buyer shall transfer the property to the seller, the transaction is a mortgage by conditional sale. The law permits for such a document. It is very surprising that the learned Single Judge without any reference to any evidence whatsoever set aside the concurrent findings of fact of both the courts below and held as follows:

"The terms of reconveyance does not appear to be genuine as such cannot be deemed to have formed part of the instrument. The facts, circumstances and evidence together with the deed of kabala having not carefully considered by the courts below, the decision arrived at by the courts below does not appear to be correct decision."

Thus, the concurrent findings were wrongly set aside in revision and the learned Single Judge exceeded his jurisdiction not vested in law.

8. The plaintiff filed a suit for redemption of mortgage and both the courts below found that a suit for redemption of mortgage is maintainable and the same having been filed within 60 years from the accrual of the cause of action the suit was not barred by limitation. The learned Single Judge wrongly held that the suit for redemption is barred by limitation. A reference to Article 148 of the Limitation Act clearly shows that the limitation of filing such a suit is 60 years and as such the learned Single Judge wrongly held that the suit was barred by limitation.

9. It is on record that this document was executed and registered on 26-3-62 and ten years expired on 25-3-72. President's Order No. 88 of 1972 came into operation on 3-8-72. Thus, it appears that prior to the promulgation of P.O. 88 of 1972 the period of mortgage expired on 25-3-72. The learned Single Judge wrongly held that the mortgage money was to be paid on or before 25.3.72 and held that the condition ceased to be operative after promulgation of P.O. 88 of 1972 and P.O. 136 of 1972 and amendment of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Single Judge failed to consider that the filing of a suit for redemption of mortgage in a civil court is wholly different from filing of an application under P.O. 88 of 1972 before the revenue authority. We fail to understand how the learned Single Judge could hold like this in an independent civil suit for redemption of mortgage and opine that the suit is not maintainable. These are two independent proceedings. The reference of P.O. 88 of 1972 is wholly irrelevant for the purpose of the suit and the learned Single Judge totally misconceived the law governing the suit for redemption of mortgage and most illegally reversed the judgment of affirmance of the lower appellate court.

10. Before parting with the case it may be mentioned that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division took note of the case of Bangladesh Vs. Haji Abdul Gani Biswas and others, 32 DLR(AD) 233. The reference of that case in the context of the present case is wholly irrelevant. The historical background of the legislations mentioned in P.O. 88 of 1972 in respect of subsisting usufructuary mortgage is hit by section 95A of the State Acquisitions and Tenancy Act which is meant to protect the helpless raiyat. A raiyat in Bangladesh cannot enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than which is capable of enjoyment for a maximum period of 7 years and the raiyat will get back his property under Section 95 of EBSAT Act. I am afraid that the reference of this case shows total non-application of judicial mind of the learned Single Judge.

<u>11. P.O. No. 88 of 1972, P.O. No. 136 of 1972. and P.O. No. 24 of 1973 amending the provision of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951 and inserting the provision of section 95A therein came up for consideration in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Haji Abdul Gani Biswas and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. In that case it was held, amongst others, "as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed." That conclusion was arrived at in view of the contention that an application for restoration of possession of the mortgaged land in respect of a transaction past and closed was not maintainable. P.O. No. 88 of 1972 created special forum for restoration of mortgaged property. But it did not take away right of redemption available to a mortgagor by filing a mortgage suit under Order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter High Court Division was totally wrong to held that the suit was not maintainable as the transaction was past and closed.</u>

12. For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. Consequently, the appeal is allowed with costs and the suit is decreed.

Bimalendu Bikash Roy Choudhury, J: I agree with the judgment of My Lord, the Chief Justice.

A M Mahmudur Rahman, J: I agree with the judgment of My Lord, the Chief Justice.

Mahmudul Amin Choudhury, J: I have the privilege of going through the judgment to be delivered by My Lord the Chief Justice but I failed to persuade myself in agreeing with the decision.

16. As the facts involved in this appeal as well as leave granting order has already been incorporated in the judgment of My Lord the Chief Justice. I refrain myself from repeating it further but I shall deal only with the facts involved for my decision including the evidence on record and the legal position.

17. In this suit the plaintiff prayed for a decree declaring that principal "mortgage deed together with interest thereon has been fully redeemed on the enjoyment of the usufruct of the mortgaged property" and also for other relief in the form of recovery of khas possession. Now the main question is whether the kabala dated 26.3.1962 executed by the plaintiff in favour of the predecessor of the defendant is a mortgage or not. If it can be found that the document in question is an usufructuary mortgage, the plaintiff has a relief as prayed for but not otherwise. admittedly the document dated 26.3.1962 is a sale deed and there is a stipulation at the bottom side of the kabala in the following terms:-

“প্রকাশ থাকে যে বর্তমান সন হইতে আগামী দশ বতসরের মেয়াদের অঙ্গীকারে আপনার নিকট নিম্ন তপছিল বর্ণিত জমি বিক্রয় করিয়া এতদ্বার্থে স্বেচ্ছায় স্বজ্ঞানে অত্র সাফ কবলা দলিল লিখাইয়া সম্পাদন করিয়া দিলাম।”

and it has also mentioned as follows:-

“ফেরত দেওয়ার অঙ্গীকারে বিক্রয় করিলাম দশ বৎসর ম্যাদ মধ্যে ফেরৎ দলিল করিয়া দিবেন।”

From these recital the trial court as well as the appellate court found that the document dated 26.3.1962 is an usufructuary mortgage to which the High Court Division did agree. In the plaint itself it has been averred that the plaintiff executed the sale deed in favour of the recipient of the kabala embodying condition specifying the transaction as mortgage but it is the definite case of the defence that the document in question is out and out a sale deed and the aforesaid portion has been subsequently inserted behind the back of the recipient of the kabala at the instance of the plaintiff influencing the scribe. Before the trial court both the parties adduced oral and documentary evidence. The questioned kabala has been marked Exhibit I which was produced by the defence and it appears from this kabala that there is such an endorsement at the bottom side of the kabala.

18. The question is whether a particular document is a mortgage or a sale deed has to be determined on condition that on such payment the buyer shall transfer the property to the seller and the period of repayment i.e. a short period being indicative of a sale and a long period of a mortgage and also inadequacy of price and that there is a stipulation indicating a mortgage. Here in the present case the plaintiff's contends that the sale price in the questioned document is too low which is indicative of the fact of mortgage and that there is also a stipulation. This stipulation ac-cording to the defence, has been made behind their back and when they came to know of this they confronted the seller who admitted that this has been subsequently inserted. But he has not done anything to correct the mistake saying that the property has already been sold to the defendant and as such he need not worry and relying on this assurance the defence has not taken recourse to any legal proceedings for correcting the mistake. It is the definite case of the Plaintiff that on such stipulation the kabala was executed by him. The trial court as well as the appellate court lost sight of the fact that the plaintiff has changed this position while deposing as P.W.1. Before the trial court on oath the plaintiff deposed as follows:

"Not a fact that the defendant did not execute any other deed of agreement of re-conveyance. The defendant executed a separate agreement of reconveyance. The paper is submitted, Wasir Mukter wrote a separate deed of agreement".

In his evidence P.W.1 further stated as follows:

"Not a fact that there was no agreement of reconveyance"

These sentences escaped the notice of the trial court as well as of the appellate court. These statements of the plaintiff on oath clearly indicate that there was a separate deed of reconveyance which was written by scribe Wasir Mukter and such a deed of reconveyance must be with the plaintiff who deposed that this has been submitted. So the plaintiff has given a go bye to his plaint case and on dock he came up with a case of separate deed of reconveyance. It is the definite case of the defence that the portion which has been quoted above in the kabala was subsequently inserted and this admission of the plaintiff in his examination-in-chief clearly lent support to the defence version of the case. The plaintiff has not taken into evidence the deed of reconveyance which was allegedly executed by the predecessor of the defendant. Had this been proved and taken into evidence then the situation could have been in favour of the plaintiff but that has not been done for reason best known to the plaintiff. He has not filed that document and no explanation has been given for not filing such an important document. The plaintiff in Court it appears was not banking on the aforesaid recital in the kabala genuineness of which has been challenged by the defence.

<u>19. It is well settled that the plaintiff is to prove his own case. He cannot get a decree banking upon the defects in the defence version of the case. When the plaintiff has categorically deposed of a separate deed of reconveyance non-production of which cast a doubt in the plaintiffs case. He is now trying to bank upon certain recitals in the questioned kabala. In the document itself there are recital in may parts that the document is a safkabala and it has also been stated as follows:-</u>

<u>ইহাতে আমার কি আমার স্থলবর্তী ওয়ারিশগণের সর্ব্ব দাবী দাওয়া ত্যাগ ও রহিত হইল। যদি ভবিষ্যতে কেহ কোন প্রকার দাবী দাওয়া করে কিম্বা তবে তাহা সর্ব্বাদালতে বাতেল বলিয়া গণ্য হইবেক।</u>

<u>So this indicate that this is a document of sale and the stipulation as regards return of the land has not been admitted by the defence. In such a situation onus lies heavily on the plaintiff to prove that the transaction is a mortgage. It is well settled that if the document is of a lesser price then the price prevalent at the date of execution then the document may be construed as a deed of mortgage. Admittedly the price mentioned in the kabala is Tk.1,500/-. To prove that this amount is a lesser a nount the plaintiff has not produced any other sale deed of the relevant period nor adduced any oral evidence. From the side of the defence several documents have been produced to prove that the price indicated in the questioned document is the proper price and not a lesser price. The trial court as well as the appellate court has not it appears considered these documents of the defence which was very much necessary for holding that the questioned document is a deed of mortgage. When the allegation is that the recital as regards mortgage has been subsequently inserted the trial court as well as the appellate court ought to have considered this aspect of the matter. The evidence both oral and documentary have been led from the side of the defence but nothing has been considered and simply on consideration of the recital made in the kabala Ext. I itself, the genuineness of which as regards the endorsements have been seriously challenged, the trial court as well the appellate court ought not to have decreed the suit relying only on the endorsement. The plaintiff himself admitted the existence of a separate deed of reconveyance which has not been produced before any of the courts below which escaped the notice of the trial court as well as of the appellate court and there is also no consideration of the circumstance as regards the prevalent price of such lands at the relevant time which would have indicated the nature of the questioned document. The trial court as well as the appellate court has therefore wrongly decreed the suit.</u>

20. Before the trial court from the side of the plaintiff 2 witnesses have been examined. P.W. 1 is the plaintiff himself and P.W. 2 is one Chand Mia who is an attesting witness of the questioned document. The scribe has not been examined and no explanation has been given from the side of the plaintiff for his non-examination. The scribe ought to have been examined to prove that when the document was written and executed the last portion indicating the mortgage was there in the kabala and that has not been subsequently inserted as alleged by the defence. This non-examination of the scribe led to an adverse presumption against the plaintiff to the fact that had been examined he would not have supported the plaintiffs version of the case of mortgage.

20. From the perusal of the materials available it appear that the plaintiff has not taken any step for proving the tests that Ext. 1 is a deed of mortgage. Even P.W.2 has, in his evidence, not stated that the price as mentioned in the kabala was a lesser price and that has been fixed for making the kabala a deed of mortgage. Nothing has been stated by this P.W.2 in this respect. Rather he stated categorically that "consideration was fixed at Tk. 1,500/-" So there was absolutely no evidence either oral or documentary to prove that the price as mentioned in the document is a lesser price.

21. It appears from the evidence of D.W. I that he categorically stated that the record of right has been corrected in the name of his predecessor and in support of that Exhibit-D series have been produced. In his examination-in-chief D.W.1 categorically stated that when the insertion of promise of redemption was found out the recipient of the kabala brought the matter to the notice of the plaintiff who admitted that the same was done through mistake and begged apology. This D.W.1 was confronted on this during cross-examination. There also he answered the question as follows:-

“নাঃ জমি সম্পর্কে যে শর্ত লেখা হয়েছিল সাব কবলা দলিলে সে জন্য আমার বাবা বাদীকে জিজ্ঞেসা করে কেন তোমরা সাব কবলা দলিলে লিখেছ এই সব কথা (বন্দকী) তখন বাদী মাফ চাইলে বাবা মাফ করে দেন। এরপর আমরা দলিল সংশোধনের কোন চেষ্টা করিনি।”

This statement D.W. 1 in his examination-in-chief and also in cross-examination indicate that the recital in the kabala as regards mort-gage is a subsequent insertion and nothing has been produced and no evidence led to discard the evidence of D.W.1 and the defence case. When there is contest over the insertion of certain recitals in the questioned document and when defendant No.1 was specific in his evidence the plaintiff ought to have produced more materials in support of his case. The test as aforesaid to find out the real intent could not be proved by the plaintiff. In view of the clear defence evidence and inadequate and contradictory evidence led from the side of the plaintiff it cannot be found that the questioned transaction is an usufructuary mortgage.

22. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the High Court Division committed wrong and illegality in interfering with the concurrent finding of fact arrived at by the final court of fact but when the appellate court committed wrong and illegality in the finding of fact which was based on non-consideration and misreading of material evidence on record the High Court Division may interfere and the same has been done in the present case. There was total non-consideration and misreading of the aforesaid aspect of the evidence both by the trial court as well as by the appellate court. Here the question is of non-consideration and misreading of material evidence. It is surprising that on the face of such type of evidence and circumstances how the trial court as well the appellate court can pass such a decree. Here in the present case the evidence led from the side of the parties and non-examination of the scribe and the facts and circumstances mentioned above prove that the transaction is not a mortgage but a sale out and out. The factual aspect of the case and the evidence adduced are all in favour of the defence. There was no proper appreciation of the case in the light of the evidence adduced by the trial court as well as by the appellate court. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has not therefore exceeded his jurisdiction in interfering with the matter and come to his finding on appreciation of the evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case. It is well settled that the High Court Division may interfere in a case where there is total non-consideration or misreading of the evidence on record and the finding arrived is contrary to evidence. Here I find that the finding arrived at by the trail court as well as by the appellate court was based on total non-consideration and misreading of the evidence on record and as such perverse. The trial Court as well as the appellate court shirked their responsibilities in properly and legally evaluating the evidence and facts and circumstances of the case while disposing the matter in question.

23. Having given my best consideration to the materials on record both oral and documentary and the legal position I hold that the trial court as well the appellate court committed goes illegality in decreeing the suit and the High Court Division rightly set aside the same and there is nothing to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division.

The appeal is a accordingly dismissed without costs. Order of the Court By a majority decision the appeal is allowed with cost.

End.
